# WiseOwl COBOL — Conformance & Processor-Dependent Element Disposition

> **STATUS: LIVE conformance record (ISO/IEC 1989:2023 §4.2.16).** This document is the implementor's user
> documentation required by §4.2.6 (processor-dependent elements), §4.2.7 (optional elements), and §4.2.13
> (obsolete elements): it states, for every processor-dependent language element in Annex A.3 and every optional
> facility this compiler does **not** implement, whether support is claimed. Every syntactically-detectable
> unsupported element is NAMED at compile time, on the channel its licence chooses: an Annex A.3
> **processor-dependent** facility is accepted with a named WARNING (**COBOL1578 / 1778**, §4.2.6
> third paragraph, which MANDATES that warning), and an Annex A.4 **optional module for which no support is
> claimed** is REFUSED with a named ERROR (the **COBOL1560 / 1705 / 1706 / 1707** band, §4.2.7 and Annex
> A.4.1). **COBOL1580 (VALIDATE) is the one element that is A.4 and yet warns**, and it is a CHOICE rather
> than a mandate — see §4 (kb/Work PB709). This document is the
> authoritative catalogue behind both. Default `--std` = COBOL-2023.

## 1. Conformance summary (§4.2.16)

WiseOwl COBOL is a **standard-conforming** COBOL implementation targeting ISO/IEC 1989:2023, with correct support for
the 1985, 2002, and 2014 editions selected by `--std`. It implements the required nucleus and the standard modules
except the optional/processor-dependent facilities listed as **not supported** below; the per-module
optional-element dispositions are §5 (only Claimed/Partial rows there are claimed). Per §4.2.6, an
implementation need not implement processor-dependent elements for which support is not claimed; per §4.2.7, an
optional element is implemented only when support is claimed. All four **documented non-support facilities**
(§4) are now recognized at compile time with a NAMED diagnostic. Two of them are ACCEPT-INERT WARNINGS:
MCS SEND/RECEIVE → **COBOL1578**, which satisfies §4.2.6 ¶3's MANDATORY warning mechanism for its Annex A.3
element, and VALIDATE → **COBOL1580**, which does NOT —
VALIDATE is Annex A.4.14 and appears nowhere in Annex A.3, so §4.2.7 obliges only that its non-support be
identified in this document, and warning rather than refusing is our documented choice (kb/Work PB709). The
program compiles, runs, the facility is inert, and no
associated exception condition is raised (§14.6.13.1.1 licenses this). **SCREEN handling is a REFUSAL** —
**COBOL1560** (the data / environment surface) and **COBOL1707** (the procedure surface), both Errors,
at every edition where the words are reserved — because Annex A.4.1 admits an optional element's syntax
"only when support for that language element is claimed", which is a prohibition on ACCEPTING and not a
licence to accept-and-flag. The A.4.8 (FORMAT / SELECT WHEN, **COBOL1705**) and A.4.13 (WRITE / REWRITE
FILE, **COBOL1706**) declines are refusals for the same reason. Commit and rollback (A.4.3, **Claimed**) is
**provided for every organization §9.1.18.2 admits** — RELATIVE and INDEXED files in the keyed store engine, SEQUENTIAL
and LINE SEQUENTIAL files (the print stream included) in a transaction journal — complete for the sequential
and keyed organizations alike: an OPEN OUTPUT that replaces a RELATIVE or INDEXED file, a DELETE FILE that removes one and an OPEN that creates one are journaled in the same transaction journal (the keyed CAPTURE of DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.2.14, kb/Work PB3492), so a ROLLBACK restores such a file as at the last COMMIT (§14.9.36.4 GR3; the NOTE under §14.9.10.4 GR15) and a DELETE FILE after a CLOSE under commit control proceeds (§5, A.4.3; §4 item 2).

> ⚖ **The warning band and the hard errors are DELIBERATELY asymmetric, and the axis is whether a program can
> still mean what it says.** For an Annex A.3 element §4.2.6 ¶3 requires a warning mechanism and adds that "The
> implementor is not required to produce executable code when unsupported processor-dependent language elements
> are used" — so both severities conform there, and the choice is ours to make and to explain. For an Annex A.4
> element neither sentence applies: §4.2.7 asks only for the documentation, and A.4.1 makes refusing the default
> reading — so warning on the A.4.14 VALIDATE statement is a choice we owe an explanation for, and it is below.
> **The 1578–1580 band warns** because those facilities are *additive*: a program with a SEND, a COMMIT or a
> VALIDATE has a well-defined meaning with the facility inert, and the rest of the program is unaffected.
> Compiling and running it is more useful than refusing it. **SCREEN handling left that band on 2026-09-02**
> (kb/Work PB260): it is not additive in practice — `ACCEPT screen-name-1` and `DISPLAY screen-name-1` are
> token-identical to their format-1 DEVICE forms, so "inert" meant *silently binding the other statement* and
> moving the wrong data — and A.4.1's licence for an unclaimed OPTIONAL module reads the other way from
> §4.2.6's for a PROCESSOR-DEPENDENT one. A.4 unclaimed ⇒ the syntax is not accepted at all.
> **`ARITHMETIC IS STANDARD-BINARY` is a hard error (COBOL0806)** because it is *pervasive*: §8.8.1.4.1 makes
> it "a method of evaluating an arithmetic expression, an arithmetic statement, the SUM clause, and certain
> integer and numeric functions", in effect for the whole unit the moment the phrase is written, so there is
> no inert reading — compiling it with the clause ignored would silently run the whole program under a different
> arithmetic than the source selected, and the divergence would appear as wrong VALUES, not as a missing
> facility. A warning nobody reads plus wrong answers is the worst of the available outcomes; refusing is the
> honest one. `ARITHMETIC IS STANDARD` (removed 2023) and the removed/introduced edition gates are errors for
> the same reason.

> ℹ **The former warning dead spot is closed (kb/Work PB137).** A bare `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` after any
> open operand list — a `DISPLAY` operand tail, an `EVALUATE … WHEN` arm's first statement, the
> arithmetic receiver lists — now parses as its statement at the editions where §8.9 reserves the words:
> the `cobolWord` alternatives for the two words carry a reservation predicate, so no operand list can
> absorb them at 2023 while both remain ordinary user-defined words below 2023 (which is itself the §8.9
> rule). The named warning fires in every position, the statements bind with IDENTITY
> (`BoundCommitRollback`), and §14.9.7.3/§14.9.36.3 SR1 (recursive source elements, functions and
> methods included) and SR2 (SORT/MERGE input/output procedures) reject at compile time (COBOL1690).
> `VALIDATE` keeps the old absorption behavior (its own facility row).

## 2. Annex A.3 — processor-dependent language element disposition

Each row is one A.3 item. **Claimed** = standard-conforming support is provided. **Not claimed** = not implemented
(a §4.2.6 warning is emitted where the element is syntactically detectable). **N/A** = the element is a property
of an unsupported facility.

| A.3 # | Element | § | Disposition | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Significand/exponent >31/>3 digits in float literal / numeric-edited PICTURE | 8.3.3.3.3 / 13.18.40 | **Claimed** (all four) | WiseOwl COBOL supports the standard floating-point usages and STANDARD-DECIMAL arithmetic, so item 1's latitude is unavailable and the FULL forms are provided: a floating-point literal's significand of up to 36 digits and exponent of up to 4 digits (kb/Work PB99 — the value range is A.1 item 82's determination), a floating-point numeric-edited PICTURE with a 36-digit significand and a 4-digit exponent (kb/Work PB66, D21) |
| 2 | ARITHMETIC IS STANDARD-BINARY | 11.9.5 / 8.8.1.4 | **Not claimed — REVISITABLE** | ⛔ **The ground is PROCESSOR-DEPENDENCE, not obsolescence** (this row said "Obsolete feature" until 2026-08-31, which names a fact that grants nothing). **A.3 item 2**: "The ARITHMETIC IS STANDARD-BINARY clause in the OPTIONS paragraph is dependent on the capabilities of the processor" — and **§4.2.6** is what makes declining it conforming: the decision to claim support "is within an implementor's discretion", the absence "shall be specified in the implementor's user documentation" (this row), and a compile-time warning mechanism is required (COBOL0806 — see §1 on why an error). Obsolescence is *not* a licence: Annex **F.2**'s preamble reads "A conforming implementation shall support obsolete language elements **except** for elements that are also optional or processor-dependent" — so the exception is doing the work, and the obsolescence only corroborates. **REVISITABLE by the standard's own words**: F.2 item 3 ("STANDARD-BINARY arithmetic and STANDARD BINARY Intermediate Data Item. These features have not been implemented as of the writing of this revision by any COBOL provider") adds "Unlike other obsolete features, it is intended that interest in these facilities will be **reevaluated** during the next revision". Every rule conditioned solely on the mode carries this ONE determination (a derived verdict — `inventory-schema.json` `derived-verdicts.standard-binary-only`); NATIVE and STANDARD-DECIMAL are provided. Decision: kb/Work PB198. |
| 3 | ARITHMETIC IS STANDARD-DECIMAL | 11.9.5 | **Claimed** | Full SDIDI consumption (P10): `CobolDec` engine, decimal128 range ECs |
| 4 | Asynchronous messaging (MCS) facility | E.3.2 | **Not claimed** | Documented non-support (§4) — inter-run-unit communication not provided. Every rule conditioned solely on the facility carries this ONE determination, by owner decision R43 (a derived verdict — `inventory-schema.json` `derived-verdicts.mcs-only`); witnesses `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.6.11-Normal-run-unit-termination/w59_mcs_facility_witness`, `conformance:cases/4.2.10-Nonstandard-extensions/pb374_ec_mcs_names_accept_inert` |

EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED is raised from that one site; with checking off the §14.6.13.1.3 #8 implementor choice is to continue and return `"="` |
| 26 | STANDARD-1 phrase of RECORD DELIMITER | 12.4.5.11 | **Not claimed — and so is the clause's other arm** | **The WHOLE RECORD DELIMITER clause is declined, on two different grounds that reach one disposition, and it is diagnosed by name as COBOL1778 (accept-inert Warning) at every edition on both arms** (kb/Work PB292). ⛔ **This row said only "Reel-device delimiter; mass-storage model only" until 2026-09-05, and the compiler emitted NOTHING** — `recordDelimiterClause` parsed and no binder read it, so a program writing `RECORD DELIMITER IS STANDARD-1` compiled and ran clean at 85/2002/2014/2023 and this table's own "a §4.2.6 warning is emitted where the element is syntactically detectable" was false here. **STANDARD-1** is item 26's processor dependence made concrete by §12.4.5.11.4 GR2 — "If STANDARD-1 is specified, the external medium shall be a tape drive" — and WiseOwl COBOL provides no reel device (rows 28–30, 33–34), so GR3's ISO/IEC 1001:2012 7.1.2 framing is unreachable. **feature-name-1** is not an A.3 item at all: §12.4.5.11.3 SR2 makes the available names the implementor's to specify and A.1 item 150 makes providing them optional — this implementation provides **none** (§7, item 150), so §12.4.5.11.4 GR4 has no method to associate. **Accept-inert rather than refuse**, because §12.4.5.11.4 GR1 — "Any method used shall not be reflected in the record area or the record size used within the function, method, or program" — makes the framing invisible to the program: the file still round-trips through GR5's implementor method (§7, item 151), so unlike an inert FORMAT clause (§5, A.4.8) nothing a program can observe changes. Witness `conformance:cases/12.4.5.11-RECORD-DELIMITER/pb292_record_delimiter_witness` + `conformance-test:DocumentedNonSupportWitnessTests` (both arms, 85/2002/2014/2023) |
| 27 | CODE-SET clause | 13.18.13 / A.3 item 27 | Partial | **The identity-correspondence sets are CLAIMED** (kb/Work PB110): `NATIVE`, `STANDARD-1`/`STANDARD-2` (ISO/IEC 646 IRV — the native set's first 128 characters, so the §12.3.7.4 GR7 c correspondence is the identity), `UTF-16` and the `ASCII` code-name convert as the identity, byte-exact (golden `2023/pb110_code_set_identity`). The ISO/IEC 646 sets (`STANDARD-1`, `STANDARD-2`, `ASCII`) hold only 128 characters, so a record character above U+007F has no associated coded character (§13.18.13.4 GR6 b) and its WRITE or REWRITE is refused with '91' — '71' on a line sequential file — before anything reaches the medium (§7, A.1 item 187); an `EBCDIC` record character above U+00FF is refused the same way, at the statement, for every organization (kb/Work PB1150, PB1542; goldens `85/pb1542_code_set_unrepresentable_85`, `2023/pb1542_code_set_line_sequential`). **AND ONE GENUINE ALTERNATE DEVICE CODE SET IS NOW CLAIMED TOO** (kb/Work PB793): the `EBCDIC` code-name, whose §12.3.7.4 GR7 i correspondence with the native set is IBM CCSID 37 (§7 item 183), converts on every record crossing the medium — §13.18.13.4 GR6 a on input, GR6 b on output — for every organization (golden `2023/pb793_code_set_ebcdic`, which also reads the same physical file through a description carrying NO CODE-SET clause to show the medium really holds EBCDIC). **What is converted:** the record's data. The framing this processor adds AROUND a record — the §9.1.7.2 record-length header of a VARYING or keyed file, and a line sequential file's line delimiter — is not data of the record and stays in the native encoding; §9.1.7.2 leaves that framing implementor-defined, and keeping it native is what lets one framing serve a converted and an unconverted file alike. **The code set is deliberately NOT a validated fixed file attribute** — see §7 item 129. Both formats parse (the 2002 national half gated `code-set-national-2002`), SR1/SR2/SR3 are checked (COBOL1672; a LOCALE alphabet is COBOL1669). **What remains not provided:** an alphabet whose on-medium representation is neither the identity nor a single-byte code with a known native correspondence — a literal-phrase alphabet's remapped ordinals (the ordinal numbering itself is A.1 item 186's determination in §7; no medium encoding of a remapped alphabet is provided), UTF-8 / UCS-4 as variable-width medium encodings — is refused with COBOL1672 naming A.3 item 27 ("dependent upon a device capable of supporting the specified code"), never a silent identity |
| 28–30 | CLOSE REEL/UNIT, FOR REMOVAL, WITH NO REWIND | 14.9.6 | Partial | **No reel/unit device is provided**, so every physical file is §14.9.6.4 GR2 category (a) Non-unit (sequential) or (d) Non-sequential — the determination and the closing operations it settles are §7's A.1 item 24 row. All three phrases are ACCEPTED and execute their Non-unit Table 14 cell exactly: REEL/UNIT [FOR REMOVAL] is symbol e (successful, the file stays open, `'07'`), WITH NO REWIND is c,g (the file IS closed and a successful close reports `'07'`). What is not provided is the unit-media behaviour of columns (b)/(c) — unit swaps, volume pointers, rewind |

What is not provided is the unit-media behaviour: an actual reel to leave unrewound. | 40 | SOURCE phrase of RECORD KEY / ALTERNATE RECORD KEY | 12.4.5.12.2 / 12.4.5.6.2 | **Claimed (2002 and later)** | The `record-key-name-1 SOURCE IS { data-name-2 } …` key form is PROVIDED on both clauses (kb/Work PB1099 Q1; owner rule R65: a processor-dependent element is declined only where the processor truly lacks the capability, and this one does not). The key is §12.4.5.12.4 GR2 / §12.4.5.6.4 GR2's "concatenation of all occurrences of data-name-2 in the order specified": a record key is a LIST of byte windows end to end at every layer that carries it (`FileModel`'s `RecordKey`, the runtime `KeySegment`, the key descriptors of the keyed store's meta page), data-name-1 being the one-window case, so uniqueness, ordering, READ / START / DELETE and START's partial key (§14.9.41.4 GR17 a)/b)) treat the concatenation as one key. The record-key-name (§8.3.2.2.24) has the class and category of data-name-2 (SR5 / SR6) and is named by READ … KEY (§14.9.30.3 SR11), START … KEY (§14.9.41.3 SR7) and COLLATING SEQUENCE OF (§12.4.5.7.3 SR5), bare or qualified by its file-name (§8.4.2.2.2 Format 6); every syntax rule stated of data-name-2 is screened on each operand. ANSI X3.23-1985 prints data-name-1 only, so the phrase is COBOL0900 at 85 (VCR row 7.36, a derived provisional 2002 edge). The former refusal, COBOL1954, is retired. Witnesses `conformance:cases/12.4.5.6-ALTERNATE-RECORD-KEY/pb1099_record_key_source`; `conformance:cases/12.4.5.6-ALTERNATE-RECORD-KEY/pb1099-record-key-source-85`; `conformance-test:FileControlKeyRuleSpecTests` (the SOURCE section) |
| 41–42 | Cultural collating for keys / multiple alt keys with differing collating | 12.4.5.7 | **Partial** | The file-control COLLATING SEQUENCE clause (§12.4.5.7, Format 1 + Format 2 per-key) is supported for **alphanumeric** keys under a declared SPECIAL-NAMES alphabet — per-key weighted ordering/START/uniqueness on the greenfield IndexedConnector (COBOL1582/1583), and — owner decision Q3 (2026-08-18; kb/Work PB101, determination L8) — for a key whose alphabet is declared `ALPHABET … IS LOCALE`: **LOCALE-based cultural collating IS provided** (§A.3 item 41's own latitude): the key orders by the derived CLDR/UCA collation of the locale named, or, for `IS LOCALE` without a locale-name, of the locale current at the OPEN, and that order is a fixed file attribute (§12.4.5.7.4 GR1): every OPEN freezes the key sequences before §14.9.27.4 GR10's comparison, so a `SET LOCALE` while the file is open never reorders it, and an OPEN of an existing file while a locale of a different order is current is the file attribute conflict, '39' (golden `cases/12.4.5.7-COLLATING-SEQUENCE/pb3331_locale_key_sequence_fixed_at_open`). **Each key takes the sequence of its own CLASS** (§12.4.5.7.4 GR2/GR3, kb/Work PB1074): alphabet-name-1 reaches only keys of class alphanumeric and never reorders or re-judges the uniqueness of a national key, which takes the native national sequence (GR5) or alphabet-name-2 (GR3); SR1/SR2/SR7 are screened on the clause as written (COBOL1583). A NATIVE or UCS-4 national alphabet on a national key is the native national sequence and is supported. **A national alphabet defined by literals or LOCALE on a national key is NOT provided** (Annex A.3 item 41): it is declined by name and REFUSED, COBOL1584, because an inert compile would order the key by a different sequence than the one written |
| 43 | Zero-length record for relative/sequential files | 13.18.43.3 SR7/SR8 | **Claimed — on BOTH organizations the item names, at every supported edition** | The capability is PROVIDED: `RECORD IS VARYING IN SIZE FROM 0 TO n DEPENDING ON d` compiles with no diagnostic, a zero-length record round-trips through a WRITE and a READ, and §13.18.43.4 GR15's length register reads back 0 (goldens `conformance:cases/8.5.4-Zero-length-items/pb721_zero_length_record` — a sequential file **and** a relative one in one program, because A.3 item 43 names both — and `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb721_zero_length_record_85`, its COBOL-85 twin). ⛔ **This row read "Not claimed — Minimum record length is 1" until 2026-09-13, and that note was measurably false on both arms** (kb/Work PB721): the compiler had always accepted and round-tripped a zero minimum, so the §4.2.6 ¶3 warning a declined element owes was neither owed nor present, and the conformance record contradicted the compiler it describes. Claiming it is also what §13.18.43.3 SR7 requires of the FRONT end independently of the capability — "Integer-2 shall be greater than or equal to zero" is the express override of §5.5 1)'s "unsigned and nonzero" default for `integer-n`, so `FROM 0` is legal source and refusing it would reject legal COBOL; §8.5.4 item 5 confirms the result is a real zero-length item, and §13.18.43.4 GR16's closing sentence contemplates the count reaching zero on a READ INTO. The negative half is pinned too: a NEGATIVE minimum cannot be written at all (`conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb721-record-varying-negative-minimum`, `…-record-contains-negative-minimum`). |

## 3. Behavior determinations (§4.2.6 / Annex E — pinned implementor choices)

- **D-SEQ — the statement-sequence placement rules, and what "a discreet block of code" is** (kb/Work PB397).
  Three syntax rules are stated over a SEQUENCE of statements and are refused at compile time at every edition
  (none carries an edition qualifier): §14.9.14.3 SR1 — a Format 1 (bare) EXIT "shall appear in a sentence by itself
  that shall be the only sentence in the paragraph or in a section without paragraphs" (COBOL2966); §14.9.17.3 SR2
  — a Format 1 GO TO appearing "in a consecutive sequence of imperative statements within a sentence … shall appear as
  the last statement in that sequence" (COBOL2967); §14.9.42.3 SR1 — "The STOP statement shall be specified only as
  the last statement in any discreet block of code" (COBOL2968). **(a) The sequence** is a consecutive run of
  IMPERATIVE statements inside one sentence, or inside one phrase of another statement (an IF THEN or ELSE phrase, an
  inline PERFORM body, an ON SIZE ERROR phrase) (kb/Work PB2610). A CONDITIONAL statement ends the run: §14.5.1 says "Any
  statement with a conditional phrase that is not terminated by its explicit scope terminator is a conditional
  statement", and the rule binds only "a consecutive sequence of imperative statements". So `GO TO P IF A DISPLAY "Y".`
  and `GO TO P ADD 1 TO A ON SIZE ERROR DISPLAY "Z".` are legal. `GO TO P IF A DISPLAY "Y" END-IF.` is refused,
  because the delimited IF is imperative (§14.5.3.2). `IF A GO TO P END-IF DISPLAY "X"` is legal, because the GO TO
  ends its own phrase, and `IF A GO TO P DISPLAY "X" END-IF` is refused. **(b) "A discreet block of code"**
  is undefined by the standard (the spelling is the printed one); the implementor latitude is settled by CLAUDE.md
  rule 1's order: the standard does not decide, GnuCOBOL 3.2 compiles all four violating shapes without a diagnostic (measured), and IBM Enterprise COBOL and Micro Focus
  document the STOP rule as a statement last in "a sequence of imperative statements within a sentence" — so the block
  is read as the SAME sequence §14.9.17.3 SR2 names, for STOP RUN, including (a)'s end at a conditional statement:
  `STOP RUN IF A DISPLAY "Y".` is accepted, as IBM's and Micro Focus's wording ("a sequence of imperative statements")
  admits. "The STOP statement" of §14.9.42 is STOP RUN alone;
  the X3.23-1985 STOP literal (deleted 2002) communicates to the operator and then CONTINUES with the next statement,
  so a statement after it executes and it is not governed (`STOP "HALT" DISPLAY "A".` compiles at 85). A narrower reading (only sentence-level
  sequences) would admit `IF A STOP RUN DISPLAY "X" END-IF`, whose DISPLAY can never execute. **(c) Format 1 GO TO**
  includes the 1985 target-less `GO TO.` (that edition's Format 1; its procedure-name is optional there); the
  Format 2 DEPENDING GO TO is not constrained, since control falls through when no name is selected (§14.9.17.4 GR2).
  **(d) An EXIT inside another statement** (`IF A EXIT END-IF`) is not "in a sentence by itself": the sentence is the
  IF. A paragraph is §14.4.3's, so the sentences after a section header or the procedure division header form one
  (unnamed) paragraph and a section without paragraphs is one such paragraph. Witnesses:
  `conformance:cases/14.9.14-EXIT/pb397-exit-not-alone`, `conformance:cases/14.9.17-GO-TO/pb397-go-to-not-last`,
  `conformance:cases/14.9.42-STOP/pb397-stop-not-last`, `conformance:cases/14.9.14-EXIT/pb397_sequence_placement_legal`,
  `conformance:cases/14.9.17-GO-TO/pb2610_go_to_before_conditional`,
  `conformance-test:StatementSequencePlacementTests`.

- **D-PROP — what `>>PROPAGATE ON` propagates, and from where** (kb/Work PB1119). §7.3.21.4 GR2 says "any exception
  condition raised and not handled … shall be propagated as though a GOBACK RAISING LAST statement were executed",
  while the two processing orders it feeds name the directive in exactly two places: §14.6.13.1.3 6) for a FATAL
  condition with checking enabled (not EC-FLOW-GLOBAL-EXIT / -GOBACK), after 5)'s declarative, and §14.6.13.1.5's
  EXIT/GOBACK item 3 for an exception OBJECT in the activating element. §14.6.13.1.4, the order for a NONFATAL
  condition, has no propagation step — its 4) continues the statement. **(a) A nonfatal level-3 condition is not
  propagated**: the specific processing order governs, so an unhandled EC-OVERFLOW-STRING under PROPAGATE ON
  continues exactly as under OFF (`conformance:cases/7.3.21-PROPAGATE/w73d2_pb1119_propagate_on`, "B CONTINUES"). **(b) A MAIN program
  propagates nothing**: §7.3.21.1 propagates "to the activating runtime element" and a run unit's main program has
  none — the literal GOBACK there is a STOP that ignores RAISING (§14.9.18.4 GR3), which would end a failing run
  unit NORMALLY — so 7)'s abnormal termination stands (`conformance:AutomaticPropagationTests.MainProgram_HasNoActivator_Terminates`).
  **(c) An activator's re-propagated OBJECT is typed at run time**: "an applicable class or interface … specified in
  the RAISING phrase of the procedure division header in the activating element" is an `is` test over that header's
  classes (FACTORY OF: the factory type) and interfaces; no match stages EXCEPTION EC-OO-EXCEPTION
  (`conformance:AutomaticPropagationTests.ExceptionObject_ItemThree_ObjectOrEcOoException`). Implemented at the one
  fatal default, `EcEmitter.EmitSelection` (and the EC-I-O arm of `__IoCheckEc`, which §14.6.13.1.3 3) sends on to
  6)), with the element's ON/OFF folded by `PropagateState`.

- **D-GLOBAL-EXIT — EC-FLOW-GLOBAL-EXIT is never set** (kb/Work PB3102). §14.6.13.1.6 Table 13 names it ("EXIT PROGRAM
  in a global Declarative") as a Fatal condition, and §14.6.13.1.3 6) mentions it beside EC-FLOW-GLOBAL-GOBACK, but the
  standard states no general rule that SETS it. The sibling is set by §14.9.18.4 GR6 (a GOBACK executed within the range
  of a global declarative); §14.9.14.4 GR3 gives an EXIT PROGRAM only GOBACK's GR3 and GR4, not GR6, and the one
  normative statement about EXIT PROGRAM in a global declarative is §14.9.14.3 SR2, which the compiler enforces at compile
  time. The name is catalogued and accepted wherever an exception-name may be written, and the implementation never
  raises it: inventing a raise site for a condition the standard never sets would be behaviour with no rule behind it.
  Held by `unit:EcRaiseSiteRegistryDriftTests.EveryCataloguedLevel3Name_IsDeclaredAndRaised_OrDeclinedWithAReason`.
- **D-MCS-NR — the exception-name is EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTER; the standard's other spelling EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTOR is
  not a name** (kb/Work PB3149; a defect in the printed standard, recorded here and not coded around). The ISO PDF prints
  both spellings, and the transcription matches it at every site. §14.6.13.1.6 Table 13, which "is a list of the
  exception-names and their attributes", has the row `| EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTER | NF | RECEIVE statement |`, and the
  alphabetic Index spells it the same way. §E.3.2 3) spells it EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTOR in its list of the Asynchronous
  messaging facility's new exception conditions. Annex E is informative and only summarizes changes; it defines no
  exception-name. §7.3.25.3 SR2 binds the TURN directive's operand to Table 13: "Exception-name-1 shall be one of
  the exception names listed in 14.6.13.1". So the normative name is the Table 13 spelling, and no general rule raises
  either spelling (§14.9.31.4, RECEIVE, raises EC-MCS-INVALID-TAG and EC-MCS-REQUESTOR-FAILED only). The -OR
  spelling of the sibling EC-MCS-REQUESTOR-FAILED is consistent between Table 13 and E.3.2, so only NO-REQUESTER
  differs. GnuCOBOL 3.2 agrees: `libcob/exception.def` registers EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTER (1A05) and no -OR alias.
  Accepting EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTOR as well would be a nonstandard extension (section 3.2 below) that nothing asks for. So
  `ExceptionCatalog` catalogues EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTER only (a COBOL-2023 name, accepted inert like every EC-MCS name,
  section 4 item 1), and EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTOR is an unknown exception-name: COBOL0711 at every edition that has the TURN
  directive. Witnessed by `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb3149_ec_mcs_no_requester_table13` and
  `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb3149-ec-mcs-no-requestor-unknown`. Confirmed by the owner on 2026-10-18 ("keep
  EC-MCS-NO-REQUESTER only"; kb/Work PB3149, "Owner confirmation").

- **D-TW1 — a period, comma or semicolon written immediately before a closing pseudo-text delimiter is a
  SEPARATOR, so `==STOP RUN.==` holds the text-words `STOP` `RUN` `.`** (kb/Work PB1350). §8.3.5 2)/3) make those
  characters separators only "when followed by a space", and read literally `RUN.==` would form the one text-word
  `RUN.` — a pseudo-text that no source text can ever match, since source text writes the sentence period before a
  space or a line end. But §8.3.5 8) lets the separator space OPTIONALLY precede every separator but three, and the
  closing pseudo-text delimiter is not one of the three, so `==STOP RUN.==` and `==STOP RUN. ==` are the same
  pseudo-text written with and without an optional space and must form the same text-words. Everywhere else the
  rule is applied as printed — `ZZ.ZZ`, `Z,ZZ9` and `X.COPY` are single text-words. Written once, in
  `TextWordScanner.SeparatorFollows`; witnessed by `unit:TextManipulationTextWordTests.ReplaceStatement_PeriodInsidePseudoText`
  and `conformance:cases/7.2.2.5-Text-words/pb1350_text_words_85` (`[ZZZ]`).
- **D-B2 — the figurative constant SPACE against a BOOLEAN receiving operand is the boolean character '0'**
  (kb/Work PB425). The standard does not define the value, and §14.9.25.4 GR2 makes the case reachable:
  `MOVE "" TO PIC 1(4)` is legal source (Table 16's Alphanumeric sending row gives "Yes" against a Boolean
  receiving operand, and §14.9.25.3 SR7's prohibition names figurative constants *written in the source*, which
  a zero-length literal is not), and GR2 then treats the literal "as if it were the figurative constant SPACE".
  Table 17 gives SPACE against a Boolean receiving operand the category **boolean**, but §8.3.3.6.4 GR5 defines
  the space format only as "one or more of the character space in the computer's runtime coded character set"
  and names no boolean value, while §8.3.3.4.3 SR2 admits only '0' and '1' in a boolean item. WiseOwl COBOL fills
  with the boolean character '0' — the only boolean character the standard attaches to a fill (§14.6.8.6 aligns
  a boolean receiver "with zero fill or truncation to the right"; §8.3.3.6.4 GR4 gives the ZERO format "one or
  more of the boolean character '0'"), and the same answer GR3 gives a boolean zero-length literal, so the two
  GR arms agree. Written once, in `FigurativeConstants.FillChar` — the compiler's one fill-character
  computation; witnessed by `conformance:cases/8.3.3.2-Alphanumeric-literals/pb425_zero_length_literal_move` (`A-BOOL=[0000]`).
  *(Unrelated to the superseded D-B1 boolean-representation determination in `DATA_MODEL_DESIGN.md`.)*
- **D-B3 — the usage of a boolean literal is DISPLAY, so a MOVE of one to a group deposits its '0'/'1' characters**
  (kb/Work PB3562). A MOVE to an alphanumeric group is §14.9.25.4 GR4's "alphanumeric to alphanumeric elementary
  move, except that there is no conversion of data from one form of internal representation to another", so the
  sender's representation, and therefore its usage, decides the bytes deposited. A boolean *function* has a stated
  usage — §15.2 2) "Boolean functions have an implicit usage bit", §15.13.4 1) "a boolean item of usage bit" — and so
  does a national literal (§8.3.3.5.4 GR3 a), "usage NATIONAL"), so each deposits its own representation (packed bits,
  UTF-16BE pairs: `MOVE FUNCTION BOOLEAN-OF-INTEGER(102 8) TO G` deposits the one byte X"66"). A boolean *literal* has no
  stated usage: §8.3.3.4.4 GR3 gives only its value, "the sequence of occurrences of boolean-character-1". WiseOwl
  COBOL reads it as what it is written with, the characters '0' and '1' "from the computer's coded character set"
  (§8.3.3.4.3 SR2): usage DISPLAY, one byte a position, so `MOVE B"01100110" TO G` deposits the eight characters
  01100110. That is the answer the compiler's one static-usage reader (`IntrinsicArgumentRules.StaticUsageOf`) already
  gave every argument screen (a boolean literal passes CONCAT's display-usage screen), and the same usage a boolean
  item written without USAGE BIT has (§13.18.60.4 GR7); the alternative, packing the literal as bits, would make one
  literal two usages. A zero-length boolean literal is not affected: GR3 makes it the figurative ZERO before the sender
  is asked. Written once, in `OperandText.NonElementaryMoveSender`, which every group-move sender channel (MOVE, an
  implicit MOVE such as WRITE FROM, a CALL / INVOKE argument into a group formal) reads - directly where the formal is
  known to the activating element, and through the argument's second alphabet where it is not (kb/Work PB3587): a
  Format-1 CALL, or a CALL located at run time, cannot see the formal, so it states a BY CONTENT argument's `Sending`
  with its characters (what an elementary formal reads) and, for a sender of usage national or bit,
  its representation (`MoveSending.StorageImage`, produced by `OperandText.StorageImageIfDiffers` / `StorageImageConverter`
  from the same codec), which a plain-group formal's record is filled from (`CobolArgAdapt.Text`); an INVOKE literal
  crosses as the bound literal, its category kept (`BoundInvokeArg.StringLiteral`), so a national literal is usage
  national there too. Pinned by `GroupMoveSenderChannelDriftTests`;
  witnessed by `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3562_boolean_literal_group_move` and
  `conformance:cases/14.2-Procedure-division-structure/pb3587_content_group_formal_usage_values`.
- **D-B4 - a numeric literal, and the value of a numeric function, sent to a group store their DIGITS ONLY** (kb/Work
  PB3570, PB3613; owner decision 2026-10-23, on a point of implementor latitude). A MOVE to a group item is §14.9.25.4 GR4's move, "treated exactly as if it were an
  alphanumeric to alphanumeric elementary move, except that there is no conversion of data from one form of internal
  representation to another": it preserves the sender's representation, and a numeric literal has none, so the standard
  does not say what `MOVE -456 TO G` stores. CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence for implementor latitude is the standard,
  then GnuCOBOL, whose literal data holds the digits without the sign or the decimal point - and an elementary
  alphanumeric receiver already drops the sign by GR6 a) ("the operational sign is not moved"), so the group move now
  agrees with it. WiseOwl COBOL sends the digits of the literal's value, in the order written, with neither sign nor
  decimal point: `MOVE -456 TO G`, `MOVE +456 TO G` and `MOVE 456 TO G` store 456, `MOVE -4.56 TO G` stores 456,
  `MOVE -0.05 TO G` stores 005 (leading zeros are digits), and a floating-point literal sends the digits of its
  SIGNIFICAND as written, never its exponent nor the digits of its scaled value (`1.5E+3` sends 15, `12.0E+2` sends 120,
  `0.5E-1` sends 05, each measured against cobc 3.2.0; the same value written `0.05` sends 005, so the digits follow the
  notation, as GnuCOBOL's literal data does, and `1.0E+6144` does not become 6145 characters); the group then aligns left with space fill or truncation to the right
  (§14.6.8.5). The same characters cross a CALL ... AS NESTED or INVOKE BY CONTENT argument into a plain-group formal
  (§14.2.3 GR9, "otherwise, a MOVE statement"). This supersedes kb/Work PB1113's determination, which kept the literal's
  own characters, sign included. **The value of a numeric or integer FUNCTION is the same sender** (kb/Work PB3613): §15.2 4)-5)
  give it "an operational sign" and no usage, and §15.4.1 leaves a returned value's "characteristics and representation" to
  the implementor under native arithmetic, so §14.9.25.4 GR4 has no internal representation of it to preserve, exactly as for
  a literal, and the one determination covers both: `MOVE FUNCTION MIN(N 3) TO G` (N = -15) stores 15 and `FUNCTION MIN(M 3)`
  (M = -1.5) stores 15, the same characters an elementary alphanumeric receiver takes (GR6 a); under DECIMAL-POINT IS COMMA
  the separator is no digit either, and a floating-point value sends its significand digits as a literal does). A call the
  compiler folds to a literal and the same call evaluated at run time send the same characters. GnuCOBOL sends the function's
  own internal field instead (`1u` for the S99 minimum, a 4-byte binary for INTEGER, `15` for ABS), which is no rule for a value
  the standard gives no representation, so the determination follows the literal, not the engine. The same characters cross
  a CALL ... AS NESTED, a Format-1 CALL and an INVOKE argument BY CONTENT into a plain-group formal; a function-identifier is a
  MOVE sender (§14.9.25.4 GR1), so §14.8.2.2 rule 2 admits it there (only an arithmetic expression, which is no MOVE sender, is
  refused; so is the same function, item or numeric literal ENCLOSED IN PARENTHESES, `(FUNCTION MIN(N 3))`, `(N)` or `(3)`, which is
  no longer an argument that "consists merely of a single identifier or literal", §14.9.4.4 GR8, whatever tree the binder reduces it
  to: kb/Work PB3678, `pb3678_parenthesized_function_group_formal_refused`; kb/Work PB3760,
  `pb3760_parenthesized_literal_group_formal_refused` and its INVOKE and user-defined function siblings. A literal's sign is part of
  it, §8.3.3.3.2 rule 2, so `-3` is still the literal and `(-3)` an expression). An ITEM sends its storage image (a signed DISPLAY item its overpunched sign), which D-B3's codec already gives.
  Written once, in `OperandText.NonElementaryMoveSender`, whose digit rule is `CobolNum.GroupDigits`; witnessed by
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3570_numeric_literal_group_move`,
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3570_floating_literal_group_move`,
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.2-Procedure-division-structure/pb3570_numeric_literal_group_formal`,
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3613_numeric_function_group_move`,
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3613_numeric_function_group_move_comma` and
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.2-Procedure-division-structure/pb3613_numeric_function_group_formal`.
  **A Format-1 CALL sends the SAME digits** (kb/Work PB3677): the activating element cannot see the formal there, and it used to
  cut an SDIDI value (a numeric function that returned one, or a STANDARD-DECIMAL expression) to the receiver-less 6 fraction
  digits before any formal could (`0.0001` sent `0000100`, the value 2 sent `2000000`). GR9 moves the argument "without
  conversion" and fills a numeric formal by a COMPUTE "without the ROUNDED phrase", so only the formal cuts the value: it
  crosses at its own exponent (`CobolArgAdapt.SdidiValue`), witnessed by
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.2-Procedure-division-structure/pb3677_format1_sdidi_function_value`.
  **A numeric function's value reaches a numeric or character formal as its VALUE in a Format-1 CALL too** (kb/Work PB3969): §15.4.1
  leaves "the characteristics and representation of the returned value" to the implementor under native arithmetic, so GR9's
  first regime has no image of it to move "without conversion", and the value is the sender exactly as in the second regime and
  in GR10 ("if the formal parameter is numeric, a COMPUTE statement without the ROUNDED phrase"; otherwise the MOVE of the value).
  `CALL "Q" USING BY CONTENT FUNCTION MAX(W 0)` with W = 1.25 shows `+1.25` in a PIC S9V99 formal (it showed `+0.00`, the leading
  positions of the value's 38-digit container), `FUNCTION INTEGER(W)` shows `1` in a PIC X(5) formal as `MOVE FUNCTION INTEGER(W)
  TO X5` does. Witnessed by `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.2-Procedure-division-structure/pb3969_format1_numeric_function_value`.
- **D-B5 — a boolean item RECEIVING characters converts each one: '1' is boolean one, every other character boolean
  zero** (kb/Work PB3666; owner decision 2026-10-24, on a point of implementor latitude). Table 16 (§14.9.25.3) admits
  an alphanumeric or national sending operand against a boolean receiving operand, and §14.6.8.6 transfers the data
  "after any necessary conversion, into the corresponding boolean positions of the receiving data item, with zero fill
  or truncation to the right" (JUSTIFIED per §13.18.32). But a boolean character is "the value zero or one" (§3.21), no rule
  converts a character that is neither, and §14.6.13.2 1) calls a later reference to non-boolean content undefined with
  EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE, so the standard leaves the conversion to the implementor. Before the determination a MOVE of
  `"AB"` to `PIC 1(5)` stored the characters themselves, so DISPLAY showed `AB000` while `B-NOT` of the same item
  gave `11111` (the operators read a position outside `{'0','1'}` as zero). WiseOwl COBOL converts EACH transferred
  character at the store: `'1'` to boolean one and every other character (a `'0'`, a letter, a space, a national
  letter) to boolean zero, then aligns with zero fill or truncation to the right (left, under JUSTIFIED). It is the
  rule the operators already apply and the rule an ACCEPT into a boolean item applies (§14.9.1.4 GR1,
  `AcceptSource.DeviceBoolean`), so DISPLAY of the item and the operators over it agree for both usages (USAGE DISPLAY
  `PIC 1` and USAGE BIT) and every other character store inherits it. GnuCOBOL 3.2 gives no precedent (probed 2026-10-24: it
  warns that USAGE BIT is not implemented and stores a `PIC 1(5)` item in one byte, and its USAGE DISPLAY `PIC 1` moves
  text as a number, right-aligning `"101"` as `00101` against §14.6.8.6's zero fill to the right); IBM Enterprise COBOL
  has no boolean category. The paths that deposit characters into a boolean item and now convert: the elementary
  MOVE and every statement that MOVEs (READ INTO, MOVE CORRESPONDING, INITIALIZE ... REPLACING BOOLEAN DATA, a CALL
  argument landed by §14.2.3 GR9, the element MOVE of a variable-length group MOVE between corresponding dynamic-capacity
  tables, §14.6.9.2), a reference-modified boolean receiver, STRING into a USAGE DISPLAY boolean item (§14.9.43.4 GR3 a)),
  a group sender into a USAGE DISPLAY or USAGE NATIONAL boolean item (§14.9.25.4 GR4's alphanumeric move; into a display
  item it zero-fills where it used to space-fill), a READ or RETURN into an elementary boolean record area that no other
  description shares (§14.9.30.4 GR13 c); §14.9.34.4 GR3; a record area shared with another record of the FD
  (§13.18.33.4 GR3) or with a SAME RECORD AREA peer (§12.4.6.4.4 GR2) holds the record's bytes for every description and a
  READ leaves them as they are, as the restore of an APPLY COMMIT item does, §14.9.36.4 GR3), and COMPUTE's boolean result. **The GR4 arm converts the DECODED characters, never the
  bytes:** GR4 has "no conversion of data from one form of internal representation to another", so the sender's BYTES
  fill the receiving area unchanged, and the item's characters are then decoded from them (a national item's UTF-16BE
  pairs, `ReceivingStore.StorageCharacters`) and converted like any other character store (`MOVE GN TO BN` with GN holding
  `N"101"` stores `101`; `MOVE GA TO BN` with GA holding `A1Z1` stores `0000`, because the pairs x4131 x5A31 x2020 x2020
  are no national `1`). Converting the bytes before decoding them is the defect PB3666's review R1-1 removed. **The one
  exemption is USAGE BIT:** a GROUP sender into a USAGE BIT item leaves the item's bits the first bits of the sender's bytes
  (`MOVE GA TO BB` with GA holding `1A` stores the bits of x"31", `00110`), and every bit pattern is a valid boolean value,
  so DISPLAY and the operators agree there without a character conversion. Every STORE into a boolean item converts its
  characters. That includes a GR4 group move (the decoded characters of a national or display receiver; a USAGE BIT
  receiver's bits are all valid) and a READ or RETURN into an elementary record area that no other description shares. A
  boolean item can still hold a character other than 0 or 1 only through another description of the same storage, which no
  store into the item reaches: a group receiver (GR4 moves the group's bytes), a REDEFINES view, a record area shared with
  another record of its file or with a SAME RECORD AREA peer (a READ or RETURN fills the area's bytes), an APPLY COMMIT
  restore (ROLLBACK returns the saved image), or storage shared through a BY REFERENCE argument,
  EXTERNAL, BASED or ADDRESS OF. That content is undefined (§14.6.13.2 1)), and the boolean operators read such a position
  as zero. (`MOVE "A1Z" TO G` leaves `A1Z` in a boolean member of the group G.) VALUE cannot reach it (§13.18.63.3 SR10: the literals of a boolean item's VALUE clause are boolean
  literals), UNSTRING refuses a boolean receiver (§14.9.48.3 SR4) and a .NET host's string landing into a boolean formal is
  REFUSED when it holds a character other than `0` or `1` (`HostLanding.RequireClass`). Written once, in
  `CobolBool.FromCharacters` and its fitting store `CobolBool.Store` (`RuntimeApi.StrStoreBoolean` is the only emitter of
  that store); witnessed by `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3666_boolean_receiver_converts_characters` and
  `conformance:wiseowl/cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3666_dynamic_table_group_move`, and `unit:CobolBoolTests.Store_ConvertsEachCharacterThenFits`.
- **D-DL1 — §14.9.20.4 GR7's length-zeroing is the GR6c arm's rule, not a post-pass over all three
  sending-operand arms** (2026-09-20; kb/Work PB418 + PB415, rows `GR-14.9.20.4-7` and `SR-14.9.20.3-8`).
  GR7 is printed without a condition — *"When a dynamic-length elementary item is initialized, its length is
  set to zero"* — and read that way it erases the sending operand GR6a and GR6b have just designated, so
  `INITIALIZE D ALL TO VALUE` would not restore D's VALUE and `INITIALIZE D REPLACING ALPHANUMERIC DATA BY
  "ABC"` would store nothing, for the whole dynamic-length population. **WiseOwl COBOL applies GR7 only where GR6c
  supplies the sender** — i.e. where the item qualified through GR5c3 (the DEFAULT phrase) or GR5c4 (neither
  REPLACING nor VALUE specified). Four reasons, none of them a preference:
  **(i)** the standard states the SAME action at the other occasion WITH the carve-out spelled out —
  §14.6.2.3.2 GR7, *"The length of each dynamic-length elementary item that is specified without a VALUE clause
  is set to zero"*; **(ii)** §8.6.4 makes a dynamic-length item's initial-state length the VALUE clause's
  length, and §14.9.20.4 GR6a3 demands a sender that *"produces the same result as the initial value of the
  data item as produced by the application of the VALUE clause"* — under the unconditional reading **no sender
  can satisfy GR6a3** for this population, i.e. a general rule becomes unsatisfiable rather than merely
  narrowed; **(iii)** §14.9.20.3 SR8 designates literal-1 / identifier-2 as *the* sending operand under
  REPLACING, and the unconditional reading makes that designation inert for every dynamic-length receiver;
  **(iv)** GR7 is NECESSARY only on the GR6c arm — §8.3.3.6.4 GR3b gives a bare figurative constant a length of
  one character, so GR6c's *"Figurative constant alphanumeric SPACES"* would otherwise leave the item at
  length 1 instead of §13.18.19.4 GR1's minimum of zero. **Rejected reading:** §14.9.20.4 GR7 as an unconditional
  post-pass, which is what WiseOwl COBOL did before this determination. Written once, in
  `InitializeBinder.ElementaryAction`; witnessed at both poles by
  `conformance:cases/14.9.20-INITIALIZE/initialize_dynamic_length` (the GR6c arm → `LEN=00`) and
  `conformance:cases/14.9.20-INITIALIZE/pb418_initialize_dynamic_length_senders` (the GR6a/GR6b arms, the figurative-VALUE
  one-character case, and the GR5c ordering against `THEN TO DEFAULT`).
- **D-DL2 — the SIZE of a dynamic-length RECEIVING operand is its maximum size** (2026-09-22; kb/Work PB871).
  §8.5.1.10.4 fixes a dynamic-length item's size only where it is a SENDING operand or reference-modified —
  *"treated as a fixed-length data item whose length is the dynamic-length elementary item's current length"* — and
  for a receiving operand gives the new CONTENT (*"the new value becomes the content of the item"*), not a size.
  Three statements are written over the receiver's size itself: STRING (§14.9.43.4 GR6/GR8, *"the number of
  character positions in the data item referenced by identifier-3"*), UNSTRING without DELIMITED BY (§14.9.48.4
  GR11b, *"the size of the current receiving area"*) and ACCEPT format 1 (§14.9.1.4 GR3/GR4). **WiseOwl COBOL reads
  that size as the item's MAXIMUM size (§8.5.1.10.1)**: an item "for which the number of character positions
  allocated to the data item may vary during program execution" can receive as many as it may hold. For STRING,
  GR7 (*"only the portion of the data item referenced by identifier-3 that was referenced during the execution
  of the STRING statement is changed"*) still governs, so the new length is the old content's, extended through
  the last position written, and a position between the old end and the pointer is a space — the character
  §14.9.39.4 GR39 gives every position a dynamic-length item grows by. **Rejected reading:** the CURRENT length,
  which makes an empty dynamic-length item unwritable by STRING (every character an overflow) and makes UNSTRING
  examine zero characters. Written once for the emitters (`ReceivingStore.DynamicReceivingSize`, beside the one
  elementary character receiving store `ReceivingStore.Characters`) and read through the ONE receiver-size reader
  `ReceivingStore.CharacterPositions` — by ACCEPT format 1's device transfer (kb/Work PB1013, which also answers an
  ANY LENGTH receiver's size with its argument's, §13.18.2.4 GR1 b)) and by UNSTRING's examination size
  (`ReceivingStore.ExaminationSize`, kb/Work PB979); witnessed by `conformance:cases/14.9.43-STRING/pb871_dynamic_length_receivers`
  (STRING into an empty item, into a longer one, through a grown gap and past the maximum; UNSTRING with and
  without DELIMITED BY).
- **D-DL3 — the DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause: the PREFIXED length field bounds the item, the layout is the
  item's form in the record a file holds, and no physical-structure-name is supported** (kb/Work PB829, PB1094;
  rows `FMT-12.3.7.2`, `GR-12.3.7.4-19`). §12.3.7.4 GR18
  sizes the PREFIXED length field ("If SIGNED is specified, the length field is a signed binary field"; SHORT the
  shorter one) and GR19 puts a binary-zero delimiter after DELIMITED data. WiseOwl COBOL's length fields are exactly
  those binary fields (32-bit, or 16-bit with SHORT), so §8.5.1.10.1's candidate "the largest integer that can be
  stored in an item of the usage specified in the PREFIXED phrase" is GR18's own table value — 65535 for SHORT
  PREFIXED, 32767 for SIGNED SHORT PREFIXED; 4294967295 and 2147483647 exceed the implementor maximum (item 62)
  and bound nothing. "The maximum length associated with dynamic-length-structure-name-1" (§13.18.19.3 SR4) is
  that capacity bounded by the implementor maximum (a DELIMITED-only structure: the implementor maximum); a larger
  LIMIT is COBOL2258. **The LAYOUT is realized in the record image** (kb/Work PB1094, which refuted this
  determination's earlier premise that "no operation gives the item an addressable byte image": a WRITE does).
  §8.5.1.10.3 lets a dynamic-length item sit "within the record they are subordinate to", which is what a record on
  a medium is, and §12.3.7.4 GR18 / GR19 then say what the item looks like there: *"data described with
  dynamic-length-structure-name-1 is prefixed by a length field"* and *"a delimiter shall directly follow the data"*.
  So a structured item occupies **`[length field][data][delimiter]`** in a record a file or a sort store holds, the
  length field present for PREFIXED and the delimiter for DELIMITED, in that order whichever order the clause wrote
  them (a structure with both has both). **Representation** (the standard leaves it implementor-defined, GR18's
  "capable of supporting" and GR19's "data of the length of an alphanumeric character"): the length field is the
  item's current length in CHARACTER POSITIONS as a binary integer **most significant byte first** (the
  implementation's binary byte order, A.1 item 205), **four characters** for PREFIXED / SIGNED PREFIXED and **two**
  for SHORT PREFIXED / SIGNED SHORT PREFIXED (SIGNED changes the range, never the bytes: a length is never
  negative), one image character per byte; the delimiter is **one character position of zero bits** — one
  character for an alphanumeric item, **two** for a national item, whether it is a member of a group or is itself
  the record (its image is its UTF-16BE byte pairs, D-N1: the image of a group is its storage, A.1 items 57 and 63;
  kb/Work PB3441). **The program never sees these characters:** §8.5.1.11.2 makes a
  variable-length item behave "as though it were in fact contiguous with its neighbors whenever a procedural
  operation is applied to a group containing it", so a MOVE, a comparison, DISPLAY or READ … INTO of the record is
  over the data alone. A record has TWO FORMS: the *contiguous* image (the data alone, what the procedural
  view is) and the *medium* image (what the file holds: each structured member framed). They are produced and
  consumed in ONE place, `CobolContiguousLayout` (`MediumImage` / `MediumExtents` on a WRITE, REWRITE or RELEASE;
  `Decompose` on a READ or RETURN), over the per-member layout `CobolDynStructure`, and the frame's extent table
  (D-FRA (v)) keeps describing the stored image, so a key behind a structured member, the sort store and the fixed
  form (D-FRA (vi)) need no second rule. **Sizes include the structure**: the record on the medium physically
  contains the length field and delimiter, so §13.18.43.4 GR8's size of a record description, GR9 / GR10's
  minimum and maximum, every RECORD clause integer a syntax rule compares against them (§13.18.43.3 SR3 / SR4), the
  bytes a RECORD VARYING … DEPENDING ON item holds (GR13 a), GR15) and the fixed length a Format 1 file's records
  have (GR6 — each member then at its MAXIMUM extent, length field + maximum size + delimiter, blank padded)
  all count them; `FileModel.MaxDynamicExtent` / `MinExtent` are the one place. **Reading**: the frame's extent table
  says where each member's extent ends and the structure says what is inside it (length field first, else up to the
  delimiter; an extent that ends in its delimiter is exactly the data before it, so data that itself holds a binary
  zero survives); a record that carries NO table (a file another program wrote, a Format 1 file) is taken
  apart by the structures themselves, and a member with no structure takes what is left beyond the fixed material and
  the minimum (length field + delimiter) of the structured members after it — so with NO table a plain member
  followed by a structured one is read as the take step reads it (D-FRA), and data that holds the delimiter of a
  DELIMITED-only member ends there. A length field larger than the record holds is clamped to what is there (a record
  that ends inside its own structure gives what is left) and no condition is set: §14.6.13.2 rule 5's
  EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE speaks of a dynamic-length item's own internal format, which here is a native string and is
  always well formed, and the standard defines no status for a medium record that disagrees with its structure.
  **LINE SEQUENTIAL**: the characters below U+0020 are outside a line sequential
  file's character set (A.1 item 115), and a length field (whose first byte is zero) and a delimiter are such
  characters, so a WRITE of a record that holds a structured member to a LINE SEQUENTIAL file is the status '71' of
  §14.9.51.4 GR23, exactly as for any record holding a binary field — an unstructured dynamic-length member
  (§13.18.19.3 SR3) is unaffected. **Rejected readings:** keeping the structure off the medium because the item is
  a native `string` outside the record (§8.5.1.10.3's other option — it makes GR18 and GR19 unobservable, and the
  clause's purpose is the layout a second program reading the file sees); putting the structure in the
  contiguous image (it would break §8.5.1.11.2's procedural view, which is why the two forms are separate);
  counting the structure bytes against nothing (a record of maximum content then exceeded the RECORD clause's own
  bound and the WRITE failed '44'). §12.3.7.3 SR32 ("The implementor shall
  specify the names supported for physical-structure-name-1") is answered with the EMPTY set: every layout the
  carrier could honour is already expressible with PREFIXED / DELIMITED, so a physical-structure-name is refused by
  name (COBOL2257) rather than silently mapped to one of them. Witnessed by `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/pb829_dynamic_length_structure`
  (a 70000-character sender stores 65535 / 32767 / 70000 / 70000 / LIMIT 10), `conformance:cases/13.18.19-DYNAMIC-LENGTH/pb829-dynamic-length-structure-limit`
  and, for the layout in the record, `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/pb1094_dynamic_length_structure_record_image` (every
  PREFIXED / SIGNED / SHORT / DELIMITED form and a plain member, read back as the characters the file holds),
  `…_elementary_record` (a record that is the item: alphanumeric and national), `…_organizations` (indexed
  variable and Format 1, relative, SORT USING / GIVING and procedures) and `…_record_size` (the Format 1 fixed form
  and RECORD VARYING … DEPENDING ON).
- **D-UN3 — which side of UNSTRING's all-national rule a NUMERIC receiver stands on** (2026-09-22; kb/Work
  PB980, row `SR-14.9.48.3-3`). §14.9.48.3 SR3 is category-worded: *"If any of identifier-1, identifier-2,
  identifier-3, identifier-4, identifier-5, literal-1, or literal-2 are of category national, then all shall be of
  category national."* SR4 then admits identifier-4 *"as usage display and category alphabetic, alphanumeric, or
  numeric; or as usage national and category national or numeric"*. A numeric receiver is never category national,
  so SR3 read by category alone would forbid every national sender from reaching SR4's usage-national numeric
  receiver, leaving that arm of SR4 unusable — no reading of the two rules together supports that. **WiseOwl COBOL
  reads SR4's own pairing into SR3: a usage-national numeric identifier-4 stands with the national operands, a
  usage-display numeric identifier-4 with the others**; every other operand answers by its §8.5.2.1 class through
  `IntrinsicArgumentRules.ClassOf`, and a figurative delimiter (GR7: it takes identifier-1's class) never mixes.
  **Rejected readings:** category alone (above), and exempting numeric receivers entirely, which would admit a
  usage-display numeric receiver beside a national sender where SR4's pairing says otherwise. Implemented in
  `StringUnstringBinder.BindUnstring` over the shared `AllOrNothingClass` predicate (COBOL2306); witnessed by
  `conformance:cases/14.9.48-UNSTRING/pb979_unstring_any_length_national` (national sender into two usage-national numeric receivers)
  and `conformance:cases/14.9.48-UNSTRING/pb980-unstring-national-mix`.
- **D-FNUSE — a numeric, integer, index or boolean function-identifier is not "described … as usage display or
  national", so it is no STRING character operand, no INSPECT identifier-n and no numeric integer operand opposite a
  character operand of a relation** (owner 2026-10-24 and 2026-10-25; kb/Work PB3665, PB3691,
  rules `SR-14.9.43.3-1`, `SR-14.9.22.3-2`, `GR-8.8.4.2.1-6`). §14.9.43.3 SR1 requires every identifier of STRING but the POINTER to be
  *"described implicitly or explicitly as usage display or national"*, and §14.9.22.3 SR2 requires *"an elementary item
  described implicitly or explicitly as usage display or national"* of INSPECT's identifier-3 … identifier-n. A
  function-identifier references *"the unique data item that results from the evaluation of a function"* (§8.4.3.2.1),
  and §15.2 describes that item by the function's type: an alphanumeric function has *"an implicit usage display"*
  (1)), a national function *"an implicit usage national"* (3)), a boolean function *"an implicit usage bit"* (2)); the
  numeric (4)), integer (5)) and index (6)) functions are given a class, a category and (for the first two) an
  operational sign, and **no usage**. §15.2's opening sentence (a function *"may be used anywhere a sending data item
  of that class and category may be specified"*) and §15.4.1 (the returned value's characteristics are the
  implementor's) leave the usage of a numeric value open, and the choice is the owner's: **WiseOwl COBOL reads the
  silence as "not described as usage display or national", so only the alphanumeric and national functions are
  admitted** — `STRING FUNCTION UPPER-CASE(S) …`, `INSPECT … FOR ALL FUNCTION LOWER-CASE(P)` — and `STRING FUNCTION
  INTEGER(N) …`, `STRING … DELIMITED BY FUNCTION ORD(C)`, `STRING FUNCTION BOOLEAN-OF-INTEGER(N 4) …` and the INSPECT
  forms are refused (COBOL1626, COBOL0847). The same refusal reaches `FUNCTION LENGTH(item)`, which the binder
  FOLDS to a number: it is the function it folds, never "a numeric literal", and the diagnostic says so (a real numeric
  literal keeps the literal wording, §14.9.43.3 SR1). UNSTRING needed no new rule: SR2 (category alphanumeric or
  national) already refused the numeric and boolean functions, and its delimiter now names the folded LENGTH as
  category numeric. **GnuCOBOL 3.2 is no precedent**: `cb_emit_string` checks usage only for a data item (a literal
  carries a `TODO`, a function call falls to `default: break;`), and stores the raw four bytes of
  `cob_intr_integer`'s binary field (`FUNCTION INTEGER(N)` with N = 7 gives `\a\0\0\0`), so the precedence stops at the
  standard. Implemented once: `IntrinsicSig.ImplicitUsageOf` (the §15.2 usage by type) behind
  `IntrinsicArgumentRules.FunctionIsNotDisplayOrNational`, asked by `StringUnstringBinder.Sr1Offence` and
  `StatementValidation.CheckInspectFunctionUsage`; pinned by `DisplayOrNationalUsagePredicateDriftTests`; witnessed by
  `conformance:cases/14.9.43-STRING/pb3665_string_function_usage_controls` and
  `conformance:cases/14.9.22-INSPECT/pb3665_inspect_function_usage_controls` (the admitted functions) and the
  `pb3665-*` refusals.
  **The relation condition (owner 2026-10-25, "Refuse it per the spec"; kb/Work PB3691).** §8.8.4.2.5 (`cite.py
  --check` OK) reads *"The numeric integer operand shall be an integer literal or an integer numeric data item of usage
  display or national."* A numeric, integer or index function-identifier is neither: it is not a literal (§8.4.3.2.1:
  it references a data item, and the folded `FUNCTION LENGTH(item)` is that function, never "an integer literal"), and
  §15.2 4), 5) and 6) describe the item it returns without a usage. So `IF FUNCTION INTEGER(N) = "0007"`, `IF "0007" =
  FUNCTION ABS(N)`, `IF FUNCTION LENGTH(N) = "4"`, the same pairs as EVALUATE subject/object, SEARCH WHEN, PERFORM UNTIL
  and abbreviated combined relations, and the national forms, are refused with **COBOL2532** exactly as a COMP item is
  (no new code), through the SAME reader STRING and INSPECT ask (`IntrinsicArgumentRules.FunctionIsNotDisplayOrNational`,
  called by `RelationComparability.IsNumericIntegerOperand`); an index function (`FUNCTION MAX` over index items) opposite
  a character operand was already refused by §8.8.4.2.13 (COBOL2533). The measured reason it mattered: §8.8.4.2.5
  treats the integer operand "as though it were moved, according to the rules of the MOVE statement, to an elementary
  data item of the same length in terms of character positions as the number of digits in the integer", which needs the operand's digit count — a display item has one (its PICTURE),
  a function result has none the standard states — so `IF FUNCTION INTEGER(N) = "0007"` (N PIC 9(4) VALUE 7) compared
  the function's literal-form text (A.1 item 92) and answered not equal, where `IF N = "0007"` answers equal.
  **GnuCOBOL 3.2** also answers not equal there (and accepts a COMP item, which WiseOwl refuses, COBOL2532), so it is
  no precedent for the admission. Admitted still: a numeric or integer function against a NUMERIC operand (`IF FUNCTION
  INTEGER(N) = 7`, row 1), an alphanumeric or national function against a character operand (`FUNCTION UPPER-CASE(S) =
  "ABCD"`, §15.2 1) and 3)), and an integer display item or literal against a character operand. `--permissive` keeps the
  refused pair as COBOL2532's warning, the character comparison of the function's text, as for the other operands.
  **`SendingValueTemp.FunctionValuePic` is not a usage claim and no admission rule reads it.** The returned-value item's
  USAGE DISPLAY there is the implementor's representation (§15.4.1: *"the characteristics and representation of the
  returned value are defined by the implementor"*) that gives the nominal item its digit capacity for IN-ARITHMETIC-RANGE
  (A.1 item 92; `FUNCTION LENGTH` measures the temporary DISPLAY shows, kb/Work PB3951); the question "described … as usage display or national" is asked of the operand as written, through
  `IntrinsicSig.ImplicitUsageOf` (§15.2), and `DisplayOrNationalUsagePredicateDriftTests` pins that `RelationComparability`
  asks it and never reads a returned-value `PicInfo`. Witnessed by `conformance:cases/8.8.4.2-Simple-relation-conditions/pb3691_relation_function_operands`
  (the admitted pairs) and the `pb3691-*` refusals.
- **D-FRA — the record area of a file whose record is a dynamic-length item, a variable-length group or a pointer,
  and the record image such a record sends and receives** (2026-09-22; kb/Work PB981, row `GR-13.18.33.4-3`).
  §13.18.33.4 GR3 makes every level-1 entry of an FD or SD *"implicit redefinitions of the same area"*, and no rule
  forbids those records from being a dynamic-length item, a variable-length group (§8.5.1.12.1) or a level-1
  pointer (§13.18.60.3 SR14); §12.4.6.4.4 GR2 extends the same sharing to the files of a record-area SAME clause.
  The standard does not say where such an item lives — *"Dynamic-length elementary items may be physically located
  in memory within the record they are subordinate to, or they may be located elsewhere in the computer's memory"*
  (§8.5.1.10.3), its internal structure is implementor-defined (§8.5.1.10.2), and a pointer has no character image
  here (A.1 items 210/216) — but it does say how the item BEHAVES: *"a variable-length data item behaves in all
  respects as though it were in fact contiguous with its neighbors whenever a procedural operation is applied to a
  group containing it"* (§8.5.1.11.2). GnuCOBOL, IBM Enterprise COBOL and Micro Focus do not admit a dynamic-length
  item in the file section at all (IBM 6.4: WORKING-STORAGE, LOCAL-STORAGE and LINKAGE only), so there is no
  implementation to follow. **WiseOwl COBOL's determination:** (i) such a record is an OUT-OF-LINE record — it does not
  overlay the file's character record area, which the file's other records share as before; (ii) a READ or RETURN
  makes the CURRENT RECORD, at its own length, available in every out-of-line record of the area (and of the
  SAME-clause peers): a dynamic-length record takes it as its new content (§8.5.1.10.4), a variable-length group is
  decomposed left to right — each dynamic-length item takes as many characters as the record holds beyond the
  fixed material still to come, up to its maximum size, and the fixed members take their own positions (a
  dynamic-capacity table is never a member here: it "may be defined in any place, other than the file section",
  §8.5.1.9.1 3)) — and a pointer record is not reached (it has no character image, so its value is
  unchanged); (iii) a WRITE, REWRITE or RELEASE of an out-of-line record sends its contiguous image at its current
  extent — the variable-length group's members concatenated exactly as DISPLAY shows them (A.1 item 57), a
  dynamic-length record's content, a pointer record's zero-length image; (iv) the implicit RECORD clause
  (§13.18.43.4 GR5, *"defined by the implementor"*; A.1 item 147 in §7, for an FD and an SD entry alike) is **Format 2** when a record is variable-length — minimum with
  every dynamic item at zero length, maximum with each at its maximum size (GR8) — and Format 1 otherwise, as
  before; **an EXPLICIT Format 1 clause keeps the file FIXED** whatever its records hold (§13.18.43.4 GR6, "Format 1 is
  used to specify fixed-length records"; §9.1.6 makes the record type and size fixed file attributes every program
  using the file shares — kb/Work PB1562; the form such a record takes is (vi)), integer-1 being the file's record
  size and the area's width, which §13.18.43.3 SR3 keeps every description within; and SR3 / SR4 now SCREEN such a record — GR8 b)'s maximum for a dynamic-length item is its
  maximum size (§8.5.1.10.1: the smallest of its LIMIT, the largest integer its prefixed usage stores and the
  implementor maximum, A.1 item 62) and its minimum is zero (§8.5.4 item 4), so `RECORD CONTAINS 20` over an
  unbounded dynamic member is COBOL2010 (it used to be skipped, on the ground that GR8 had nothing to sum);
  (v) **a variable-length group record is sent WITH ITS EXTENT TABLE** (kb/Work PB1053) — each
  variable-length component's fixed-run offset and current length — because with two or more such components the
  contiguous image alone cannot be inverted (a record `"AA" "KEY" "CCCC"` and a record `"AAKEY" "CCC" "C"` are the
  same characters, and the fixed member between them would be read from the wrong ones). The table is implementor
  information "on the physical storage medium" beside the record — the §9.1.7.2 licence the record-length header
  already uses — and, like that header, it is never "reflected in the record area or the record size" (§12.4.5.11.4
  GR1): the record is still exactly the contiguous image of (iii). Every organization that FRAMES its records
  carries it (a RECORD VARYING record-sequential frame, every relative and indexed frame — `RecordFraming`), the
  sort store carries it from RELEASE (and the USING transfer) to RETURN (and the GIVING transfer), and a READ /
  RETURN hands it back beside the current record. The split in (ii) then uses the record's own table whenever the
  receiving group's components CORRESPOND to it — "Two dynamic-length elementary items correspond if they start
  at the same relative byte positions within their groups" (§8.5.1.12.2) — and the table describes the very
  characters received; each component takes exactly the characters it was written with, so every layout
  round-trips, however many variable-length members flank a fixed one or sit side by side. A record that carries
  no table — written through a character record or at a RECORD VARYING DEPENDING length other than its composed
  one, held in a LINE SEQUENTIAL file (a line is plain text with no frame: (x)), or received by a non-corresponding group — is split by the take step of (ii): exact for ONE
  variable-length member wherever it sits, the earlier member taking the excess with several. An in-place
  sequential REWRITE (§14.9.35.4 GR16 fixes the frame's size) replaces the frame's table with the new record's when
  it has as many components, and otherwise VOIDS it (every offset -1, which corresponds to no layout) rather than
  leave a table describing the replaced record. (vi) **a file of FIXED-length records carries a variable-length record
  in its FIXED FORM** (kb/Work PB1562; `CobolContiguousLayout.ToFixedForm`) — a file whose RECORD clause is an explicit
  Format 1 (§13.18.43.4 GR6) is plain blocks of integer-1 bytes with no frame, and §9.1.6 makes its record type and
  size attributes the SAME for a second program that describes the file as `RECORD CONTAINS 20` over `PIC X(20)`,
  which must read the same bytes. So (v)'s table has nowhere to live, and no control information that depends on one
  program's record description can be added to the physical record (§13.18.43.4 GR2 licenses control information
  "required by the operating environment", and the environment's requirement is a function of the file's type and
  size, not of a description the other program does not have). Each such record therefore occupies the ONE shape
  every record of the file shares: every dynamic-length member at the position it has when it holds its MAXIMUM size
  (its §8.5.1.10.1 maximum size — the LIMIT — which is the maximum §13.18.43.4 GR8 b) sums for the record, as PB1276 reads it, so
  that `A` limit 9, `KY` X(3), `C` limit 8 are bytes 1-9, 10-12 and 13-20),
  space padded, the remainder of the integer-1 bytes spaces; a READ takes each member back at that width and drops
  its trailing spaces, so a member that does not end in a space round-trips exactly. **The one loss is stated:** in
  a fixed-size field a trailing space is padding, never data (the same convention as a line sequential record,
  §14.9.51.4 GR21), so `"AB "` is written as `"AB"`'s bytes and reads back with length 2. The form is the same in
  every organization — sequential, relative and indexed (witnessed for each: `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb1562_variable_group_under_fixed_record_clause`, `…/pb1880_variable_group_under_fixed_record_clause_relative` and `…/pb1880_variable_group_under_fixed_record_clause_indexed`, which also pin the invalid-key, delete and start arms) — and an indexed RECORD KEY a dynamic member precedes is
  one plain window at its fixed-form offset, the key a second program names (§9.1.7.4: a key's number of components, length and relative positions "are fixed file attributes"); a REWRITE's record-name-1 size is the
  maximum layout (§13.18.43.4 GR13 — the number of bytes in the record — compared by §14.9.35.4 GR16), and a dynamic-length ELEMENTARY record is its content padded to integer-1 and read back
  without the padding. A file whose RECORD clause is Format 2 or 3, or is absent (the implied Format 2 of (iv)),
  keeps (v): its frames are variable-length records. **Rejected readings:** framing the Format 1 file as
  variable-length records with the extent table (the first PB1562 landing: a second program describing the file as
  `PIC X(20)` got OPEN '39' on a relative file and read the framing bytes as data on a sequential one); keeping the
  contiguous image and padding it (the table cannot be carried, and the split is lost — the original defect); a
  trailing-space-exact encoding (information-theoretically impossible in integer-1 bytes: 20 bytes cannot hold
  every length pair of two dynamic members and their content). **Rejected readings of the whole:** refusing the source (the
  previous staged-loud posture; no rule forbids it); treating the file's character bytes as the dynamic item's
  storage (the item's content would be bounded by the area and padded by it, contradicting §8.5.1.10.4's "the new
  value becomes the content of the item"); a length-prefixed record image FOR AN ITEM THAT NAMES NO STRUCTURE (the
  length field is the representation a DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause names, §8.5.1.10.2, and an item whose clause
  names none has not asked for it — a NAMED structure is given exactly that form in the record, D-DL3 — and for the
  unstructured item it would put the lengths INSIDE the record
  a character record of the same area, a RECORD VARYING DEPENDING item and a key position all read, where (v) keeps
  them in the frame); refusing at bind a record the take step cannot invert (legal source, and the physical form
  is the implementor's to choose); the take step alone for every record (the previous posture — PB1053 measured
  `A=[AAKEY] KY=[CCC] C=[C]` for the record written as `AA` / `KEY` / `CCCC`). **EXTERNAL** (kb/Work PB1026): §13.18.22.4 GR4 b)
  makes "the data contained in all record description entries" of an EXTERNAL file external, so an out-of-line
  record of such a file is run-unit storage of its own, shared by every describer — keyed by the FILE's
  externalized name (GR5) and the record's ordinal among the file's out-of-line records in declaration order,
  since GR5 externalizes no record name; a pointer-class record is carried the same way (§13.18.22.3 SR4 restricts
  the clause "specified for a data item", and here it is specified for the file). (A SORT/MERGE or indexed key that
  follows a variable-length member is D-KWV below.) **(vii) A WRITE, REWRITE or RELEASE under a SAME RECORD AREA
  clause makes the released record available in the other records of the area** (kb/Work PB1195; §14.9.51.4 GR4,
  §14.9.35.4 GR6, §14.9.32.4 GR3 — *"The logical record is also available as a record of other file-names
  referenced in the same SAME RECORD AREA clause ..., as well as the file associated with record-name-1"*), through
  the same two halves a READ uses: the shared CHARACTER area takes the record's image when the released record is
  itself out of line, and each OTHER out-of-line record of the area (`FileModel.OutOfLineRecordsOfArea`) takes the
  record at its released length (GR13) with its extent table — only after a SUCCESSFUL statement, and decided at
  compile time so a program with no out-of-line record in the area renders as before. The READ side is completed
  alike: a file whose every record is out of line has no character window of its own, and its READ now reaches the
  character window of a clause peer (`SequentialIoEmitter.EmitRecordAreaStore`). **(viii) A record holding an OCCURS DEPENDING table of VARIABLE-LENGTH elements** (kb/Work PB2497) — each occurrence holds a dynamic-length item, so §8.5.1.12.1 makes it a variable-length group — is a record type like any other: a WRITE, REWRITE or RELEASE sends the first K occurrences' current images, K being data-name-1's value at the start of the statement (the sending operand's count, §13.18.38.4 GR8 a for a data-name-1 outside the record, GR8 b for one inside it; when the file description has the VARYING phrase of the RECORD clause, GR9 has the program set it to the occurrences written), with the extent table of (v), which then describes exactly the components of those occurrences. The record's LENGTH cannot say how many occurrences it holds (the elements have no fixed width, and data-name-1 is data, not layout), so a READ or RETURN takes the count from, in order: **the record's own extent table** when it travelled and describes the record — the number of components it describes, each occurrence bringing the same number (`OdoTail.CountFrom`); **the maximum** for the fixed form of (vi), where every occurrence sits at its fixed-form position (the writer pads the occurrences it holds and the file's fixed length fills the rest with spaces, which is their fixed form); and otherwise **data-name-1**: the record is decomposed at the table's maximum — the receiving record area's maximum length, §13.18.38.4 GR8 b) — which places a data-name-1 the record holds itself (§13.18.38.3 SR20 puts it before the table: *"The data item defined by data-name-1 shall not occupy a byte position within the range of the first byte position defined by the data description entry containing the OCCURS clause and the last byte position defined by the record description entry containing that OCCURS clause"*), and then again at data-name-1's value, clamped to the table's bounds; a data-name-1 outside the record keeps its value from the start of the statement (GR8 a).
