- **PERFORM VARYING … AFTER under TEST BEFORE — the reset/augment ORDER (§14.9.28.4 GR13 e) 2; the ISO text and the
  NIST CCVS-85 corpus disagree)**: GR13 e) 2's true branch is ordered "a. the induction variable associated with the
  current condition is set to its initialization value", then "b. the condition to the left of the current condition
  becomes the current condition", then "c. the induction variable associated with the new current condition is
  incremented by its associated augment value". GR12 does item identification for the FROM operand "each time … is
  used in a setting or augmenting operation" and GR13's closing paragraph gives every such change "immediate effect",
  so an AFTER level whose FROM reads the level to its LEFT is reset from that level's **pre-augment** contents. For
  `PERFORM VARYING A FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL A > 3 AFTER B FROM A BY 1 UNTIL B > 3` the rule therefore runs the body
  **eight** times — (1,1)(1,2)(1,3)(2,1)(2,2)(2,3)(3,2)(3,3), leaving A=4 and B=3. **NIST NC201A PFM-TEST-F4-23
  ("ORDER OF INITIALISATION OF VARYING IDENTIFIERS", referenced to the 1985 text as `VI-114 6.20.4 GR10(d)1`) asserts
  SIX** — i.e. the opposite order, augment-then-reset. **Pinned choice: the ISO text governs, at EVERY edition.**
  Process rule 1 makes the standard the oracle and the CCVS corpus a regression net; `docs/VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE.md`
  records no change to §14.9.28 across 1985/2002/2014/2023, so there is no edition on which the CCVS order could be
  the conforming one, and an edition-gated split would have to be invented rather than cited. The rule text was
  verified against the canonical PDF page 718 (prose, no figure). NC201A's golden consequently records
  `FAIL* PFM-TEST-F4-23` with `COMPUTED= 8 / CORRECT = 6` and a `001 TEST(S) FAILED` footer — the ONE golden in
  `tests/nist/valid` that carries a CCVS failure; the allowance is declared `CCVS-DEFECT` in `tests/nist/corpus.tsv`
  and audited in both directions by `CorpusManifestTests.GoldensCarryingACcvsFailure_AreExactlyTheDeclaredCcvsDefects`.
  The TEST AFTER arm is unaffected and is **not** symmetric: GR13 c) 4 is the one sub-step of GR13 that states the
  increment BEFORE the reset, and that arm implements exactly it. Witnesses:
  `conformance:cases/14.9.28-PERFORM/pb436_varying_after_from_outer`; `SpecPinnedNistTests.NC201A_VaryingAfterFromOuterInductionVariable_RunsEightBodies`.
  (kb/Work PB436.)
- **Normal completion of a declarative — "a fatal exception occurs within the scope of the declarative" (§14.6.13.1.2 1),
  spec silent on three points)**: the rule makes a declarative that falls off its end "not complete normally" when a
  fatal exception occurs within its scope. **Pinned choices: (a) "occurs" is read as "is RAISED"** — checking for it is
  enabled (§14.6.13.1.1: with checking off nothing is set to exist, so nothing occurs); **(b) the scope is DYNAMIC and
  run-unit wide** — a fatal raised in a procedure the declarative PERFORMs or a program it CALLs is within it, and the
  mark reaches every open declarative; **(c) a RESUME that §14.9.33.4 GR1 made a CONTINUE marks only the open
  declaratives of ITS OWN program instance** ("specified in this … program"). The disposition after a declarative falls
  off its end is by FATALITY, not by how it completed, wherever a rule does not key on normal completion (§14.9.49.4
  GR13, GR7 b)/c), GR12 b)/c)), so only a USE procedure invoked while a format 1 SORT is active (§14.9.40.4 GR17,
  kb/Work PB1177) and the MERGE (§14.9.24.4 GR7, GR12) implicit transfers tell a not-normal fall-off from a normal one. **(d) A Format 4 (EXCEPTION OBJECT) declarative's not-normal fall-off is
  treated as normal**: §14.6.13.1.5 names only the normal case ("completes normally, execution continues as specified

  (a MERGE GIVING file whose implicit OPEN fails: a declarative that completes normally BYPASSES the file, one that

  TERMINATES the MERGE) and `unit:DeclarativeActivationRecordTests`.
  (kb/Work PB1122.)
- **An exception object converted to EC-OO-EXCEPTION is "propagated" (CALL / INVOKE NOT ON EXCEPTION) only when it is
  RAISED in the activator (§14.9.4.4 GR3 i), §14.6.13.1.5 items 1 and 4, spec silent on the pairing)**: GR3 i) runs the
  NOT ON EXCEPTION phrase unless "an exception condition is propagated from the called program". An object that a USE
  AFTER EXCEPTION OBJECT declarative of the activator takes IS raised there. An object no declarative takes becomes,
  by items 1 and 4, "as if EXCEPTION EC-OO-EXCEPTION were specified in the RAISING phrase", and a RAISING condition is
  raised in the activator only "if checking for that exception condition is enabled in the activating runtime element"
  (§14.9.18.4 GR1 b)). **Pinned choice: with EC-OO-EXCEPTION checking OFF in the activator nothing is raised, so the
  call completes normally and its NOT ON EXCEPTION phrase RUNS; with checking ON the condition is raised and the NOT
  ON EXCEPTION phrase does not run** — the reading the NAMED GOBACK … RAISING arm already follows (kb/Work PB606).
  The last exception status after an unraised conversion is left holding the exception object. Witnesses

  `conformance-test:OoSpineTests.GobackRaisingObject_NoF4_ActivatorUnchecked_RaisesNothing`;
  `conformance-test:FatalRaiseSelectionTests.ObjectPropagation_ActivatorChecked_NoHandler_TerminatesAbnormally`.

  of a global declarative" a CONTINUE. A global declarative may PERFORM a local declarative (§14.9.49.3 SR4), so the

  PROGRAM INSTANCE that declares the GLOBAL declarative**, the same test as §14.9.18.4 GR6's "specified in the same
  program" (the per-instance `__useActive[global ids]`). A RESUME in a program CALLed from a global declarative runs in

- **Exception-checking PERFORM — RESUME NEXT STATEMENT in a WHEN skips WHEN COMMON (§14.9.28.4 GR17/GR19, spec silent)**:
  GR17 passes control to imp-4 (WHEN COMMON) "at the completion of the execution of imperative-statement-2"; a RESUME

  taken. **Pinned choice: a WHEN that RESUMEs (NEXT STATEMENT) does NOT run WHEN COMMON.**
- **Exception-checking PERFORM — where control goes after WHEN OTHER's imperative-statement-3 (§14.9.28.4 GR18, a GENUINE
  STANDARD DEFECT: two consecutive sentences, two destinations)** (kb/Work PB438). GR18 prints, one after the other, "At the
  completion of the execution of imperative-statement-3, control is passed to the end of the PERFORM statement or, if WHEN COMMON
  is specified, to imperative-statement-4" and "At the completion of the execution of imperative-statement-3, control is passed
  as indicated in General rule 14.9.29 or, if WHEN COMMON is specified, to imperative-statement-4". Both are on the printed page
  (PDF page 719), so the duplication is the standard's, not the transcription's; the second sentence's "General rule 14.9.29"
  names a CLAUSE number (14.9.29 is the RAISE statement) where a general-rule number belongs. **Pinned reading: the second
  sentence, with its broken cross-reference read as General rule 20, exactly as GR17 and GR19 word the same hand-off.** After
  imperative-statement-3 (and imperative-statement-4 when WHEN COMMON is specified) GR20 decides: a NONFATAL condition resumes
  with the implicit CONTINUE immediately after the statement of imperative-statement-1 that raised it, so the rest of
  imperative-statement-1 still runs; a FATAL one proceeds as 14.6.13.1.3 (abnormal termination) unless a RESUME redirects it.
  *Why, from the text and not from the code:* (1) GR20 itself says "the processing in General rules 17, 18, and 19 is completed,
  return depends on whether the exception condition was fatal or nonfatal" - it names GR18, and that return would be vacuous for
  a WHEN OTHER whose first sentence had already sent control to the end of the PERFORM; (2) the first sentence cannot be the
  rule alone, because with WHEN COMMON both sentences hand control to imperative-statement-4 and GR19 then passes it "as
  indicated in General rule 20" - so a WHEN COMMON written beside a WHEN OTHER would turn "abandon imperative-statement-1" into
  "resume in place", and one WHEN OTHER whose destination depends on whether an unrelated phrase is present is no reading of GR18;
  (3) a named condition (GR17, returning by GR20) would otherwise resume in place where an unnamed one (WHEN OTHER) abandons imperative-statement-1, though GR14 enables both the same way and
  GR17 and GR18 select the same handler machinery. §14.9.28.4's own cross-clause statement, §14.6.13.1.4 item 2, describes only a
  PERFORM "that contains a WHEN phrase that specifies the exception-name" and says the WHEN phrase's statement "completes as
  specified in the rules for the PERFORM statement" - GR20; it is silent on WHEN OTHER, which GR18 supplies, and that silence is
  the one consideration the other way. This is not implementor latitude (CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence never starts: the ISO
  text controls, through GR20); the project's earlier scout note that "the first sentence already gives the correct destination"
  (`PHASE-13-remaining-waves-scout.md`) is superseded by this entry. Realized in one place: `ControlFlowEmitter.EmitMatcherArms`
  sends the WHEN OTHER arm through the same `__RunF3` return path (`EcEmitter.EmitRunF3`) as a named WHEN, so GR17, GR18 and GR19
  cannot drift. Witnesses: `PerformFormat3BehaviorTests.WhenOther_NonfatalWithoutResume_ContinuesInPlace`,
  `WhenOther_NonfatalWithCommon_RunsCommonThenContinues`, `WhenOther_Fatal_ThenTerminates` and
  `conformance:cases/14.9.28-PERFORM/pb438_f3_when_other_nonfatal_resumes_in_place`; the test that stood for GR18 before wrote
  RESUME NEXT STATEMENT inside the WHEN OTHER, which prints the same output under either reading.
- **D-F3S — the reach of an exception-checking PERFORM's WHEN phrase: dynamic within the activation, bounded by it
  (§14.9.28.4 GR1, GR17, GR20; §14.6.13.1.4 2); §9.1.12 1); the clauses word the scope three ways)** (kb/Work PB442).
  GR17 reads "during the execution of imperative-statement-1", §9.1.12 1) "an active PERFORM statement", §14.6.13.1.4
  2) "the executed statement is within imperative-statement-1", and GR1 puts in the range "all statements that are
  executed as the result of a transfer of control in the range", a CALLed program's included. **Pinned reading, which
  the standard's own propagation rules decide:** (a) **within one activation the reach is the PERFORM's dynamic
  range** — a condition raised in a paragraph PERFORMed (or reached by GO TO) from imperative-statement-1 selects the
  WHEN exactly as one written inside it, and GR20's "statement in imperative-statement-1 in which the exception
  condition occurred" is the statement that raised it, the one §14.9.33.4 GR2 a) 1. names for RESUME NEXT STATEMENT;
  (b) **it stops at the activation boundary** — an exception status indicator "exists for each function, method, or
  program" (§14.6.13.1.1), so a condition raised in a CALLed program, an activated function or an INVOKEd method is
  processed there (its own conditional phrase, its own exception-checking PERFORM, its own USE statements), and it
  reaches the activator only when propagated: GOBACK / EXIT … RAISING raises it "in the activating runtime element"
  (§14.9.18.4 GR1 b)), as does `>>PROPAGATE ON` (§14.6.13.1.3 6)), with the CALL or INVOKE as the statement it
  occurred in (§14.9.33.4 GR2 a) 2.) — and there the activator's WHEN selects it. Reading (b) is also the one the
  design recorded as the owner's default (`docs/CONDITIONS_EXCEPTIONS_DESIGN.md` D12 (d)). (c) **Enablement stays
  lexical and is a separate question**: GR14's implicit TURN is a directive "assumed before the first statement in
  imperative-statement-1", and a TURN enables checking for the statements "that follow in the compilation group"
  (§7.3.25.4 GR6), so a raise in a PERFORMed paragraph written outside the PERFORM is raised, and so reaches the WHEN,
  only where checking is enabled at that paragraph's text; an I-O statement there whose EC-I-O checking is off raises
  nothing, and §14.9.49.4 GR6 then runs its USE AFTER STANDARD EXCEPTION procedure. Realized by one mechanism: each WHEN
  frame carries the activation that pushed it, and the frame walk stops at the first frame of another activation
  (`ExceptionEngine.RunTopFrame`), so every activation mechanism is bounded by the run unit's one activation record.
  Witnesses `conformance:cases/14.9.28-PERFORM/pb442_f3_when_activation_scope` (the PERFORMed paragraph, a CALLed program holding an
  exception-checking PERFORM of its own, GOBACK … RAISING), `conformance:cases/9.1.12-Input-output-exception-processing/pb442_f3_when_method_scope` (an I-O
  raise in an INVOKEd method of a class holding such a PERFORM) and `conformance:cases/9.1.12-Input-output-exception-processing/pb442_f3_when_io_enablement`
  (reading (c): a READ in a PERFORMed paragraph written before, and after, a `>>TURN`).
- **Exception-checking PERFORM — the implicit POP ALL and the END-PERFORM line's reference format (§14.9.28.4 GR14, the
  spec states the order, not the line)**: "Immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase, there is an implicit POP ALL",
  and ALL includes SOURCE FORMAT (§7.3.22.4 GR2). A reference format is a property of a physical LINE (§6.5), so the
  op is a boundary between lines: **pinned choice: the restored format governs the line that holds END-PERFORM itself**
  (the phrase is text following the POP, and §7.3.24.3 1) makes a format govern "the source text … following the
  directive"), and the implicit PUSH takes effect after the line that ends imperative-statement-1. A handler may thus
  switch format and write END-PERFORM in the layout of the format it started in. Where the unrestored format makes that
  line unreadable, the front end finds the phrase in the physical text and verifies the guess by re-parsing (kb/Work
  PB1066; `DESIGN-frontend-grammar.md`).
- **SET SIZE OF — the storage-physically-unavailable EC-STORAGE-NOT-AVAIL leg (§14.9.39.4 GR38 third sentence)**:
  **implemented, not assumed away.** All three of GR37/GR38's outcomes are live and each sets the nonfatal
  EC-STORAGE-NOT-AVAIL under `>>TURN EC-STORAGE-NOT-AVAIL CHECKING ON`: a value that does not evaluate to a
  nonnegative number gives length 0 (GR37: a floating-point NaN is not a number, and −∞ is negative, so both take
  it — `2023/pb2647_set_size_not_finite`, kb/Work PB2647); a value above the item's §8.5.1.10.1 **maximum size**,
  +∞ included (an infinity is a number in ISO/IEC 60559), is clamped to that
  maximum (GR38 second sentence); and, when the host cannot hand over the storage that expansion needs, **the size
  is not changed** (GR38 third sentence) — an `OutOfMemoryException` at the growth site inside
  `CobolDynString.SetSize`, which returns the item unchanged instead of letting a framework exception escape into
  generated code. The condition is raised ONCE per statement: a request that already took the clamp leg has set it
  to exist. Goldens `2023/ec_storage_not_avail` (a LIMIT-phrase item) and `2023/pb463_dyn_implementor_maximum` (an
  item with none).
  ⚠ **This row used to pin the opposite** — "a dynamic-length elementary item is a managed .NET `System.String`,
  always allocatable within the runtime string limit, so the … branch is unreachable" — and that was a claim about
  code nobody had checked. It was false in both directions (kb/Work PB463): the item's maximum size was the LIMIT
  phrase with `-1` meaning "no phrase", the clamp SKIPPED that sentinel, and so an item written without a LIMIT had
  no bound at all — a SET SIZE request of 2³²+k silently wrapped to k, and one between `int.MaxValue` and 2³² threw
  a raw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` out of generated code. The maximum size is now computed by the one producer
  `CobolDynString.MaxSizeOf` for EVERY dynamic-length item (A.1 item 62 below), which makes the clamp the one
  path for an over-large request and the narrowing exact by construction rather than by inspection. The integer-2
  literal form is compile-time bounded by SR34 (`SetBinder.BindSetSize` over `SetLiteralAmount`, COBOL2113 —
  kb/Work PB458; the sentence stood here for a screen nobody had written until then), so its out-of-range
  cases are compile diagnostics, not this runtime EC.
- **SET SIZE OF — "truncated to the nearest integer" (§14.9.39.4 GR37 second sentence) is TRUNCATION TOWARD
  ZERO** (kb/Work PB464). "If arithmetic-expression-5 evaluates to a number that is not an integer, the result of
  arithmetic-expression-5 is truncated to the nearest integer" pairs two operations that differ: truncating 2.7
  discards the fraction (2), rounding it to the nearest integer selects 3. It is the standard's only use of the phrase
  (one occurrence in the whole document), so no sibling use calibrates it. **Determination: the fraction is
  discarded, 2.7 gives 2, a half does not round away from zero (2.5 gives 2), and 0.9 gives length 0 with no
  condition** — a nonnegative amount that is merely fractional raises nothing, because the only conditions GR37/GR38
  name are "not a nonnegative number" and "greater than the maximum size". **Why this and not the other:** the
  standard gives "truncation" a defined meaning of its own, the ROUNDED MODE IS TRUNCATION mode that every
  arithmetic statement without a ROUNDED phrase takes (§14.7.4.3 GR2), and defines that mode in the very idiom the SET SIZE rule
  uses: "rounded to the nearest value nearer to zero" (§14.7.4.3 GR10; §11.9.11.2 GR2 e) for the intermediate
  value). "Truncated to the nearest integer" is that idiom compressed — the nearest integer in the toward-zero
  direction. **Order of the tests:** the sign test (GR37 first sentence) and GR38's "evaluates to a number that is
  greater than the maximum size" are asked of the EVALUATED value, before the truncation, so −0.5 takes GR37's leg
  and 9.5 against a maximum size of 9 takes GR38's clamp and sets the condition (the length, 9, is the same either
  way); the truncation only chooses the length stored. **The amount is read in its own domain:**
  `CobolDynString.SetSize` has one overload per evaluation carrier (binary64, SDIDI, scaled `Int128`, unsigned-wide
  `UInt128`), and `SetEmitter.SetSizeCall` maps each `NumXCarrier` onto its own, so 2.99999999999999999 truncates to
  2 and not, through its binary64 image 3.0, to 3 — the same discipline CONTINUE AFTER already follows
  (`StatementEmitter.ContinueAfterCall`, kb/Work PB1529). Goldens `2023/pb464_set_size_fraction_truncates` (2.7, 2.2,
  2.5, 0.9, 8.9, the grow case, the 17-digit near-integer and the fractional amount above the maximum) and the
  refusal below 2023 `pb464-set-size-fraction-below-2023`.
- **EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE / EC-DATA-OVERFLOW applied to EVERY floating-point usage (§14.6.13.2 item 3 / §14.9.25.4
  GR6 d)4.a)**: the standard scopes these to a "standard floating-point usage" (the ISO/IEC 60559 FLOAT-BINARY-32/64/128
  and FLOAT-DECIMAL-16/34 forms — §13.18.60 item 19; FLOAT-SHORT/-LONG/-EXTENDED and COMP-1/COMP-2 have
  implementor-defined representation, §13.18.60 item 21, with implementor-specified exception conditions per
  §14.6.13.1). In the typed-native model EVERY floating-point usage is a native IEEE `float`/`double`, so **pinned
  choice: WiseOwl COBOL raises both ECs for all floating-point usages uniformly** — mandatory for the standard usages,
  an implementor determination (which the standard delegates) for FLOAT-SHORT/-LONG/-EXTENDED and COMP-1/COMP-2.
  EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE (fatal) fires when a NaN/±Infinity float sending operand is referenced (both the numeric-value and
  the string-image read paths) except in a class condition, a sign condition, a same-usage MOVE, or VALIDATE;
  EC-DATA-OVERFLOW (fatal) fires when a MOVE's algebraic value is farther from zero than the receiver's usage
  permits — §14.9.25.4 GR6 d)4.a verbatim: "If the algebraic value of the sending operand is farther from zero
  than is permitted by the usage specifications of the receiving data item, the EC-DATA-OVERFLOW exception
  condition is set to exist, and the content of the receiving data item is undefined." Both default OFF
  (byte-identical to a pre-slice build). Goldens `2023/ec_data_not_finite`, `2023/ec_data_overflow`,
  `2023/pb271_float_receiver_overflow`.
  ⛔ **THAT TEST IS ON THE ALGEBRAIC VALUE, WHICH MEANS IT MUST HOLD THE DECIMAL SENDER** (kb/Work PB271). It
  used to be inferred from an IEEE cast: a single-precision receiver asked whether a FINITE double had become
  ±Infinity, and a double receiver was a bare cast on the premise that "a double receiver cannot overflow from
  a finite double". Both premises assumed the sender reaching them was a finite double. A STANDARD-DECIMAL
  intermediate reaches ±9.999…E+6144 and collapses to ±Infinity in the conversion, so `MOVE 1.0E+400 TO` a
  FLOAT-BINARY-64 (or -32, or FLOAT-LONG) stored +Infinity and raised NOTHING, at every checking level — and
  owner decision D-B made that literal legal in the DEFAULT arithmetic mode, so the shape reached ordinary
  programs. The screen is now on the `CobolDec` itself, before the conversion.
  ⚠ **What a DEFAULT build does is unchanged and is its own determination:** checking is off by default
  (§14.6.13.1.1) and GR6 d)4.a makes the receiver's content undefined in the overflow case, so WiseOwl COBOL
  performs the ISO/IEC 60559 conversion and keeps its result — ±Infinity for an over-range value, zero for an
  under-range one, which is not this EC in either direction. `2023/pb271_float_receiver_overflow` pins that
  half; `2023/ec_data_overflow` pins the checking-ON half.
  **Documented gaps:** (a) a floating-point NUMERIC-EDITED MOVE receiver is not covered by the EC-DATA-OVERFLOW seam
  (§14.9.25.4 GR4 also names it) — deferred until floating-point numeric-edited PICTUREs are supported; (b) a
  multi-receiver `ADD/SUBTRACT … TO/FROM` with several float receivers under EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE checking can
  half-commit earlier receivers before a later non-finite receiver's read raises — only observable under USE-F3 +
  RESUME NEXT STATEMENT, where a fatal-EC-interrupted statement already leaves undefined results (§14.6.13.1.3), a
  precise follow-on.
- **The counter registers' declared description — LINAGE-COUNTER, PAGE-COUNTER, LINE-COUNTER** (§8.4.3.14.4 GR1 /
  §8.4.3.15.4 GR1; NOT an Annex A.1 item — the registers' size and usage are simply unspecified, so this is a pinned
  implementor choice, kb/Work R26, PB1153, PB1746): all three registers are **unsigned integers** per their GRs, so
  `LOWEST-ALGEBRAIC` of any of them is **0** and `SMALLEST-ALGEBRAIC` is **1**. **LINAGE-COUNTER**: GR1 ties its
  size to "the page size specified in the LINAGE clause" — `HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC(LINAGE-COUNTER OF f)` folds to the
  LINAGE literal's value directly (`LINAGE IS 66 LINES` → 66); with a data-name operand the page size is set at
  run time, and the compile-time capacity is the MAXIMUM that operand can specify, its PICTURE's all-nines.
  **PAGE-COUNTER / LINE-COUNTER**: the standard gives them no size and no usage, so CLAUDE.md rule 1's latitude order
  (ISO → GnuCOBOL → IBM / Micro Focus) takes **GnuCOBOL's, surveyed with cobc 3.2.0 (kb/Work PB1746)**: `build_report`
  (cobc/tree.c) declares both `CB_USAGE_UNSIGNED_INT`, an **unsigned 32-bit binary integer**. WiseOwl COBOL's
  description is therefore the shape of `BINARY-LONG UNSIGNED` (`PicInfo.ReportCounterItem`, the one statement of it;
  the `OCCURS DYNAMIC` CAPACITY register is the same shape): capacity **4,294,967,295**, `HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC` folds to
  it, the character image is **10 digits**, and `FUNCTION LENGTH` / `BYTE-LENGTH` are **4**. The survey, against
  cobc 3.2.0: `DISPLAY PAGE-COUNTER` prints `0000000001` (10 digits); `MOVE PAGE-COUNTER TO` a `PIC X(4)` item stores
  `0000`; `MOVE 5000000000 TO PAGE-COUNTER` leaves `0705032704` (the 32-bit value) and `ADD 1` to 4,294,967,295 leaves
  `0000000000`; `STRING` refuses the register ("must be USAGE DISPLAY or NATIONAL"); `FUNCTION LENGTH(PAGE-COUNTER)`
  and `PERFORM PAGE-COUNTER TIMES` are syntax errors there (WiseOwl COBOL admits both, §15.50.3 r1 and
  §8.4.3.15.3 SR1 — the standard decides what GnuCOBOL does not take); `HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC(PAGE-COUNTER)` prints
  `294967295` and a `MOVE` of the register to `PIC X(14)` shows 9 digits (cobc's attribute digit count for
  `UNSIGNED-INT` is 9 where its DISPLAY prints 10 — a GnuCOBOL inconsistency WiseOwl COBOL does not copy: the
  description is one 10-digit item, as `BINARY-LONG UNSIGNED` is here). **Runtime:** the report engine stores the
  counters in a `long` and reduces every assignment modulo `CobolReport.CounterModulus` (2³²), so a page advance
  past the capacity, or `MOVE 5000000000 TO PAGE-COUNTER`, wraps exactly as cobc's does;
  `ReportCounterDescriptionDriftTests` pins the runtime modulus to the compiler's description.
  (§8.5.2.12 items 3/4/5 make the registers category-numeric DATA ITEMS, which is what admits them to the
  §15.43.3/§15.58.3/§15.83.3 r1 argument position at all.) **The same capacity answers the §8.8.4.4.4 GR3 g)/m)
  class conditions** (kb/Work PB1401): `LINAGE-COUNTER OF f IS FARTHEST-FROM-ZERO` is true exactly when the
  register holds the capacity `HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC` folds to, and `IS NEAREST-TO-ZERO` when it holds 1 — one
  statement of the description (`AlgebraicRanges.DescribeCounter`) serves every surface, so they cannot disagree. A
  register `IS NUMERIC` is always true (GR3 n) 1. c.: its content is a value the register holds), and
  `IS IN-ARITHMETIC-RANGE` is always true (every capacity lies inside every mode's intermediate).
  **The registers' implicit DESCRIPTION** (kb/Work PB1153, PB1199, PB1318, PB1746): **LINAGE-COUNTER** is the unsigned
  integer item **`PIC 9(d) USAGE DISPLAY`**, d the digits of the page size (`LINAGE IS 20 LINES` → `9(2)`; a
  data-name page size → its PICTURE's digits) — GR1 gives it a size in digits, which is a DISPLAY item's; GnuCOBOL's
  `UNSIGNED-INT` LINAGE-COUNTER (a 10-digit image whatever the page size) contradicts that GR, so the standard decides.
  **PAGE-COUNTER / LINE-COUNTER** are the unsigned 32-bit binary integer above. Consequences: `DISPLAY LINAGE-COUNTER`
  after `LINAGE IS 20 LINES`, OPEN OUTPUT and one WRITE shows `02`; `DISPLAY PAGE-COUNTER` after INITIATE shows
  `0000000001`; `MOVE LINE-COUNTER TO` a `PIC X(4)` item stores the leftmost four of the 10 digits (§14.9.25.4 GR6 a));
  every register is an integer for `PERFORM … TIMES`. **Usage screens follow the description:** STRING's identifiers
  "shall be described … as usage display or national" (§14.9.43.3 SR1) and §8.8.4.2.5's numeric integer operand "shall
  be … of usage display or national", so **LINAGE-COUNTER takes a STRING sender and an alphanumeric relation, and
  PAGE-COUNTER / LINE-COUNTER are refused in both** (COBOL1626, COBOL2532), because those rules read the item's usage
  "described implicitly or explicitly" and the registers' implicit usage is binary. **§14.9.25.3 SR8 does not reach the
  registers**: it keys on "a data item described with usage binary-char, binary-short, binary-long, or binary-double" —
  a USAGE clause a program wrote — and §8.4.3.15.4 GR1 gives the counters no usage clause, only the category numeric and
  the unsigned-integer shape the implementor pins above; so `MOVE PAGE-COUNTER TO` an alphanumeric item is judged by
  Table 16's numeric-integer row alone and is legal (and cobc accepts it), whereas `MOVE` of a declared
  `BINARY-LONG UNSIGNED` item to one is COBOL0819 (`MoveTable16.ShapeRefusal`, kb/Work PB1746 review R1-1);
  UNSTRING's identifiers "shall reference data items of category alphanumeric or national" (§14.9.48.3 SR2), which a
  numeric register is not, so **all three registers are refused as an UNSTRING sender or delimiter** (COBOL1651;
  before PB1746 the statement compiled and split the register's image). `AlgebraicRanges.CounterRegisterDigits` /
  `CounterRegisterByteLength` / `CounterRegisterIsUsageDisplay` / `IsCounterRegister` are the one reader every consumer
  asks (`OperandText.AsString`, `IntrinsicResultType.IsIntegerOperand`, `RelationComparability`, the STRING / UNSTRING
  binder, the LENGTH / BYTE-LENGTH folds). Witnesses: `conformance:cases/8.4.3.14-LINAGE-COUNTER/pb1153_counter_register_character_image`,
  `conformance:cases/_unassigned/algebraic_counter_registers`, `wiseowl:cases/8.4.3.15-Report-counters/pb1746_report_counter_description`,
  `wiseowl:cases/8.4.3.15-Report-counters/pb1746_page_counter_advance_wraps` and the `pb1746-*` refusals.
- **Floating-point value → fixed-point receiver: the conversion manner (§14.6.8.2 r1/r2/r4; kb/Work PB77,
  2026-08-18).** §14.6.8.2 r2 leaves "the manner in which the value is converted to a fixed-point value" to the
  implementor for a FLOAT-SHORT/-LONG/-EXTENDED sending item, and r1 treats an intermediate or standard-float
  sender "as if it had been converted to a fixed-point value"; WiseOwl COBOL's FLOAT-LONG and FLOAT-BINARY-64 are the
  same `double` (item 22), and a §15.4.1 float-family returned value IS a binary64 (item 92), so ONE conversion
  serves all three: **the binary64's EXACT algebraic value, aligned by decimal point and truncated (or rounded,
  under a ROUNDED phrase) at the receiver's scale — at every magnitude** (`CobolFloat.TryExactScaled`; kb/Work
  PB623, 2026-09-05, which ANSWERED kb/Work PB90's three-way choice). A double is ±man·2^exp exactly and therefore
  always a terminating decimal, so "the value" is never in doubt: a COMP-2 holding 8.2 holds
  8.199999999999999289457264239899814128875732421875 and moves **8.1** into PIC 9V9; one holding 1.15 moves 1.14
  into PIC 9V99; one holding 0.1 moves .1000000000000000055 into PIC V9(19); **past the carrier the same expansion
  keeps supplying the low-order digits** (`CobolFloat.LowOrderDigits` — a COMP-2 holding 1.0E+40, whose exact value
  is 10000000000000000303786028427003666890752, moves 90752 into PIC 9(5); an in-carrier 1.0E+25 moves its exact
  69664) — never a saturation sentinel, which has no capacity check downstream in a MOVE and used to store ITS low
  digits (884105727 / 03715). A non-finite value reaching a fixed-point landing with checking off (NaN, ±Infinity —
  EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE at the sending read under checking, §14.6.13.2 item 3) lands ZERO. The CHECKED landing (an
  arithmetic store under ON SIZE ERROR / EC-SIZE checking) RAISES the size error past the carrier
  (`CobolFloat.ToScaled` and the checked `FromDouble` landing throw `CobolSizeError`
  EC-SIZE-TRUNCATION, item 179, kb/Work PB2967): it used to saturate and leave the receiver's capacity check to
  notice, which a 16-byte COMP-5 receiver cannot — its capacity is the whole carrier, so `COMPUTE R = FUNCTION
  VARIANCE(A, 1)` (about 2.5E+57) stored 2^127 - 1 and took NOT ON SIZE ERROR.
  **Why the exact expansion and not the shortest-round-trip decimal (PB90's option b) — the choice is not free.**
  r2's latitude covers a FLOAT-SHORT/-LONG/-EXTENDED sending ITEM only; r1 governs a standard-float item and an
  intermediate with no latitude at all ("the value is treated as if it had been converted to a fixed-point value"),
  and `COMPUTE r = <any float>` lands through an intermediate. So a different manner for COMP-2 would make
  `MOVE c2 TO r` disagree with `COMPUTE r = c2` for one value — the split PB623 exists to remove. The same
  expansion answers the ROUNDED MODE PROHIBITED question (§14.7.4.3 item 7): the double nearest 0.1 is NOT
  representable in one fraction digit, so `COMPUTE r ROUNDED MODE IS PROHIBITED = <COMP-2 0.1>` raises
  EC-SIZE-TRUNCATION and leaves the receiver unchanged, where a binary64 product test called it exact
  (`0.1 * 10.0` is exactly 1.0). Pinned by `2002|2014|2023/pb623_float_landing_exact`,
  `2023/pb77_move_past_the_carrier` and `CarrierLandingFormTests`.
- **Floating-point data item → standard-decimal intermediate data item: the conversion mechanism (§8.8.1.5.1;
  kb/Work PB1606, 2026-10-23).** §8.8.1.5.1 leaves "the mechanisms for conversion of data items described with a usage
  of float-short, float-long, or float-extended into standard-decimal intermediate data items" to the implementor, and
  §8.8.1.5.2 r1 says an operand that "cannot be expressed exactly in an SDIDI" is "rounded according to the rules in
  11.9.11"; NOTE 3 of that clause names the binary value as the case. WiseOwl COBOL, under ARITHMETIC IS
  STANDARD-DECIMAL (and STANDARD, which shares the engine): **a floating-point data item enters the SDIDI as its
  binary64's EXACT algebraic value — a double is always a terminating decimal, so "the operand value" is never in doubt —
  rounded ONCE to the SDIDI's 34 significant digits under the program's INTERMEDIATE ROUNDING mode**
  (`CobolDec.FromBinary64`; default NEAREST-AWAY-FROM-ZERO): a COMP-2 holding 0.1 enters as
  0.1000000000000000055511151231257827, a value of 34 digits or fewer (0.5, every integer below 10^34) enters
  unchanged, and under INTERMEDIATE ROUNDING IS PROHIBITED an inexact one is EC-SIZE-TRUNCATION (§11.9.11.2 r3 d).
  The same ONE conversion serves every position: an operand beside an operator, a **float item that is the whole
  expression** (`COMPUTE R = F`, `ADD F GIVING R` — before, these landed natively while `F + 0` converted through
  the shortest round-trip decimal, so one statement mode held two float conversions and `COMPUTE D = F` stored
  `.1000000000000000055` where `COMPUTE D = F + 0` stored `.1000000000000000000`), a relation operand (§8.8.4.2.4)
  and an intrinsic function's argument. It is also the value a MOVE or a native COMPUTE reads (the item above), so
  `COMPUTE D = F`, `COMPUTE D = F + 0` and `MOVE F TO D` agree. The choice follows the precedence of CLAUDE.md rule 1:
  the standard leaves the mechanism open, GnuCOBOL 3.2.0 has no standard-decimal mode and no precedent to follow
  (measured 2026-10-23: it stores a COMP-2 0.1 as 0.099999999999999991673327315311 by `COMPUTE D = F`, `COMPUTE D = F + 0`
  and `MOVE F TO D` alike, and says `F = 0.1` is true), so the choice is the implementor's, made for
  agreement with the PB623 float-landing determination above. **Consequences, stated so they are not found by surprise:** (a) a
  float item holding a decimal fraction is not equal to that decimal under standard-decimal arithmetic — `IF F = 0.1`
  with F = 0.1 (COMP-2) is false and `IF F > 0.1` true (native arithmetic compares both as binary64 and says equal);
  (b) landing into a binary float receiver follows the implied TRUNCATION (§14.7.4.3 r2 and r10): the SDIDI
  0.1000000000000000055511151231257827 is below the double 0.1, so `COMPUTE F2 = F1` and `COMPUTE F2 = F1 + 0` both
  store the double below it, 0.09999999999999999 (the same with ROUNDED, where the nearest double is chosen and
  F2 is 0.1); (c) a COMP-2 holding 1.0E+30 is 1000000000000000019884624838656, and that is what standard-decimal
  arithmetic divides; (d) a function whose argument is a float item and whose value is the SDIDI shows the SDIDI's digits
  (`DISPLAY FUNCTION ABS (F)` with F = 0.1 is `0.1000000000000000055511151231257827`, with F = 0.5 it is `0.5` — a value
  of 34 digits or fewer is held at the fewest places that carry it). **An implementor-defined APPROXIMATION is not a data item** — a §15.4.1 function's returned
  value (SIN, SQRT, a non-integer power) has no content beyond its 17th digit that means
  anything — and enters through `CobolDec.FromApproximation`, the shortest round-trip decimal, so `FUNCTION SIN (1)`
  is 0.8414709848078965 and not the 34 digits of the double's binary expansion. The floating-point numeric-edited
  receiver reads a binary64 sender the same exact way (`CobolDec.FromBinary64ToOdd`, a 38-digit round-to-odd
  significand, because the mask's rounding is the receiver's): `COMPUTE FE ROUNDED MODE IS PROHIBITED = F` with F =
  0.1 is the size error (the value is not representable in the mask), as it already was for a fixed-point
  receiver. That exact reading is for a floating-point DATA ITEM alone: a fixed-point sender (a BY CONTENT argument at
  §14.2.3 GR9's activation boundary, `MoveSending.ExactValue`) is edited by its own decimal digits, and an
  approximation (a function's returned value) by its shortest round-trip decimal (`CobolDec.FromApproximation`), so
  neither shows the binary noise of a double (0.3 is `+3.0000000000000000E-01`, never `+2.9999999999999998E-01`).
  The binary64 intermediate a multi-receiver MOVE freezes such a value into (§14.9.25.4 GR1's "temp", "an intermediate
  result item provided by the implementor") is read as the approximation it holds (`DataItem.HoldsApproximation`), so
  `MOVE FUNCTION PI TO W1 W2` edits what `MOVE FUNCTION PI TO W3` does.
  Witnesses: `conformance:cases/14.6.8.4-Floating-point-numeric-edited-receiving-data/pb1606_fixed_sender_float_edited_formal`, `conformance:cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb370_move_function_value_digits`, `conformance:cases/8.8.1.5.2-Standard-decimal-intermediate-data-item/pb1606_float_item_conversion`
  (every position, the rounding modes, the negative and the huge), `15.60.4-Returned-value-rule/arith_standard`,
  `_unassigned/pb3017_sdidi_divide_remainder_beyond_the_int128_carrier`, `CobolDecBinary64ConversionTests`.
- **The editing sign of a value the store truncates to zero (§13.18.40.5 5), §14.9.25.4 6), §14.6.8.2 5); kb/Work
  PB3664, owner 2026-10-24).** An editing sign control symbol (the fixed `+`, `-`, `CR`, `DB`, the floating `+` and
  `-`, and a PICTURE EDITING character-1 under a FOR phrase) shows the Table 8/Table 9 column for "the value of the data
  item", whose first column is "Positive or zero value", and the data item holds the value AFTER alignment and
  truncation (§14.6.8.2 5), for a numeric-edited receiver: "further alignment, zero fill or truncation, and transfer of
  digits take place as described in the general rules and editing rules in 13.18.40"). So `MOVE -0.001 TO PIC -9.99`
  stores zero and prints ` 0.00` (`+0.00` for `PIC +9.99`, `0.00  ` for `PIC 9.99CR`), and `MOVE -100 TO PIC -99`, whose
  high-order digit truncates, prints ` 00` (§8.8.4.2.4 says the same of comparisons: "Zero is considered a unique value
  regardless of the sign"). The sign is decided
  ONCE per edit, from the digit string the receiver holds (`CobolEdit.Render`), and the format-2 locale editor
  (`CobolLocaleEdit.Format`, GR18 `+`) reads the same stored value. GnuCOBOL 3.2 agrees for the edited receiver
  (`cob_move_display_to_edited` guards every `-`, CR and DB with `neg && !is_zero`, `is_zero` taken from the digits that
  land in the picture). A signed NUMERIC receiver is the adjacent case and already agrees with the same choice
  through the carrier, which has no negative zero: `MOVE -100 TO PIC S9(2)` stores `+00` (GnuCOBOL stores a
  negative-signed zero there and DISPLAYs `+00`, the representation difference documented with the sign-encoding
  determinations at Annex A.1 items 177 and 178).
  Witnesses: `conformance:cases/13.18.40.5-Editing-rules/pb3664_edited_sign_stored_value`, `CobolEditStoredSignTests`.
- **Floating-point numeric-edited receiver — the overflow, underflow, size-error and incompatible-content
  dispositions (§14.9.25.4 GR6 item 4; §14.7.5 items 3/4; §14.6.13.2 rule 4; kb/Work PB66, 2026-08-18).**
  §14.9.25.4 GR6 item 4a says a MOVE whose sending value is farther from zero than the picture permits sets
  EC-DATA-OVERFLOW "and the content of the receiving data item is undefined"; item 4b says a value nearer to zero
  than permitted "is treated as zero". WiseOwl COBOL: **under EC-DATA-OVERFLOW checking the exception is fatal at the
  store and the receiver is UNCHANGED** (a USE declarative may RESUME); **with checking off the receiver holds the
  pinned SATURATED image** — the all-nines significand at the maximum exponent with the value's sign (`9.99E+9`
  for `PIC 9.99E+9`; `-9.99999E+99` for a negative value into `-9.9(5)E+99`) — never arbitrary content; underflow
  stores the §13.18.40.5 rule-8 zero image (all digit positions zero, both signs positive; BLANK WHEN ZERO applies)
  with no exception. An ARITHMETIC statement's floating-point numeric-edited resultant takes the size error
  condition in BOTH directions (§14.7.5 items 3 and 4 — the receiver unchanged, EC-SIZE-TRUNCATION) under ON SIZE
  ERROR / EC-SIZE checking; without either, the MOVE disposition above. The receiver's ROUNDED [MODE] rounds the
  SIGNIFICAND at its last digit (§14.7.4.3 rules 3 to 10; a MOVE truncates, §14.6.8.4 rule 2): a carry out of
  the last digit renormalizes and the exponent is tested after it (`9.996` into `+9.99E+99` is `+1.00E+01`,
  §14.7.5 item 3 "after … any applicable rounding specifications"), and ROUNDED MODE IS PROHIBITED with a
  significand that cannot be held exactly is the size error condition with the receiver unchanged (§14.7.4.3
  rule 7; unchecked, it lands truncated like every unchecked store, A.1 item 70). Pinned by
  `2023/pb2638_float_edited_rounded_store`. A de-editing MOVE from content that is not a possible
  result of editing into the picture (§14.6.13.2 rule 4 — the result "is undefined") raises EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE
  (fatal) under checking with the receiver unchanged; with checking off the image is read digit-for-digit
  (a non-digit position contributes zero, a missing exponent sign reads positive). Pinned by
  `2023/pb66_float_edited_picture` and `2023/pb66_float_edited_algebraic_and_checking`. The value of
  `HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC` / `LOWEST-ALGEBRAIC` of such an item is that same saturated extreme (§15.43.4 / §15.58.4 r2 —
  zero for LOWEST of an unsigned picture); an entry whose extreme would fail IN-ARITHMETIC-RANGE for the arithmetic
  mode in effect (binary64 natively — an exponent of three or four digits — or decimal128 under STANDARD-DECIMAL)
  is COBOL1660 at the function reference (§15.43.4 r1 / §15.58.4 r1).

- **DIVIDE ... GIVING identifier-3 REMAINDER identifier-4 with a floating-point identifier-3: the subsidiary quotient
  (§14.9.12.4 6) c), 7); kb/Work PB2923, 2026-10-26).** §14.9.12.3 2) admits any elementary numeric or numeric-edited
  identifier-3, so a floating-point numeric-edited item (`PIC +9.99E+99`) and a binary floating-point item (COMP-1/-2,
  FLOAT-SHORT/-LONG/-EXTENDED, FLOAT-BINARY-32/-64; the wider FLOAT-BINARY-128 and FLOAT-DECIMAL-16/-34 are refused at the data description, COBOL1564, A.3 items 17 and 19) are legal; the PB2923 adjudication found that IBM Enterprise COBOL and Micro Focus reject them,
  and that GnuCOBOL 3.2 has no floating-point numeric-edited item, so the ISO text decides. 6) c) gives the subsidiary quotient
  "the same number of digits and the same decimal point location as" identifier-3, which a floating-point item does not
  have as a pair, so WiseOwl COBOL takes the phrase to mean **identifier-3's own shape under truncation**: for a
  floating-point numeric-edited item, the quotient truncated to the significand's digit count, normalized as in §14.6.8.4
  1), at the quotient's own exponent (1/3000 into `+9.99E+99` has the subsidiary quotient 3.33E-04, so
  `DIVIDE 1 BY 3000 GIVING FE REMAINDER R` leaves R = 1 - 3.33E-04 * 3000 = 0.001; a value past the exponent's range is the
  pinned saturated content and one nearer to zero than the item holds is zero, exactly as the item's store leaves them);
  for a binary floating-point item, the quotient truncated toward zero into the item's format (binary32 for COMP-1,
  FLOAT-SHORT and FLOAT-BINARY-32, binary64 for every other; a quotient the format holds is itself), which is the landing
  the item's own store performs under implied TRUNCATION (§14.7.4.3 10), `FloatResultant`, so the two cannot disagree. The remainder is GR7's
  expression over that subsidiary quotient: the SDIDI expression under STANDARD-DECIMAL, the binary64 one natively
  (A.1 item 123). **The stored quotient is never derived from the subsidiary quotient** (§14.9.12.4 6) b) forms and stores it,
  as §14.9.12.4 5) b) does for the statement without REMAINDER): it keeps all its digits and its exponent, rounded by the
  receiver's mode. The same adjudication measured GnuCOBOL 3.2 truncating a FLOAT-LONG subsidiary quotient at a fixed 17
  fraction digits (FLOAT-SHORT 8), so for a quotient below 1E-17 it leaves the whole dividend as the remainder; this
  compiler does not follow it because that scale is not identifier-3's. Pinned by `pb2923_divide_remainder_float_edited`, `pb2923_divide_remainder_float_usage`
  and their STANDARD-DECIMAL twins.

- **Incompatible data in a fixed-point numeric sending operand (§14.6.13.2 rule 2).** The standard makes the
  RESULT OF THE REFERENCE undefined — "the result of the reference is undefined and an EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE
  exception condition is set to exist" — so what happens to the value is an implementor determination.
  WiseOwl COBOL: **under EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE checking the exception is fatal at the SENDING READ** (a USE declarative
  may RESUME, in which case the raising statement is abandoned and every receiver it had not yet stored is
  unchanged); **with checking off the content decodes DETERMINISTICALLY** — a zoned position that is not a digit
  contributes no digit and an all-non-digit image is zero, a packed nibble above 9 contributes none, a binary
  window is read as its two's-complement value — never arbitrary content and never a trap. Only a numeric leaf
  whose storage is a character window (a REDEFINES view, or a leaf under a group used as a whole operand —
  §14.9.25.4 GR4 fills such a group "without consideration for the individual elementary or group items") can hold such
  content at all; a native-carrier leaf can only hold digits, so `IS NUMERIC` on one is the constant true
  (§8.8.4.4.4 GR3 n)1). The test itself is the standard's own — "would evaluate to false in a numeric class
  condition" — evaluated over the item's byte representation: n)1.a's digits-plus-declared-sign for DISPLAY,
  n)1.c's "valid representation for the usage" for packed (decimal nibbles, and a sign nibble where the usage
  reserves one), and n)1.c's picture-range half for binary, where a `COMP-5` / `BINARY-*` item's range is its
  CONTAINER rather than a picture (§13.18.60.4 GR12 — "the implementor may allow a wider range" — for `BINARY-*`, item 208 for `COMP-5`). For a
  CORRESPONDING statement the condition is deferred and set once after every implied statement completes, as
  §14.7.6's last paragraph requires. Pinned by `2002/pb230_incompatible_sending_sweep`,
  `2023/pb230_incompatible_corresponding` and `85/pb230_class_numeric_image`.

- **Incompatible dynamic-length and dynamic-capacity data (§14.6.13.2 rules 5 and 6; kb/Work PB1118).** A
  dynamic-length item IS a managed string, so its internal format — a length and that many characters — is always
  correctly formed, and the one way its content can disagree with "the corresponding DYNAMIC LENGTH clause" is to be
  longer than THAT clause's maximum size (§8.5.1.10.1; the minimum length is zero). Content stored through a
  description always agrees with it, because every store truncates to the maximum (§8.5.1.10.4), so a disagreement
  arises only when the item is READ through a description other than the one that stored it: a LINKAGE formal
  (§14.2.3 GR8 — "as if the formal parameter occupies the same storage area as the argument") and a member of a shared
  cell-backed area such as an EXTERNAL record described in two programs. **Those reads, and only those, ask the
  question** (`CobolDynString.Agree`): under EC-DATA-INCOMPATIBLE checking content past the maximum is the fatal
  condition at the sending reference (a USE declarative may RESUME, abandoning the statement); with checking off the
  content is read as it is, whole. A receiving-only reference is not a reference to the content (rule 5's closing
  paragraph, NOTE 2) and asks nothing. **Rule 6 is unreachable by construction:** the implementor's internal format of
  a dynamic-capacity table is one `CobolDynTable` object, and every one a program reads was constructed from that
  program's own OCCURS clause or recreated into it by a variable-length group transfer at the receiving description
  (§14.6.9.2); no storage form shares one across descriptions (an EXTERNAL record holding one is COBOL0899, a file
  record cannot hold one, §8.5.1.9.1 3), and a LINKAGE one crosses through that same recreation).
  `DynamicCapacityAgreementDriftTests` pins those construction paths. Pinned by `2014/pb1118_dyn_length_agreement`.

- **USAGE BIT — alignment and representation of data (§13.18.60.4 GR5 · §8.5.1.6.3).** Annex A.1 has NO item for USAGE BIT — it runs 208 (COMPUTATIONAL, GR6) straight to 209 (DISPLAY, GR7), and §8.5.1.6.3 is cross-referenced only by item 195 (SYNCHRONIZED) — so this determination is recorded here under §4.2.6 rather than in the A.1 register, where it sat under item 209’s number until 2026-09-03. A `USAGE BIT` item **occupies bits**, as GR5 requires. Bits per character position is **8** — §8.1.2 leaves it implementor-specified, and 8 is what makes it agree with DISPLAY's one byte per character position. Alignment follows §8.5.1.6.3 exactly: a bit item immediately following an elementary bit item **of the same level** takes the next bit position (they share a byte); any other bit item starts at the first bit of the next available byte; implicit filler advances to the next item's natural boundary and fills a trailing partial byte to an integral number of characters, and §15.50.4 r5 counts that filler. A bit group that follows a same-level bit item begins in the middle of a byte, and the byte boundaries inside it (every "first bit position of the first available byte", and an ALIGNED subject, §13.18.1.4 GR1) are boundaries of the **record**, not of the group (kb/Work PB3158). A bit group whose first item begins on a byte boundary (it is ALIGNED, say) begins on that boundary too — §8.5.1.6.3 "the alignment of the start of a group item and the alignment of the first item within that group, when the first item is a bit data item, are at the same bit position in storage" — so the filler before it belongs to the enclosing group, and a REDEFINES subject of that shape requires a byte boundary (§13.18.44.3 SR15; kb/Work PB3167). **A TABLE whose element is a bit group holding such a member** (an ALIGNED member, §13.18.1.4 GR1, or any member §8.5.1.6.3 puts at "the first bit position of the first available byte") lays out differently at each bit position it could begin at, and §13.18.1.4 GR2 ("An ALIGNED clause specified for a multiple-occurrence data item applies to each occurrence of that item") puts the ALIGNED member of EVERY occurrence on a byte of the record. **WiseOwl COBOL's DETERMINATION** (kb/Work PB3167; the owner may overturn it): the occurrences of such a table are a whole number of bytes apart — the element's width rounded up to a byte — so every occurrence begins at the same bit position within a byte as the first and is laid out exactly as the first, and implicit filler bits between occurrences (none after the last, §8.5.1.6.3 generates filler only "for the next item") make up the difference. This keeps the one length §13.18.38.4 7) gives "the subject of the entry", and it is the per-occurrence filler §13.18.55.4 8) b) states for a synchronized table ("generated for each occurrence of those data items") and IBM Enterprise COBOL's slack bytes between the occurrences of a synchronized table; GnuCOBOL 3.2 rejects GROUP-USAGE BIT ("reserved word, but isn't supported"), so it offers no reading. Rejected: laying each occurrence at the next bit position after the last, which makes the first occurrence's members sit at other offsets and its length differ from the later ones'. So `05 BA PIC 1(2) USAGE BIT. 05 SUB GROUP-USAGE BIT OCCURS 3. 10 SA PIC 1 USAGE BIT. 10 TA PIC 1(5) USAGE BIT ALIGNED.` puts SUB(k) at bit 2 + 16(k−1) and TA(k) at bit 8 + 16(k−1), and the group is 45 positions; a table whose element holds no such member is packed bit by bit, unchanged. In a record image a bit run is **packed high-order bit first** — §8.5.1.6.3 numbers positions from "the first bit position" — followed by its implicit filler bits. **The implicit filler is STORAGE of its group** (kb/Work PB3564): §8.5.1.6.3 describes the bits that advance alignment to the next item's boundary and the bits that complete the last byte of a record group — and, through §13.18.1.4 GR2, the bits between the occurrences of an ALIGNED table — "implicitly ... as a filler elementary bit data item", so a group MOVE (§14.9.25.4 GR4: an alphanumeric move, no conversion), a READ, a MOVE of m boolean positions to a bit group (§13.18.29.4 GR1b: its filler positions are part of m) and a group VALUE (§13.18.63.4 GR5: the group area is initialized without regard to the items in it) write those positions, and the next DISPLAY, comparison, MOVE or WRITE of the group reads them back: `MOVE "AB" TO G1` over `05 G1-B PIC 1 USAGE BIT. 05 G1-X PIC X.` displays `AB`. Their initial state is zero (§13.18.63), an elementary store to a neighbouring member never changes them, and INITIALIZE without the FILLER phrase leaves them alone and INITIALIZE ... WITH FILLER makes them receivers (§14.9.20.4 5) a) 2.: implicit FILLER items). The record-struct lane holds each in a hidden string field of the group's struct (`BitLayout.FillersOf` is the one list, `PhysicalModel` declares the fields, `GroupImageCodec` packs and unpacks them); a REDEFINES class, an EXTERNAL or BASED record and a LINKAGE area hold the bits in the shared bytes themselves, so both lanes read a group alike. **The three shapes registered as kb/Work PB3598, as determined.** (1) *A run that holds an OCCURS DEPENDING table.* Its tail is measured at the table's maximum count, and a stored field holds the positions past the maximum extent, which no occurrence owns. That filler is data of the group at every count: it is moved with the characters it lies in, by an ordinary group's receiving store (a group with no dynamic-length item or dynamic-capacity table is a fixed-length group, §8.5.1.12.1, so its move is an alphanumeric move of whole characters, §14.9.25.4 GR4) and by a variable-length group's, which moves it as one of "each character position that is not occupied by a corresponding table" (§14.9.25.4 GR9 a: an OCCURS DEPENDING table is no corresponding table, §8.5.1.12.2 "Two tables correspond if at least one of them is a dynamic-capacity table", so every character position moves; `OdoTail.KeepUnused`). The bits that end the current extent's last character at a count BELOW the maximum are not filler: §8.5.1.6.3 generates the filler after "the last data item in a record", which is the table at its maximum, so those bits are the first unused occurrence's, whose content "is undefined" (§13.18.38.4 7)) and which §13.18.38.4 8) a) leaves out of the operation. The two receiving stores differ there only where the standard leaves the content undefined, which is implementor latitude (§13.18.38.4 7), 8) a)), and both conform: an ordinary group's alphanumeric move writes whole characters (the sender's bits), a variable-length group's store keeps the receiver's bits of the unused occurrences, the choice made since kb/Work PB3030 (`_unassigned/pb3030_bit_odo_run_continuation`; the bits spelled for T(4) and T(2) in `pb3598_odo_bit_run_tail_variable_group` are that choice, not the standard's, and only the filler bits are bound by §14.9.25.4 GR9 a)). INITIALIZE ... WITH FILLER therefore resets the stored positions beyond the maximum extent and no in-range bit (a depending item inside the group makes the group a receiver at its maximum length, §13.18.38.4 8) b); outside it the unused occurrences are not used). Witnesses `conformance:cases/14.9.25-MOVE/pb3598_odo_bit_run_tail_travels_with_the_group` (ordinary groups) and `pb3598_odo_bit_run_tail_variable_group` (variable-length and cell-backed groups). (2) *The padding of an element of a dynamic-capacity bit table* (`05 T PIC 1(3) USAGE BIT OCCURS DYNAMIC`) is **not an implicit filler item and is not stored; it reads zero in every image** (DETERMINATION, the owner may overturn it). Each element is out-of-line storage of its own ("table data items are not required to be contiguous in physical memory. The size, location, and time of physical allocation of a dynamic-capacity table are implementor-defined", §8.5.1.9.1 3)), so §8.5.1.6.3's filler "to advance alignment to a required natural boundary for the next item within that group" has no next item to advance to; the five bits that round a 3-bit element up to its character are the rounding of its length (§15.14.4 4), which an elementary item at level 77 or 01 has too and which §8.5.1.6.3's NOTE says generates no filler); and a group MOVE carries the table's elements, never those bits ("Correspondingly numbered elements are moved according to the rules of the MOVE statement", §14.6.9.2), so no statement but INITIALIZE ... WITH FILLER could name them, and it names only the implicit filler items. Witness `unit:DynamicBitElementPadTests`. (3) *A strongly-typed group carried as a leaf vector* carries its filler after its members (see below). The filler of a strongly-typed group that crosses an activation boundary as its leaf vector travels with the vector (after its members), and the tail of a run in a record-struct group that holds the canonical of a Tier-B REDEFINES class is stored beside the class's backing (the canonical's own bits are the backing's, the tail follows them in the group's layout; kb/Work PB3597). INITIALIZE ... WITH FILLER resets the filler everywhere it is stored — in a REDEFINES class, an EXTERNAL or BASED record and a LINKAGE area through one bit item per gap of the shared bytes, in the record-struct lane through its hidden field — with ZEROES or a REPLACING BOOLEAN sender; the bits between the occurrences of an ALIGNED table are n - 1 items in both lanes, and the sender reaches each gap on its own (kb/Work PB3597). ⚠ The item's VALUE CARRIER is a `'0'`/`'1'` string, which is not observable to a COBOL program and is not a conformance claim; what is claimed is the SIZE, ALIGNMENT and IMAGE above. A boolean item with **no** USAGE clause is a different case: §13.18.60.3 SR13(b) implies DISPLAY and GR7 makes it one alphanumeric character per boolean position. **A FILE's record area follows the same image** (§9.1.2: the record area is storage; kb/Work PB680): a `USAGE BIT` record, elementary or a bit leaf in an alphanumeric group, is sent and received as its PACKED bytes — `ceil(bits / 8)` characters, the trailing filler bits as the record group holds them (zero until a move writes them; §13.18.43.4 GR4 makes the value of the filler bits that complete the last byte of a logical record undefined, so a file written by another program may leave anything there, which a READ stores and a WRITE sends back) — by every I-O verb (sequential, line sequential, relative and indexed WRITE / REWRITE / READ, `WRITE FROM` / `READ INTO`, SORT / MERGE `USING` / `GIVING` and `RELEASE` / `RETURN`), never as its `'0'`/`'1'` carrier. Witnesses: `conformance:cases/13.18.60-USAGE/pb680_bit_record_area_file_io` (sequential, relative, indexed and SORT/MERGE, read back through a second connector whose record is `PIC X`), `pb680_bit_record_area_line_sequential` (LINE SEQUENTIAL, 2023), `pb680_bit_record_area_file_exceptions` (the I-O statuses 04, 10, 35, 41, 42, 46, 47, 48 and the USE declarative on such a file) and the negative `pb680-bit-record-area-below-2002`.

- **D-SIGN1 — which subordinate items a group's SIGN clause reaches (§13.18.52.4 GR1; kb/Work PB493).** GR1 applies
  the clause "for each numeric item subordinate to the group to which it applies", narrowed only by "The SIGN clause
  applies only to numeric items whose picture character-string contains the symbol 'S'", and names no usage. But
  GR5 and GR6 place the sign on a DIGIT or CHARACTER position, which a binary, packed-decimal or floating-point item
  does not have, and §13.18.52.3 SR2 states the usage pair of the item a clause is written on: "The usage of an
  elementary item for which the SIGN clause is specified shall be display or national". **Determination:** an
  inherited clause reaches a signed numeric item of usage display or national, and a signed item of any other usage
  keeps its own representation (`01 G SIGN IS LEADING SEPARATE. 05 A PIC S9(4) COMP.` leaves A two bytes): the
  standard's own sign positions decide it, so the CLAUDE.md rule 1 precedence never reaches an implementation
  survey. (COBOL-85 instead refuses that group, D-SIGN2.) ONE rule decides it for every route by which an item acquires a clause it did not write
  (`DataBinder.WithInheritedSign`): a data division group (`InheritSignClauses`), the §13.18.49.4 GR5 SAME AS
  ancestor transform, and a REPORT GROUP description entry that is a group, whose clause reaches its printable items
  through the report entry's description (`DataBinder.EnclosingReportItem`; GR2 and GR3 precedence included).
  Witnessed by `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb493_report_group_sign_inherited` and
  `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb536_code_set_group_sign`.

- **D-SIGN2 — the COBOL-85 group SIGN subject (kb/Work PB1319; VCR row 7.40).** ANSI X3.23-1985, as the vendor
  manuals transcribe it, admits a group SIGN clause only on "a group item containing at least one such numeric data
  description entry" (one whose PICTURE contains the character S), and requires "The numeric data description entries
  to which the SIGN clause applies" to be USAGE DISPLAY. The 2023 §13.18.52.3 keeps neither restriction. At `--std 85`
  each is refused with COBOL0900 through its construct row (`sign-group-unsigned-subordinates-2002`,
  `sign-group-nondisplay-subordinate-2002`; `DataBinder.GateGroupSignSubordinates`); at 2002 and later the 2023
  rules and D-SIGN1 apply. The 2002 edge of the first restriction is QUOTED (ISO/IEC 1989:2002 Annex F.2 item 124:
  "A sign clause may be specified on any group item. Formerly, the group had to contain at least one numeric item.");
  the second is DERIVED and stated in the VCR row so it can be overturned. A subordinate that writes its own SIGN clause is outside the group's reach (§13.18.52.4
  GR2/GR3), so `01 G SIGN LEADING SEPARATE. 05 C PIC S9(3) COMP SIGN TRAILING.` is refused for C's own clause
  (§13.18.52.3 SR2, COBOL2422), never twice. Witnessed by `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb1319_sign_group_subjects_2002`,
  `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb1319-sign-group-unsigned-85` and `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb1319-sign-group-comp-85`.
  **The report arm (kb/Work PB3683).** A report group description entry's SIGN clause is narrower at 85 in two ways,
  both QUOTED from ISO/IEC 1989:2002 Annex F.2 item 123 ("The SEPARATE phrase is no longer required in a report
  description entry and the SIGN clause may be specified at the group level"): the clause needs SEPARATE CHARACTER, and
  it is written on an elementary entry only. Each is refused at `--std 85` with COBOL0900 through its construct row
  (`report-sign-without-separate-2002`, `report-group-sign-2002`; `DataBinder.ScreenReportSignClauses`, once per
  written entry); at 2002 and later §13.18.52.3 SR1 and §13.18.52.4 GR5 apply. Witnessed by
  `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb3683_report_sign_2002`, `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb3683-report-sign-without-separate-85`
  and `conformance:cases/13.18.52-SIGN/pb3683-report-group-sign-85`.

- **NUMVAL-F — a space may not SPLIT the exponent's `n` (§15.69.3 r1/r5 · §15.95.4 r1 b) 1; kb/Work PB256).**
  §15.69.3 r5 says "Leading and trailing spaces in argument-1 are ignored. Embedded spaces in argument-1 are
  ignored **except** between the first numeric digit and the last digit that precedes a letter 'E'" — i.e. its
  except-clause names only the SIGNIFICAND. Read as "elide the space and JOIN the digit runs on either side",
  that would make `"1E+1 2345"` a five-digit exponent and §15.95.4 r1 b) 5 would want the position of its fifth
  digit (9). **WiseOwl COBOL's determination is the other reading: "ignored" means the space CONTRIBUTES NOTHING
  where the format admits one, never that the runs on either side join — so an interior space ends `n` exactly
  as it ends the significand, and `FUNCTION TEST-NUMVAL-F("1E+1 2345")` is 6.** Two grounds agree. (a) §15.69.3
  r1's figure — verified on the printed page 898, not only in the transcription — draws `n` as ONE contiguous
  metavariable ("n is one, two, three, or four digits representing the exponent") with `[ space-string ]` only
  before and after it; nothing admits a space inside it, and the space in `"1E+1 2345"` is therefore the legal
  trailing space-string with `'2'` the first character in error. (b) §15.95.4 r1 b) 1 governs the case directly
  and is UNQUALIFIED as to which run — "if one or more spaces are embedded within a string of numeric
  characters, the returned value is the position of the first non-space character following the spaces" — where
  sub-notes 2, 3 and 4 of the same list each say "of the significand" explicitly; the drafters distinguished
  inside one list, so sub-note 1 reaches the exponent's digit string too. Consequences, all measured:
  `"1E+ 1234"` and `"1E+1234 "` conform (0), sub-note 5 fires only on a CONTIGUOUS fifth digit (`"1E+12345"`
  → 8), and the significand keeps its own answer (`"0 1E+2"` → 3, the standard's own example). Implemented at
  the one exponent loop in `CobolIntrinsics.Exact.cs#NvfScan`; pinned by
  `conformance:cases/15.95.4-Returned-value-rule/pb256_test_numval_f_spaces`.

- **NUMVAL-F — the exponent's sign is REQUIRED, and a text without it is refused, not read (§15.69.3 r1 · §15.3 r14 ·
  A.1 item 90; kb/Work PB3952).** §15.69.3 r1's figure puts the exponent's `+`/`-` in braces (a required choice, unlike
  the bracketed optional leading sign), so `"1.5E2"` and `"1.5e2"` do not conform. GnuCOBOL's NUMVAL-F is lenient and reads
  `"1.5E2"` as 150; the standard is silent on no part of it (the rule speaks), so CLAUDE.md rule 1's GnuCOBOL tier does not
  apply, and the function is not made lenient. `FUNCTION TEST-NUMVAL-F("1.5E2")` is 5 (the digit where the sign belongs),
  and a NUMVAL-F reference with that argument sets EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION; with checking off its result is A.1 item 90's zero
  value of the numeric type (0), in every receiver and every channel (one `CobolIntrinsics.Exact.cs#NvfScan` serves the
  value twins and TEST-NUMVAL-F). Pinned by `conformance:cases/15.69.3-Argument-rules/pb3952_numval_f_exponent_sign_required`.

- **D-TFD1 — TEST-FORMATTED-DATETIME with an argument-2 SHORTER than the format answers
  `FUNCTION LENGTH(argument-2) + 1` (§15.92.4 r1; kb/Work PB255).** The shape is reachable — §15.92.3 places no
  size rule on argument-2 and the compiler applies none — and §15.92.4 r1 is silent on it: it answers with "the
  ordinal character position at which the first error in argument-2 was detected", and when the data simply runs
  out there is no character IN ERROR to point at. **WiseOwl COBOL returns the position one past the last character.**
  Two grounds. (a) The rule's own words are about the position *at which the error was **detected***, not the
  position *of the character in error* — the wording §15.93.4 r1 b) uses for the other case ("the position of
  the first character in error"), so the drafters distinguished the two inside one family and this clause takes
  the detection reading. (b) §15.93.4 r1 c) is the standard's OWN answer for exactly this shape in the sibling
  TEST- function — an argument that "contains valid characters but is incomplete" returns
  `(FUNCTION LENGTH (argument-1) + 1)` (`cite.py --check 15.93.4 "(FUNCTION LENGTH (argument-1) + 1)"` → OK,
  rule 1) — so adopting it keeps ONE answer across the two TEST- functions instead of two conventions for one
  situation. ⚠ §15.93.4 r1 c) is cited as a CONVENTION the standard already chose for this shape, never as the
  governing rule for this function. Implemented at the three `pos >= data.Length` exits of the one analyzer,
  `CobolDate.cs#Analyze`; pinned by `conformance:cases/15.92.4-Returned-value-rules/pb255_test_formatted_datetime_bounds`.

- **D-TFD2 — the date/time format literals are case-SENSITIVE, so the §15.92.4 NOTE's own program does not
  compile (§15.3.1.2; kb/Work PB255).** §15.3.1.2 is normative about case — "four **uppercase** 'Y' characters
  representing the year subfield; two **uppercase** 'M' characters …" (`cite.py --check 15.3.1.2 "four uppercase"`
  → OK) — while §15.92.4's NOTE writes `FUNCTION TEST-FORMATTED-DATETIME ("yyyymmdd", A-DATE)` in lowercase. A
  NOTE is not normative, so **WiseOwl COBOL follows §15.3.1.2 and rejects a lowercase format**: `CobolDate.Tokenize`
  matches uppercase only and `DateTimeFormatGrammar` holds uppercase literals, so the reference draws the
  bind-time format-kind diagnostic. Recorded because every fixture in the corpus silently spells the NOTE's
  examples in UPPERCASE, and an unwritten substitution reads as agreement with the NOTE.

- **D-CORR66 — which data items are "in" a level-66 THROUGH alias for the CORRESPONDING phrase, and how they
  are qualified (§14.7.6 rule 1 over §13.18.45.4 GR2; kb/Work PB966).** Admission is not the latitude: §14.9.25.3
  SR12 asks only that the MOVE CORRESPONDING operands "specify group data items" (`cite.py --check 14.9.25.3
  "Identifier-3 and identifier-4 shall specify group data items and shall not be reference-modified."` → OK,
  rule 12), and GR2 makes a THROUGH alias exactly that (`--check 13.18.45.4 "When the THROUGH phrase is
  specified, data-name-1 defines an alphanumeric group item that includes all elementary items"` → OK, rule 2),
  so the standard controls and the alias is admitted on either side. ADD and SUBTRACT CORRESPONDING still refuse
  it, and the no-THROUGH form too, because their SR6 says "shall not be described with level-number 66".
  **The latitude is rule 1's qualifiers.** Rule 1 pairs items with "the same data-name and the same qualifiers, if
  any, up to, but not including, D1 and D2" (`--check 14.7.6` → OK, rule 1), and the alias is in no included
  item's qualifier chain: those items are subordinate to the renamed record, not to the alias. **WiseOwl COBOL reads
  GR2's own words: the alias includes ELEMENTARY items and no groups, so each included item stands directly in the
  alias with no qualifier between.** It corresponds by data-name alone with an item at the first level of the
  other operand. A name the alias includes twice falls to rule 6, and rules 4 and 5 still exclude an included
  item under an OCCURS or REDEFINES entry inside the window, as they would under a group subordinate to D1. The
  rejected reading treats the record's intermediate groups inside the window as qualifiers, but GR2 does not
  include them in the alias. No model implementation offers a reading to follow: the owner's precedence (ISO,
  then GnuCOBOL, then IBM or Micro Focus) reaches them only where the standard is silent, and IBM Enterprise
  COBOL and Micro Focus are understood to refuse a level-66 CORRESPONDING operand outright. That was not measured
  here (the implementer host has no GnuCOBOL install). Implemented at `CorrespondingBinder.cs#CorrMembers` over
  `RenamesInfo.IncludedElementaryItems`, and pinned by `conformance:cases/14.7.6-CORRESPONDING/pb966_move_corresponding_through_alias`.

- **D-CORRFILLER — an item under a FILLER group corresponds (§14.7.6 rules 1 and 5; kb/Work PB229).** Rule 1
  excludes the data item that is itself "implicitly or explicitly described with the keyword FILLER" and pairs items
  with "the same data-name and the same qualifiers, if any, up to, but not including, D1 and D2" (`cite.py --check
  14.7.6` → OK, rule 1). The qualifiers are names: "Qualification is the specification of superordinate names from
  the hierarchy to which a user-defined name belongs. The superordinate names are called qualifiers" (`--check
  8.4.2.2.1` → OK), and a FILLER group has none to give (`--check 13.18.20.4 "Under no circumstances shall a FILLER
  item be referred to explicitly."` → OK, rule 1). So an item subordinate to a FILLER group has the qualifiers it
  would have beside that group, and **WiseOwl COBOL pairs it with a namesake standing there on the other side**, for
  MOVE, ADD and SUBTRACT CORRESPONDING alike. Rule 5 is where the standard names the intermediate groups that cut
  their subordinates off, "when the group item contains an OCCURS or REDEFINES clause" (`--check 14.7.6` → OK,
  rule 5), so a FILLER group carrying either clause still excludes its whole subtree. The standard controls here,
  so the owner's precedence (ISO, then GnuCOBOL, then IBM or Micro Focus) never reaches the model implementations;
  GnuCOBOL, which matches CORRESPONDING members by name one level at a time, is understood to skip a FILLER group's
  subtree, which this reading departs from (not measured: the implementer host has no GnuCOBOL install). The rejected
  reading, which this compiler held until PB229 on "the legacy/NIST-proven" behavior and no clause, cut off every
  FILLER group's subtree and silently skipped the pair. The same reading already governed rule 6's uniqueness count,
  which stands a FILLER group's subordinates at the group's level (kb/Work PB1111). Implemented at
  `CorrespondingBinder.cs#CorrMembers`, pinned by `conformance:cases/14.7.6-CORRESPONDING/pb229_corresponding_filler_group_rule4`.

- **D-RW1 — reserved words added for nonstandard extensions (§4.2.10; kb/Work PB655).** §4.2.10: "An
  implementation that introduces additional reserved words as nonstandard extensions conforms to this Working
  Draft International Standard, even though the additional reserved words may prevent translation of some
  conforming compilation groups", and "Documentation associated with an implementation … shall specify any
  reserved words added for nonstandard extensions" (`cite.py --check 4.2.10 "shall specify any reserved words
  added for nonstandard extensions"` → OK). This is that specification. Every OTHER keyword the lexer tokenizes is
  a legal user-defined word wherever ISO §8.9 leaves it free (reservation-gated per edition) and, for a §8.10
  context-sensitive word, everywhere outside its context — `CobolWordsDriftTests` proves that join empty. The
  words below are reserved at EVERY edition although ISO reserves none of them, following GnuCOBOL (the model
  implementation for implementor latitude), because each spells a vendor construct this compiler recognizes:
  **COMP-1, COMP-2, COMP-3, COMP-4, COMP-5, COMPUTATIONAL-1, COMPUTATIONAL-2, COMPUTATIONAL-3,
  COMPUTATIONAL-4, COMPUTATIONAL-5, END-JSON, END-XML, ENTRY, JSON, XML**. Each is a reserved word of GnuCOBOL 3.2
  (`cobc/reserved.c`, no context test). CHANNEL, END-INVOKE, END-MERGE, END-METHOD, END-SORT, GENERIC, PACKED and
  REMARKS were on this list until 2026-09-29 and are NOT reserved: ISO §8.9 does not reserve them, GnuCOBOL 3.2
  has no entry (REMARKS: a context test normal code never meets), so they are user-defined words and the vendor
  constructs they spell are recognized by position (owner: follow ISO) — except CHANNEL, whose vendor SPECIAL-NAMES entry `CHANNEL integer IS mnemonic-name` (and its `RESERVE integer [CHANNELS]` twin) no ISO format prints and nothing implements, so it is refused as a syntax error and CHANNEL is a user word everywhere (kb/Work PB2727), and END-INVOKE, END-SORT and
  END-MERGE, which spell NO construct at all: Table 12 (§14.5.1) gives INVOKE, SORT and MERGE no explicit scope
  terminator (`cite.py --check 14.5.1 "Statement names are identified in Table 12"` → OK; §14.9.23.2's INVOKE format
  ends at `[ RETURNING identifier-4 ]`), so `INVOKE … END-INVOKE`, `SORT … END-SORT` and `MERGE … END-MERGE` are
  not recognized — the word is an ordinary user word in the position after the statement (a syntax error after
  INVOKE, an undefined GIVING file after SORT/MERGE) — and none of the three has a lexer token (kb/Work PB758,
  decision R58 for END-INVOKE and the same ISO text for the other two; negatives
  `pb758-invoke-end-invoke-after-returning`, `pb758-invoke-end-invoke-after-using-returning`,
  `pb758-sort-end-sort-is-not-a-terminator` and `pb758-merge-end-merge-is-not-a-terminator`). The single source is
  `tests/version-matrix/cobol-words.json` `extensionReserved`; `CobolWordsDriftTests` fails when this list, that array and the lexer disagree,
  and `NonstandardExtensionRegisterDriftTests` fails when it and the `ReservedWords` of the §3.2 register's rows disagree
  (each word is reserved on the account of one extension row).
  ⚠ DETERMINATION (owner may overturn): reserving them keeps the vendor forms recognizable by name; the rejected
  reading — admitting them as user words at every edition — would make each vendor construct ambiguous with a
  data reference in every operand list.

- **D-RW2 — METHOD is reserved at COBOL-2002 and COBOL-2014 and is a user-defined word at COBOL-2023 (§4.2.8, §8.9;
  kb/Work PB2623).** §4.2.8: "An implementation shall recognize as reserved words all the COBOL reserved words
  specified in 8.9, Reserved words" (`cite.py --check 4.2.8 "shall recognize as reserved words all the COBOL reserved
  words specified in 8.9"` → OK). The printed 2023 §8.9 list runs MERGE, MESSAGE-TAG, METHOD-ID, MINUS, MODE (PDF page
  236, printed page 206; `cite.py --check 8.9 "METHOD-ID"` → OK) and has no METHOD, and §8.10 lists none either. An
  earlier generator revision added METHOD to the 2023 set as an "OCR omission"; rendering the page refutes that, so
  the line is gone and METHOD follows every other 2002/2014 word the 2023 list dropped (POSITION, COBOL, …): reserved
  at 2002 and 2014, a user-defined word at 85 (no OO) and at 2023. The standard still SPELLS METHOD in the END METHOD
  marker (§10.7.2; `cite.py --check 10.7.2 "METHOD, and INTERFACE are underlined"` → OK) and in EXIT METHOD (`cite.py --check E.2 "EXIT METHOD statement"` → OK; the 2002 and 2014 statement,
  removed at 2023); those keyword positions read the word whether or not the program also declares a data item of that
  name (`methodKeyword`, generated into `CobolWords.g4` from the row's `keywordWhereFree` determination in `cobol-words.json`, the rule MESSAGE, MULTIPLE and ORDER share; kb/Work PB3794). ⚠ DETERMINATION (owner may overturn): the standard's own text decides — a
  word its list does not reserve is not reserved (§4.2.8, §8.3.2.1 rule 1) — so the alternative, treating the
  omission as a typo and keeping METHOD reserved at 2023, would be an added reserved word that §4.2.10 3) obliges this
  document to list, and would refuse a program the standard permits. Pinned by `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2623_method_is_a_user_word_at_2023`,
  `negative/pb2623-method-reserved-at-2002-2014` and `MethodUserWordTests`.

- **D-RW3 — the COBOL-85, 2002 and 2014 reservation flags, and how they meet the removed-construct rows (kb/Work
  PB656).** §8.9 decides the 2023 flags only; the repository holds no 1985, 2002 or 2014 text, so CLAUDE.md rule 1's
  precedence gives the earlier editions' flags to GnuCOBOL: its per-standard word lists (`scripts/gen-reserved-words.ps1`,
  facts only) and, for a facility's edition edges, its 3.2 dialect files `cobol2002.conf` / `cobol2014.conf`. ISO
  Annex E.2 item 25 ("The following reserved words have been added", `cite.py --check E.2 "The following reserved words
  have been added"` → OK) speaks about one edge only, because E.1 lists "the substantive changes between the previous
  COBOL standard and this" one (`cite.py --check E.1 "substantive changes between the previous COBOL standard and
  this"` → OK): its 16 words were user-defined at 2014, which the generator ASSERTS of the 2014 list, and it says
