GR7 e)'s implementor-defined execution of a non-COBOL method therefore never occurs. **The standard class BASE is no exception** (kb/Work PB2985): §16.2's NOTE ("The standard class BASE need not be implemented in COBOL", cite.py OK 16.2) permits the implementation language, and the runtime's BASE / `__FACTORY_BASE` are C#, but the class "shall be described with an IMPLEMENTS clause that references the interface defined here" (§16.2) — COBOL text whose New and FactoryObject carry an ACTIVE-CLASS returning item — so WiseOwl COBOL treats New and FactoryObject as COBOL methods of that interface: §14.9.23.4 GR7 c) governs them through a universal object reference exactly as it governs a user method of the same interface (the same ACTIVE-CLASS returning item, `CobolObject.CheckActiveClassReturning`), and the observable behavior does not depend on the language the class happens to be written in. The standard class has no source to carry a checking directive, so "checking enabled in the activated method" is read as always enabled (`BASE.__CobolInvoke` passes true): the exception condition is then set exactly when the activating runtime element checks for it. COBOL-2002, 2014 and 2023 (COBOL-85 has no INVOKE). How a REPOSITORY class specifier that names no definition of the compilation group is resolved is open under kb/Work PB1086. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_invoke_dotnet_member_universal`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1-invoke-dotnet-class-new`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1-invoke-dotnet-member-typed`; `conformance:cases/14.8.3.3-Elementary-items/pb2985_active_class_returning_universal_invocation` |
| DOC-A.1-104 | **I-O status — the value placed when more than one value applies**, §9.1.13.1, required — A.1 says the internal procedure need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway so that a program can rely on the value it tests | **Exactly one I-O status value is placed per execution of an input-output statement, and the choice is fixed, never timing-dependent.** (1) **An unsuccessful value always wins over a successful one**: a successful-completion warning ('0x') never displaces a status that begins with another digit (`FileRegistry.NoRewindPhraseEffect` tests the first digit). (2) **Among unsuccessful values, the statement's preconditions are tested in the order its general rules state them, and the first one that fails supplies the status**: for a sequential READ, the open mode ('47') first, then a preceding unsuccessful READ or START ('46'), then the first READ of an absent OPTIONAL file ('10'), then a record locked by another file connector ('51'), and only then the physical retrieval (`FileConnector.SequentialReadGuard`). So a failing READ keeps its '47', '46' or '10' rather than reporting a '51' for a record it would never have read. For a REWRITE or a DELETE RECORD, the open mode ('49', §14.9.35.4 GR3 / §14.9.10.4 GR1) is tested before a record locked by another file connector ('51', GR11 / GR6), so a connector that is not open in the I-O mode — closed, or open INPUT — answers '49' even while another connector holds the record it names (`FileConnector.MutationOpenModeGuard`; kb/Work PB1194). A WRITE tests its open mode ('48', §14.9.51.4 GR3) before the record's size ('44', GR14) and the record's content ('91', item 110, which no general rule states), and all three before the release and invalid key rules (GR29, GR33, GR38 to GR42: '34', '21', '22', '24'); a REWRITE tests '49' (§14.9.35.4 GR3), then sequential access's '43' (GR5; ahead of the record lock '51' of GR11, and the same for DELETE RECORD's GR2 and GR6: a sequential-access statement names no record after any statement but a successful READ, `FileConnector.SequentialMutationTarget`, so the registry's lock check finds nothing to conflict on and a RETRY phrase waits for nothing; kb/Work PB3416), then '44' (GR20) and '91', then the record it replaces ('23', GR21/GR23) and the key rules: the record's own rules are written once, `KeyedConnector.RecordRulesFailure`, for every keyed WRITE and REWRITE, and the sequential organization tests '44' ahead of the line sequential '71' (GR23) and '91' (kb/Work PB2751). **The line sequential REWRITE states its own order in §14.9.35.4 GR17 — a) the part-record READ '44', b) a record of more bytes than the line replaced '44', d) a character outside the line sequential character set '71' — and tests it in that order** (kb/Work PB2834), b) measuring the record's bytes ON THE MEDIUM (`LineSequentialEncoding.ChannelLength`): where a character has no byte image (a lone surrogate under UTF-8, a character the CODE-SET alphabet does not represent) the medium bytes of the record are undefined, and b) counts that character at the FEWEST bytes any image could give it, one — so b) is judged only on what holds whatever image the character might have had, a record that exceeds the line even then is '44', and one that does not is '71'. **The record-lock ceiling ('54' / '53', §12.4.5.9.4 GR7) is the last check of a WRITE or REWRITE that requests a new lock**, because the lock is the statement's effect on success (§14.9.51.4 GR11, §14.9.35.4 GR12): every organization's WRITE and REWRITE asks it, through `FileConnector.CommitGate`, once its own rules (open mode, size, content, keys, boundaries) have passed and before it changes the file, so the statement still fails with the file untouched and a record that breaks its own rules answers that rule's value (kb/Work PB2848). (3) **Between two successful values, a value the statement's own general rules assign wins over a value only described in §9.1.13.2**: an `OPEN INPUT … WITH NO REWIND` of an OPTIONAL file that is not present reports **'07'** (§14.9.27.4 GR11), not '05' (§9.1.13.2 item 4 a)). The first READ of that file still reports the at-end '10', so the information '05' would have carried is not lost. (4) **A sequential-access REWRITE or DELETE RECORD whose record has been deleted through another file connector since the READ that accessed it is unsuccessful with '23'**, for both keyed organizations: §14.9.10.4 GR5 says a deleted record "can no longer be accessed", so the record GR5 (REWRITE) and GR2 (DELETE) name does not exist, which is §9.1.13.5 3) a)'s condition. The relative organization used to re-create the record on the REWRITE and report a DELETE of nothing as '00' (kb/Work PB2751). Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/9.1.13.2-Successful-completion/pb317_open_no_rewind`; `conformance:cases/14.9.10-DELETE/w73b_pb1194_mutation_open_mode_first`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2751_keyed_write_rule_order`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2834_ls_rewrite_size_before_charset`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2848_lock_ceiling_after_record_rules`; `unit:CommitGateDriftTests` |
| DOC-A.1-106 | **I-O status 0x — the value of x**, §9.1.13.3 item 1, optional (documented if provided) | **Not provided.** No input-output statement ever sets an I-O status of '0' followed by a letter: the successful-completion values WiseOwl COBOL produces are the standard's '00', '02', '04', '05', '06', '07' and '09' (`FileStatusCode`), and its implementor-defined I-O statuses are the fatal '90' and '91' (item 110). Because no '0x' value exists, the COBOL-2023 latitude on whether an upper-case and a lower-case x are equivalent does not arise. | `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_dns_a1_106_no_0x_io_status` |
| DOC-A.1-111 | **LEAP-SECOND directive — whether a value greater than 59 seconds may be reported, and the maximum**, §7.3.17.4 GR2 (with §14.9.1.4 GR11, §15.21, §15.99), required + documented | **NO — the seconds position never holds a value greater than 59, with `>>LEAP-SECOND ON` or OFF, so the maximum is 59.** Every reported time comes from the one run-unit clock (`RunUnit.Current.Clock`, a .NET `DateTimeOffset`, which cannot represent a leap second): `ACCEPT … FROM TIME` (`AcceptSource.Time`, seconds in positions 5–6 of HHMMSScc), `FUNCTION CURRENT-DATE` (`CobolDate.CurrentDate`) and, from COBOL-2014, `FUNCTION FORMATTED-CURRENT-DATE` (`CobolDate.FormattedCurrentDate`), and `FUNCTION WHEN-COMPILED`, whose stamp is the compile-time clock reading baked into the program (`ProgramEmitter`). `>>LEAP-SECOND ON` is recognized from COBOL-2002 on (`LeapSecondDirectiveProcessor`) and changes only the ARGUMENT side of the date and time functions, where a seconds value of 60 is accepted — see item 112, which also records that SECONDS-PAST-MIDNIGHT never returns 86,400 or more. Pinned at the one instant where a 60 could arise, the last tick before the 2016-12-31 leap second (23:59:59.9999999 UTC), with ON specified, ON implied by a bare `>>LEAP-SECOND`, OFF specified and OFF implied: the run-time sources through the `WISEOWL_COBOL_CLOCK` seam (`LeapSecondReportedSecondsPinTests`, at 2002 and 2023) and the WHEN-COMPILED bake through `IntrinsicBinder.CompileClock` (`WhenCompiledStampTests.WhenCompiled_LeapSecond*`), every one expecting second 59 with hundredths 99. The live-clock goldens `l1g4_leap_second_on_reported_seconds`, `l1g4_leap_second_off_reported_seconds` and `l1g4_leap_second_off_explicit_2002` are layout witnesses only. | `conformance-test:LeapSecondReportedSecondsPinTests.ReportedSeconds_On_LastTickBeforeLeapSecond_NeverExceeds59`; `conformance-test:LeapSecondReportedSecondsPinTests.ReportedSeconds_ImpliedOn_BareDirective_LastTickBeforeLeapSecond_NeverExceeds59`; `unit:WhenCompiledStampTests.WhenCompiled_LeapSecondOn_LastTickBeforeLeapSecond_Bakes59`; `unit:WhenCompiledStampTests.WhenCompiled_LeapSecondImpliedOn_BareDirective_LastTickBeforeLeapSecond_Bakes59` |
| DOC-A.1-117 | **Listings — whether and when produced by the compiler, and the effect of logical conversion**, §7.3.18.3 GR1 + §6.5 (Clause 7), required + documented | **The compiler NEVER produces a source listing**, in any edition and under any option: the `cobol` command has no listing option, and a compilation writes only the assembly, its runtime configuration and the generated C# source (`<name>.g.cs`), which is not a listing of the COBOL source. Diagnostics go to standard error and identify the source line and column. Because there is no listing, **`>>LISTING` (ON, OFF, or with no operand) and `>>PAGE` are accepted and have no effect** (§7.3.18.3 GR1; §7.3.19): they are syntax-checked and hold no state (`DirectiveStateRegistry`, NONE HELD), and they compile from COBOL-2002 on. Like every `>>` directive they are rejected at COBOL-85 with COBOL0900. **Logical conversion (§6.5) has no effect on a listing**, because no listing exists. | `conformance:cases/7.3.18-LISTING/pb725_directive_facility` |
| DOC-A.1-118 | **Locale specification — how the user default and system default locales are defined**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because the environment variables are the user's only control over the defaults | Both defaults are decided **once per run unit, when the run unit starts** (`LocaleState`, created with the `RunUnit`), and they are always two separate settings. **User default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_USER_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the process's current .NET culture (`CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, which on Unix follows `LANG`/`LC_ALL`); otherwise the root locale. **System default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the host's installed UI culture (`CultureInfo.InstalledUICulture`); otherwise the root locale. The variables' values are locale names in the item-119 notation, trimmed; `C`, `POSIX`, `root` or `INVARIANT` names the root locale. **At least one user default and one system default always exist**: in an environment with no locale data at all (.NET invariant globalization), both fall back to the root locale and the run unit starts normally. The current locale starts as the user default for every category (§14.6.6). A program can change the user default for the rest of the run unit with `SET LOCALE USER-DEFAULT TO …`, but it cannot change the system default (§8.2.1: the capability is not provided), so `LocaleState.SystemDefault` has no setter. Example: with `COBOL_USER_LOCALE=de-DE` and `COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE=fr-FR`, `FUNCTION LOCALE-DATE("20260924")` gives `24.09.2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO USER-DEFAULT` and `24/09/2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO SYSTEM-DEFAULT`. COBOL-2002 onward. | `conformance-test:DefaultLocaleDeterminationTests.TheUserAndSystemDefaults_AreDefinedByTheirEnvironmentVariables`; `conformance-test:DefaultLocaleDeterminationTests.AHostCultureSwitchDuringARunUnit_IsNotUtilized_ButTheNextRunUnitStartsFromIt` |
| DOC-A.1-119 | **Locale specification — manner of implementation**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because it decides which locale names a program may use | **A locale is named by a BCP 47 / CLDR language tag**, and POSIX-style spellings are accepted and normalized: `es_ES.UTF-8` is `es-ES`, `de-DE@phonebook` is `de-DE` with the phonebook collation, and `C`, `POSIX`, `root`, `INVARIANT` and the empty name are the **root locale** (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`). **A locale is available** when WiseOwl COBOL has CLDR collation data for it, a site tailoring names it, or .NET recognizes it as a culture (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable`). A name that is none of these, such as `xx-NOWHERE`, is not available (EC-LOCALE-MISSING when a program selects it with checking on). The run unit keeps a current locale for **each of the six categories**, LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC and LC_TIME, each set independently by SET LOCALE (`LocaleState`). **LC_COLLATE never comes from the host**: it is WiseOwl COBOL's own collation table generated from Unicode CLDR release 48-2 / UCA 17.0.0 data, so a locale orders text the same way on every host. **LC_CTYPE, LC_MONETARY and LC_TIME** content comes from the nearest predefined .NET culture: the tag, then its parents (`sr-Latn-RS`, then `sr-Latn`, then `sr`) (`LocaleFacts`). When no ancestor is a .NET culture, or the process runs in .NET invariant-globalization mode, that content is incomplete: the invariant culture's values stand in, and an operation that needs the category sets EC-LOCALE-INVALID when checking is on. The implementor default when the environment supplies none is the root locale (item 118). COBOL-2002 onward. | `unit:LocaleStateTests.ExternalIdentification_IsNormalized_PerDeterminationL1`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Availability_IsTheOneKnownLocaleRule`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Set_SwitchesOnlyTheNamedCategories_AndTheyPersist` |
| DOC-A.1-120 | **Locale switch — whether a switch of the current locale by a non-COBOL runtime module is recognized by COBOL**, §8.2.1, conditionally required (documented if provided) | **No, for every category.** WiseOwl COBOL never activates a non-COBOL module (a CALL cannot reach one, item 19). The only non-COBOL code that can share a run unit's process is a .NET host that activates a COBOL program, together with anything that host runs. The run unit reads the process culture **once, when it starts**, to determine its user and system default locales (item 118). After that, every locale-dependent operation uses only the run unit's own per-category state (`LocaleState`), and only SET LOCALE changes it. A later change of `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture` or the process's `LANG` by non-COBOL code is not utilized for LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC or LC_TIME. Operations that are not locale-dependent never consult the process culture: DISPLAY of a floating-point or numeric item, NUMVAL and UPPER-CASE give the same result under `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8` or `tr_TR.UTF-8` as under `LANG=C`. A host that wants a different locale sets `COBOL_USER_LOCALE` (or its culture) before the run unit starts. COBOL-2002 onward. | `conformance-test:DefaultLocaleDeterminationTests.AHostCultureSwitchDuringARunUnit_IsNotUtilized_ButTheNextRunUnitStartsFromIt` |
| DOC-A.1-122 | **National literals — number of hexadecimal digits that map to a national character**, §8.3.3.5.3 SR5, required + documented | **FOUR.** Each group of four hexadecimal digits in an `NX"…"` (or `NX'…'`) literal is one national character: the UTF-16 code unit with that value, which is also one national character position. `NX"004100420043"` is the three characters `ABC`, `FUNCTION LENGTH(NX"00410042")` is 2, and `FUNCTION ORD(NX"00E9")` is 234 (é is U+00E9). A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is written as its two surrogate code units and occupies two positions: `LENGTH(NX"D83DDE00")` is 2. A literal whose digit count is not a multiple of four, such as `NX"414"` or `NX"004100"`, is rejected with **COBOL1635** (`CobolLiteral.HexGroupViolation`, asked of every literal token by `LiteralScreen` — a keyword-omitted intrinsic argument such as `LENGTH(NX"041")` and a concatenation operand included, kb/Work PB1393). NX literals exist from COBOL-2002 on; at COBOL-85 they are COBOL0900. | `conformance:cases/8.3.3.2-Alphanumeric-literals/r03_hexadecimal_national_and_boolean_literals` |
| DOC-A.1-125 | **NULL — the value of NULL**, §8.4.3.7.4 GR1 (object references) + §8.4.3.10.4 GR1–GR3 (data, program and function addresses), required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because a pointer's NULL is visible in its storage image | **Object reference:** NULL is the .NET null reference, which never refers to an object, so `O = NULL` is true exactly when O refers to no object. **Data-pointer, program-pointer and function-pointer:** NULL is the default value of each pointer type (`ManagedPointer.Null`, `ProgramPointer.Null`, a `FunctionPointer` with no name), and it is distinct from every address `SET … TO ADDRESS OF` can produce: no data item, program or function has that address. **Storage image:** a NULL pointer of every category is eight X"00" bytes, the zero address, as in GnuCOBOL, IBM and Micro Focus. Any real address has a nonzero image (item 216). Every pointer and object-reference item starts as NULL, and SET … TO NULL restores it. The message-tag NULL (GR4) does not arise, because USAGE MESSAGE-TAG belongs to the message control system, which is not provided (COBOL1943). COBOL-2002 onward. | `conformance:cases/13.18.63-VALUE/pb557_pointer_class_initial_value_is_null`; `unit:PointerImageTests.Null_OfEveryCategory_IsTheZeroAddress`; `conformance:cases/8.4.3.10-NULL-address-pointer-and-message-tag/pb452_function_address_runtime` |
| DOC-A.1-126 | **OBJECT-COMPUTER paragraph — the default object computer**, §12.3.6.4 GR3 and GR4, required + documented | **The default object computer is the .NET runtime the program is compiled for**: the `Microsoft.NETCore.App` 10.0 shared framework (`net10.0`, named in the `.runtimeconfig.json` written beside every compiled assembly), on whatever operating system and processor it runs. There is only ONE object computer, so the default is the same whether the paragraph is written without computer-name-1 (GR3), omitted altogether with no containing source unit supplying one (GR4), or written with any computer-name (item 127: the name is accepted and identifies nothing). A program therefore behaves identically in all three cases: the same native collating sequence and character classification, and the PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE and CHARACTER CLASSIFICATION clauses have the same effect with or without a name. Same in every edition. At COBOL-85 an OBJECT-COMPUTER paragraph that carries a clause must also carry computer-name-1; a paragraph with no clauses may omit the name in every edition. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb373_object_computer_name_inert` |
| DOC-A.1-130 | **OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase — positioning of the output file with regard to physical page boundaries**, §14.9.27.4 GR18, required + documented | Physical pages have meaning for a **sequential-organization** file (record sequential or LINE SEQUENTIAL) — the files WRITE ... ADVANCING and the LINAGE clause apply to; a relative or indexed file has no pages. **OPEN OUTPUT creates the host file empty and places the output medium at its first byte, which is the TOP OF THE FIRST PHYSICAL PAGE.** The OPEN itself writes nothing — no form feed, no blank lines, no margin: a file opened OUTPUT and closed with no WRITE is **0 bytes** (`SequentialConnector.OpenWriter`). **No LINAGE clause:** because the medium is already at a page top, the first `WRITE ... AFTER ADVANCING PAGE` (or BEFORE) still repositions to the NEXT physical page as §14.9.51.4 GR25 h) says, by writing a form feed (U+000C) — so a file whose first WRITE advances PAGE begins with a form feed (`SequentialConnector.Advance`). **LINAGE clause:** at the completion of the OPEN the device is on line 1 of the first logical page, and that logical page begins at the file's first line; LINAGE-COUNTER is 1 (§13.18.34.4 GR7). The logical page's TOP margin lines are written onto the medium immediately before the first record is presented — never by the OPEN, so a LINAGE file closed with no WRITE is also 0 bytes (`SequentialConnector.BeginLinagePage`, `EmitTopMarginIfPending`). Example: `FD F LINAGE 5 FOOTING 4 TOP 2 BOTTOM 1`, OPEN OUTPUT, one plain `WRITE` of `AAA` gives THREE empty lines, then `AAA` (line terminator per item 114): the two lines of the top margin, then the line the WRITE's implied `AFTER ADVANCING 1 LINE` travels past (§14.9.51.4 GR25; the device is on body line 1 after the OPEN, and `AAA` is presented on body line 2 — §4 "DETERMINATION — a WRITE without the ADVANCING phrase is an explicit `AFTER ADVANCING 1 LINE`", kb/Work PB1027). Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/13.18.34-LINAGE/pb523_linage_margins_on_the_medium`; `conformance:cases/13.18.34-LINAGE/pb523_linage_margins_on_the_medium_85`; `conformance:cases/14.9.51-WRITE/pb1027_plain_write_is_after_advancing`; `conformance-test:PlainWriteAdvancingConformanceTests.PlainWrite_ProducesTheFileTheSpelledOutAfterPhraseProduces` |
| DOC-A.1-132 | **MODULE-NAME function — which type of dynamic-length elementary item is the returned value**, §15.65.4 r1, conditionally required + documented | WiseOwl COBOL supports more than one type of dynamic-length elementary item — alphanumeric and national, each either with the implementor-defined internal structure (no dynamic-length-structure-name, §8.5.1.10.2) or with a PREFIXED / DELIMITED structure named by a DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause (determination D-DL3 in §3) — so r1 requires the choice to be stated. **MODULE-NAME returns an ALPHANUMERIC dynamic-length elementary item with the implementor-defined internal structure** — the same type as a `PIC X DYNAMIC LENGTH` item that names no dynamic-length-structure-name: a native .NET `System.String`, one character per character position, whose maximum size is the implementor maximum of item 62 (1,073,741,791 characters). It is never national and never a PREFIXED or DELIMITED structure, so no PREFIXED length-field bound (65535 / 32767) applies to it. The value is exactly the name, with no trailing spaces (item 133): `FUNCTION LENGTH(FUNCTION MODULE-NAME(CURRENT))` in program `MNPROG` is 6, ACTIVATING in a main program is one space (length 1). Implemented as the `MODULE-NAME` entry of `IntrinsicCatalog` (result type alphanumeric), evaluated by `CobolModule.Name`. COBOL 2023 only — the function does not exist in earlier editions (COBOL1502). The witness is a value no PREFIXED structure could hold: in a RECURSIVE program 2200 activations deep, `MODULE-NAME(STACK)` is 2200 names of 30 characters, each followed by `;`, then the final single space — 68,201 characters, returned whole with no EC-BOUND-FUNC-RET-VALUE (r2). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/doc_a1_132_module_name_stack_deep`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/doc-a1-132-module-name-below-2023` |
| DOC-A.1-138 | **Parameterized classes and interfaces — manner and time of expansion**, §7.1 (with §12.3.8.4 GR5 / GR8), required + need not be documented (documented voluntarily) | **Time:** a parameterized class or interface is expanded at compile time, once per compilation group, AFTER all text manipulation — COPY, REPLACE and the compiler directives have finished, the source has been parsed, and expansion runs at the start of binding (`OoExpansion.Expand`, called from `BinderDriver`). So a REPLACE that produces a formal parameter's name inside the definition takes part in the substitution. **Manner:** each distinct expansion (`CLASS new-name EXPANDS definition USING actual …` or the interface form in a REPOSITORY paragraph) becomes an ORDINARY class or interface: the definition's own tokens re-parsed with every occurrence of each formal parameter replaced by its actual parameter (§12.3.8.4 GR5 / GR8) and the header renamed to the expansion's name. It is never a .NET generic type, and from binding onward an expansion cannot be told from a written class — its FACTORY and OBJECT data are its own (two expansions of one definition keep separate factory counters). The parameterized definition itself generates nothing. **Identity (§9.3.12):** specifiers that repeat one (expansion name, definition, actual parameters) triple, in one or several source elements, create ONE class; reusing an expansion name with a different definition or different actuals is **COBOL2240**. COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:cases/11.3-CLASS-ID/pb759_parameterized_class` |
| DOC-A.1-139 | **PERFORM statement — whether location information is available when the LOCATION phrase is not specified**, §14.9.28.4 GR14 (through §7.3.25.4 GR7), required + documented | **Not available.** An exception-checking PERFORM (Format 3, `PERFORM … WHEN exception-name …  END-PERFORM`) enables the exception conditions its WHEN phrases name over imperative-statement-1 through an implicit TURN directive (§14.9.28.4 GR14), and that implicit directive carries LOCATION exactly when the PERFORM writes `WITH LOCATION`. Without it WiseOwl COBOL saves no location information for a condition raised there — the same determination as the explicit `>>TURN` directive (item 204), so neither route yields location data the other withholds. Consequence inside the WHEN handler and after the PERFORM: `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-LOCATION` returns one alphanumeric space, `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-LOCATION-N` one national space and `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-STATEMENT` 63 spaces, while `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-STATUS` still names the condition. With `PERFORM WITH LOCATION` the full location is produced — e.g. `PL; MAIN-P; 12` and statement `RAISE`. ⛔ **An explicit TURN that already enables the name wins, in both directions:** §14.9.28.4 GR14 assumes the implicit TURN only "if checking … is not enabled for imperative-statement-1 by a TURN directive", so when a `>>TURN … CHECKING ON` in force before the PERFORM already enables a name its WHEN phrase lists, no implicit directive is assumed for that name and THAT directive's LOCATION setting governs — under `>>TURN EC-USER-X1 CHECKING ON WITH LOCATION` a PERFORM without LOCATION still yields `PL2; MAIN-P; 7`, and under `>>TURN EC-USER-X1 CHECKING ON` (no LOCATION) a `PERFORM WITH LOCATION` yields one space. The LOCATION flag travels on `BoundExceptionPerform.WithLocation` into `TurnState.WithImplicitEnable`. COBOL 2023 only (Format 3 PERFORM is COBOL0900 in earlier editions). | `conformance:cases/7.3.25-TURN/l1_exception_no_location_arms`; `conformance:cases/7.3.25-TURN/exception_statement_ambient` |
| DOC-A.1-141 | **Procedure division header rules when the activating or the activated runtime element is not COBOL — restrictions and mechanisms (parameter matching, data type representation, returning of a value, omission of parameters)**, §14.2.3 GR13, conditionally required + documented | **Supported non-COBOL language products: any .NET language, and only as the ACTIVATING element.** No non-COBOL element can be activated: no call-convention-name is defined (`>>CALL-CONVENTION` admits only COBOL, item 68), and a CALL, a program-pointer or `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` resolves only WiseOwl COBOL programs. **Mechanism:** every outermost program and every user-defined function — definition or prototype — has a generated public class `Cobol.<assembly>.<name>` in the assembly that compiled it, whose static `Call` method activates it through the same boundary a COBOL CALL crosses (§14.9.4.4 GR3), and, for a program, a static `Cancel` method (§14.9.5). This is the only host interface. **Parameter matching:** positional (§14.2.3 GR2), one `Call` parameter per USING formal in order; the C# compiler checks the count and the types; a prototype library's `Call` against a changed definition is EC-PROGRAM-ARG-MISMATCH when the definition enables that checking. **Data type representation:** a numeric item without decimal places is `long`, or `Int128` (`UInt128` for an unsigned 16-byte binary item) when its storage can hold more than `long` can; one with decimal places is `decimal` (the runtime's `CobolDec` beyond 28 digits or 28 places); a floating-point item is its own CLR type; an alphanumeric, national, boolean or edited item is `string`; an index is `long`; pointers are `ManagedPointer`, `ProgramPointer`, `FunctionPointer`; an object reference is its class's CLR type; a group is a generated record struct with `AsImage`/`FromImage`; in a group that holds a dynamic-length item or a dynamic-capacity table (a variable-length group, §8.5.1.12) a dynamic-length item is `string` and a dynamic-capacity table an array of its current capacity, and the record has no image methods, its storage having no single image (§8.5.1.9.1, §8.5.1.10.3). Values are landed by §14.2.3 GR9/GR10's COMPUTE, SET or MOVE, and a value that the landing would change in any way — a digit lost at either end, a sign dropped, a character beyond the item's length or a dynamic-length item's LIMIT, a dynamic-capacity table's array below its minimum capacity — is refused with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` (`ArgumentException` for the array) before the program is activated. BY REFERENCE is a C# `ref` parameter: the program operates on a storage of the formal's description, and the variable receives its content when the call ends; two `ref` parameters given one variable share one storage when their formals have one description and are refused with `ArgumentException` otherwise. **Return of a value:** the RETURNING item is the return value; numeric content that is not a valid representation of its description (the NUMERIC class test, §8.8.4.4.4) — in the RETURNING item or in a BY REFERENCE formal — is never converted: that variable keeps its value and `FormatException` is thrown after the other write-backs. GOBACK and EXIT PROGRAM return normally (item 65); STOP RUN and a fatal condition that terminates the run unit end the run unit as item 167 states. **Omission of parameters:** an OPTIONAL formal is a nullable `ref` parameter, and `null` passes OMITTED (§14.9.4.4 GR11). Same in every edition. | `conformance-test:HostEntryTests.AHost_CallsTheGeneratedEntries_LandingExactlyAndDecodingByTheValidityRule`; `conformance-test:HostEntryTests.AHost_PassesGroupsAsPublishedRecords_LandingEachMemberExactlyAndDecodingByTheValidityRule`; `conformance-test:HostEntryTests.AHost_PassesVariableLengthGroups_AsTheCallLanesVariableLengthCarrier`; `unit:OneHostSurfaceDriftTests.NoTest_ActivatesAProgramThroughAnUntypedRoute`; `unit:HostEntryShapeDriftTests.AGroupHoldingAComponentAndAReference_PublishesItsEntry_AsTheDescriptionsOwnCellArea` |
| DOC-A.1-143 | **Program-name — formation rules for a non-COBOL program**, §8.3.2.2.21, optional (documented if provided) | **Not provided.** WiseOwl COBOL gives no program-name a non-COBOL meaning: no call-convention-name is defined (only `>>CALL-CONVENTION COBOL` is accepted, item 68) and there is no way to declare a non-COBOL program (item 19), so every program-name — in a CALL, a CANCEL, a program-pointer SET or `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` — is formed and matched by the COBOL rules of §8.3.2.2 and resolves only to a WiseOwl COBOL program. A name that happens to spell a non-COBOL module (e.g. `CALL "System.Console"`) is simply a program that is not found: EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND, the CALL's ON EXCEPTION phrase, and a NULL program-pointer from `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule` accepts only a module that registers WiseOwl COBOL programs). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |
| DOC-A.1-148 | **RECORD clause — whether format 3 (`RECORD CONTAINS integer-4 TO integer-5`) produces fixed-length or variable-length records**, §13.18.43.4 GR17, required + documented | **Variable-length.** A file whose RECORD clause is format 3 has variable-length records in the range integer-4 through integer-5 bytes: each WRITE or REWRITE writes the record named in the statement at that record's own size, and a READ delivers the size that was written — records are NEVER padded to integer-5. On the medium each record carries the framing item 151 describes: record sequential, relative and indexed files write a 4-byte little-endian length prefix before each record, LINE SEQUENTIAL files end each record with a line delimiter. Example: `FD F3 RECORD CONTAINS 5 TO 10 CHARACTERS` with `01 R3A PIC X(5)` and `01 R3B PIC X(10)`; writing R3A = `ABCDE` then R3B = `ABCDEFGHIJ` to a record sequential file gives the 23 bytes `05 00 00 00 'ABCDE' 0A 00 00 00 'ABCDEFGHIJ'`. Format 3 differs from format 2 (`RECORD IS VARYING …`) only where the standard ties a rule to the word VARYING — the READ INTO implicit move of §14.9.30.4 GR4 b) (`VaryingRecordInfo.VaryingClause`, set by `DataBinder.BindRecordClause`). Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/l1c23_record_format3_variable` |
| DOC-A.1-153 | **Record locking — the default mode when the user specifies none**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR1 b) 2., required + documented | **No record locking** — the third option GR1 b) 2. names. A file connector whose file control entry has neither a LOCK MODE clause nor a SHARING clause, opened by an OPEN with no SHARING phrase, SETS NO RECORD LOCKS: a READ does not lock, and an explicit `WITH LOCK` phrase on its I-O statements obtains nothing (`FileRegistry.ImplementorDefaultShare`, lock mode `FileLockMode.None`). It still RESPECTS other connectors' locks, because §9.1.16 makes a locked record inaccessible to every other file connector: its READ, REWRITE and DELETE of a record another connector has locked are refused with I-O status `51`, and READ … IGNORING LOCK reads it. Example (a connector with neither clause can be open beside another connector only in the input mode, because a clause-less OPEN I-O, EXTEND or OUTPUT establishes SHARING WITH NO OTHER, item 131): A is declared `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` with `LOCK MODE IS MANUAL` and opens INPUT; B has neither clause and opens INPUT (`00`, `00`). A `READ … WITH LOCK` record 1 (`00`); B's READ of record 1 is `51`, B's `READ … IGNORING LOCK` of it is `00`, B's READ of the unlocked record 2 is `00`, and after A's UNLOCK B's READ of record 1 is `00`. A connector that must REWRITE or DELETE beside a locker declares `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` and a LOCK MODE clause (§14.9.27.3 SR8) and then is refused a locked record the same way (`pb669_lock_visibility_plain_connector`: REWRITE and DELETE of a locked record are `51`). COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:cases/14.9.27-OPEN/pb322_clauseless_reader_sees_record_lock`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb669_lock_visibility_plain_connector` |
| DOC-A.1-154 | **Record locking — the maximum number of record locks a run unit may hold**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR7, required + documented | **255** — the standard's minimum (`PhysicalFileTable.RunUnitLockMax`). The count is every record lock held by every file connector of the run unit, over all physical files. An I-O statement that would obtain a 256th lock is unsuccessful with I-O status **`53`** (§9.1.13.8 item 3) and obtains no lock; a WRITE or REWRITE refused this way changes no record (the ceiling is the last check of the statement: the organization asks it through `FileConnector.CommitGate` once its own rules have passed and before it touches the record, `PhysicalFileTable.PreflightNewLock`; so a record that breaks the statement's own rules is that rule's status, A.1 item 104 (2)). Re-locking a record the same connector already holds does not count again. When the connector's own ceiling (item 155) is also reached, `54` is reported. **The commit posture is exempt (kb/Work PB3337):** a connector under an active APPLY COMMIT clause, whose posture is §9.1.16's implicit `LOCK MODE IS AUTOMATIC WITH LOCK ON MULTIPLE RECORDS`, has no maximum but the host's — its READ locks are host region locks, and the locks of the records it changes are holdings in the file (A.1 item 152) — because Annex D.2.5's deferred commits make the count unbounded by design and GR7 lets the implementor set the maximum (docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.1.10). COBOL 2002 and later. | `unit:CobolFileLockTests.RunUnitLockLimit_256thRunUnitLock_Is53`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.A_transaction_of_300_records_meets_no_lock_ceiling`; `unit:CommitGateDriftTests` |
| DOC-A.1-155 | **Record locks — the maximum number of record locks one file connector may hold**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR7, required + documented | **15** — the standard's minimum (`PhysicalFileTable.ConnectorLockMax`). Only a connector with multiple record locking (`LOCK ON MULTIPLE RECORDS`) can hold more than one lock (GR6), and the MULTIPLE phrase is not allowed for sequential organization or access (§12.4.5.9.3 SR2), so the ceiling is reachable on relative and indexed files with random or dynamic access. An I-O statement that would obtain a 16th lock for the connector is unsuccessful with I-O status **`54`** (§9.1.13.8 item 4), obtains no lock and — for a READ — is an unsuccessful READ like any other (§14.9.30.4 GR18): no record position is established, so the next sequential READ is `46`, never the record after the refused one; a WRITE or REWRITE refused this way changes no record (`PhysicalFileTable.PreflightNewLock`), and is refused only when it is otherwise successful: the ceiling is the last check of the statement (`FileConnector.CommitGate`, asked by every organization's WRITE and REWRITE after its own rules), so a record of the wrong size is `44`, not `54` (A.1 item 104 (2); kb/Work PB2848). Re-locking a record the connector already holds does not count again; UNLOCK and CLOSE release its locks. **The commit posture is exempt (kb/Work PB3337):** a connector under an active APPLY COMMIT clause, whose posture is §9.1.16's implicit `LOCK MODE IS AUTOMATIC WITH LOCK ON MULTIPLE RECORDS`, has no maximum but the host's — its READ locks are host region locks, and the locks of the records it changes are holdings in the file (A.1 item 152) — because Annex D.2.5's deferred commits make the count unbounded by design and GR7 lets the implementor set the maximum (docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.1.10). COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:cases/9.1.13.8-Record-operation-conflict-condition-with-unsuccessful/pb338_read_lock_limit_position`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2848_lock_ceiling_after_record_rules`; `unit:CobolFileLockTests.ConnectorLockLimit_16thRecord_Is54` |
| DOC-A.1-160 | **Report writer printable item — the fixed correspondence between columns and national characters**, §13.18.14.4 GR2, required + documented | **One column per national character position** — the same one-to-one correspondence as for an alphanumeric character. A national printable item described `PIC N(n)` (explicit or implied USAGE NATIONAL, including one inherited from a group entry) occupies exactly n columns, starting at the column its COLUMN clause names, and the horizontal counter advances by n (§13.18.14.4 GR9; `DataItem.DisplayTextWidth`, used by `ReportWriterEmitter.EmitFieldPlacements`). Example: `COLUMN 1 PIC N(4) SOURCE WN1` with WN1 = N"WXYZ" and `COLUMN 6 PIC X(3) VALUE "ABC"` on one line prints `WXYZ ABC` — the national item fills columns 1–4 and column 5 stays blank. COBOL 2002 and later (national data does not exist at `--std 85`: COBOL0900). Which bytes a national character becomes in the report FILE is item 159's record structure. | `conformance:cases/13.18.14-COLUMN/pb541_report_national_item` |
| DOC-A.1-169 | **SAME SORT AREA / SAME SORT-MERGE AREA clause — extent of allocation**, §12.4.6.4 GR4 b) (§12.4.6.4.4), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **The extent is NONE.** A non-sort file named in a sort-merge-area format SAME clause never lends its storage to a SORT or MERGE: `DataBinder.BindIoControl` links only the SAME RECORD AREA format's STORAGE and gives the SORT AREA / SORT-MERGE AREA formats no storage effect (it records every format's MEMBERSHIP on its files, `FileModel.SameClauses`, which the SORT and MERGE statements read for §14.9.40.3 SR10 / §14.9.24.3 SR11 — a pair of the statement's own file-names in one barred clause is refused, kb/Work PB1139), and SORT/MERGE work storage is the run time's own managed memory, separate from every file's record area. GR4 b)'s "may be allocated" makes zero a permitted extent, and GR4 c) (the non-sort files do not share storage with each other) holds because the clause creates no sharing at all. The clause is accepted in every edition and a program that names a plain file in it sorts, reads and writes that file exactly as it would without the clause. | — |
| DOC-A.1-170 | **SEARCH ALL statement — varying of the search index during the search operation**, §14.9.37 GR9 (§14.9.37.4), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **A forward scan in occurrence order.** The initial setting of the search index is ignored: SEARCH ALL sets it to occurrence **1**, evaluates the WHEN condition, and on a false result advances it by one, until a WHEN is satisfied or the last element has been tested (`ControlFlowEmitter.EmitAllScan`). The bound is the table's maximum occurrence count, the CURRENT count of an OCCURS DEPENDING ON table, or the current capacity of an OCCURS DYNAMIC table. The last-element test happens BEFORE the advance, so the index never holds a value outside 1 through the last element — also on an unsuccessful search, where the AT END phrase sees it at the last element tested; an empty table (current count 0) is unsuccessful with no element tested and the index at 1. On success the index holds the occurrence number of the element that satisfied the WHEN. No binary search is performed, so a table whose ASCENDING/DESCENDING KEY data is not actually in sequence still finds an element that satisfies the condition when one exists. GR9 makes the final setting after an unsuccessful search undefined, so a program shall not rely on which in-range value is left. | `conformance:cases/14.9.37-SEARCH/pb447_search_all_index_stays_in_table` |
| DOC-A.1-181 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph — allowable locale-names and literal values of the LOCALE clause**, §12.3.7 GR5 (§12.3.7.4), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided (2002 and later).** `LOCALE locale-name-1 IS {external-locale-name-1 or literal-4}` accepts the SAME set of identifications in both forms: a **locale tag** — any BCP-47 tag of a CLDR locale or of a culture .NET recognizes (`fr-FR`, `de-CH`, `sr-Latn-RS`, `zh-Hant`), a `-u-` extension allowed — or the root locale spelled `INVARIANT`, `ROOT`, `C`, `POSIX` or `und`. A **POSIX spelling** `ll_CC[.codeset][@modifier]` is normalized before use (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`): underscores become hyphens, a `.codeset` suffix is ignored (the repertoire is always UTF-16), an `@modifier` that names a CLDR collation type becomes the `-u-co-<type>` extension (`de_DE@phonebook` is `de-DE-u-co-phonebook`), and any other modifier leaves a tag that names no locale. So `fr_FR`, `fr-FR`, `"fr_FR.UTF-8"` and `"fr-FR"` SELECT the same locale; the comparison is case-insensitive. Selecting the same locale is not having the same external identification: where a PICTURE clause identity is compared (the type-equivalence and parameter / returning-item conformance rules, which define the identification as "the external-locale-name or literal value" itself) the identification is compared as written, a literal value character for character (kb/Work PB1166). The word form is limited to what a COBOL word can spell (no `.` or `@`), so `.codeset` and `@modifier` spellings need the literal form. literal-4 shall be an alphanumeric or national literal (or a concatenation expression of that class), neither zero-length nor a symbolic-character figurative constant (§12.3.7.3 SR10/SR11, `COBOL0898`; every OTHER figurative constant is a literal of its class — §8.3.3.6.3 SR1, kb/Work PB1537 — so `LOCALE LA IS SPACE` names the locale `" "`, which is simply not available, and the predefined NULL is `COBOL2576`); a locale-name declared twice is `COBOL4250`. A constant-name may stand for literal-4 (13.10.3 SR2, kb/Work PB1942) and is held to the same two rules; ⚠ DETERMINATION — a word the source element declares as a constant-name is read as that constant, never as an external-locale-name-1 of the same spelling. **Availability is decided at RUN time, never at compile time**: any spelling compiles, and a locale that is not available (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable` — the root, a locale with CLDR collation data, a site `.tailor` file, or a culture .NET recognizes) raises `EC-LOCALE-MISSING` at the statement that uses it when that check is enabled; with the check not enabled the statement proceeds with the root locale's conventions (a `LOCALE-DATE` through an unavailable `"zz_QQ"` or `"fr_FR@euro"` formats as `09/24/2026`, exactly as `INVARIANT` does). Before 2002 the clause is rejected (`COBOL0900`). | `unit:LocaleStateTests.ExternalIdentification_IsNormalized_PerDeterminationL1`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Availability_IsTheOneKnownLocaleRule`; `conformance:cases/12.3.6-OBJECT-COMPUTER/pb64t1_locale_declare`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1537_figurative_literal_clauses`; `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/pb2500_locale_constant_name` |
| DOC-A.1-182 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, ALPHABET clause — coded character set referenced by the STANDARD-2 phrase**, §12.3.7 GR7 c) (§12.3.7.4), required + documented | **STANDARD-2 always references the ISO/IEC 646 International Reference Version — never a national version, under any circumstance** (no compiler option, locale or environment setting selects one). STANDARD-2 is therefore the same coded character set as STANDARD-1: its 128 characters are the first 128 positions of the native alphanumeric character set, U+0000 through U+007F, with the correspondence and ordinals item 187 states (`CodedCharacterSet.OrdinalCount` = 128; class membership `CobolClass.CodedSetKind.Ascii`). A class condition `IS alphabet-name` on a STANDARD-2 alphabet is true exactly for characters in U+0000–U+007F (`"AB~"` is, `é` is not), and a STANDARD-2 alphabet used as the PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE collates in native order. The phrase is available for alphanumeric alphabets in every edition. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1c30_standard2_is_irv` |
| DOC-A.1-186 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, ALPHABET clause, literal phrase — ordinal number of the characters not specified**, §12.3.7 GR7 k) 4. (§12.3.7.4), required + documented (the scheme, not each character) | **The ordinal number of every character is its position in the alphabet's collating sequence, counting the first position as 1, and the unspecified characters are numbered in the order GR7 k) 3. collates them.** A literal-phrase alphabet's coded character set contains every native character — 65,536 UTF-16 code units, for an alphanumeric and a national alphabet alike (`CodedCharacterSet.OrdinalCount`). The characters the literal phrase specifies take ordinals 1 through *n*, one per collating position in the order written (a THROUGH range fills successive positions; an ALSO group shares one position, and that ordinal names ALL the group's characters — literal-1 first — per GR7 k) 6.). Which of them a reference uses depends on what it needs: a reference that needs ONE character takes literal-1 alone (`SYMBOLIC CHARACTERS … IN`, GR7 k) 6.'s last sentence: "only literal-1 is used to represent the character in the native character set"), a reference that names a SET takes them all (a numeric `CLASS … IN` literal, GR12 a, so `CLASS C1 IS 1 IN AL` over `ALPHABET AL IS "B" ALSO "A" ALSO "Z"` is {B, A, Z} — the singular "a character" of GR12 a is read as the plural because the other reading would make k) 6.'s exception redundant; kb/Work PB1095). A group's ordinal is no single character to begin or end a THROUGH run, so `CLASS C IS 1 THRU 3 IN AL` over such an ordinal is refused (COBOL1671, §12.3.7.4 GR12). The characters NOT specified then take ordinals *n*+1, *n*+2, … in ascending native code order, skipping the specified ones (`CodedCharacterSet.CharAt` for one character, `CodedCharacterSet.CharactersAt` for the set). Worked example: `ALPHABET AL IS "Z" "Y" ALSO "W" "X"` has *n* = 3, so ordinal 1 is `Z`, 2 is `Y`, 3 is `X`, 4 is U+0000, 5 is U+0001, and ordinal 70 is `B` (U+0042, the 67th unspecified character). These are the ordinals `SYMBOLIC CHARACTERS … IN alphabet-name` and a numeric `CLASS … IN alphabet-name` literal use. Because an ALSO character has no ordinal of its own, the highest ordinal is 65,536 minus the number of ALSO characters (in the example, ordinal 65,535 is U+FFFF and 65,536 is `COBOL1670`). The same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1c30_literal_alphabet_unspecified_ordinals`; `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/pb1095_class_in_also_group` |
| DOC-A.1-187 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, ALPHABET clause — correspondence of the STANDARD-1 and STANDARD-2 phrases with the native character set**, §12.3.7 GR7 c) (§12.3.7.4), required + documented | **The identity on U+0000–U+007F.** Both phrases reference ISO/IEC 646 IRV (item 182), and each of its 128 characters corresponds to the native alphanumeric character with the same code: ordinal *n* of the standard set is native character U+(*n*−1), so `SYMBOLIC CHARACTERS ... IN` a STANDARD-1/-2 alphabet accepts ordinals 1 through 128 (129 or more is `COBOL1670`), and ordinal 66 is `A`. The collating sequence is the native order of those characters. Native characters above U+007F have no counterpart in the standard set: they are not members for a class condition `IS alphabet-name` (`é` is not), and no ordinal reaches them. For `CODE-SET` the correspondence converts as the identity — a record of IRV characters is written to and read from the medium unchanged. **A record character above U+007F cannot be written under a STANDARD-1, STANDARD-2 or `ASCII` CODE-SET**: §13.18.13.4 GR6 b replaces each native character "with its associated coded character as defined in the alphabet being used", and such a character has none, so the WRITE or REWRITE is unsuccessful with the implementor-defined I-O status '91' (item 110) — '71' on a line sequential file, whose character set's ceiling is the file's coded character set (item 115) — nothing reaches the medium and the record area is unchanged. The `EBCDIC` code-set refuses a character above U+00FF the same way, and every organization decides it at the output statement, a relative or indexed store included although it reaches the medium only at CLOSE (kb/Work PB1150, PB1542). The one character every CODE-SET alphabet represents although no correspondence names it is HIGH-VALUE (U+FFFF): it is written as the coded character set's HIGHEST code unit (X'7F' under ISO/IEC 646, X'FF' under `EBCDIC`) and that unit reads back as HIGH-VALUE (owner decision kb/Work R51 item 4, 'cross a byte medium as that medium's extreme byte'; `CodeSetConversion.HighUnit`, kb/Work PB1759); the native character the alphabet assigns to that unit (DEL, U+009F) then reads back as HIGH-VALUE, the CODE-SET twin of item 31's `ÿ` cost. ⚠ **The input direction is a determination**: a medium byte X'80'–X'FF' is not a character of the set, and §13.18.13.4 names no condition for reading one, so a READ carries it into the record area as the native character of the same value under its ordinary status — '09' on a line sequential file, where it is outside the line sequential character set — and a relative or indexed store re-persisted at CLOSE writes it back byte-exactly; a WRITE or REWRITE of a record holding it is refused like any other non-member. Implemented by `CodedCharacterSet` (128 ordinals; its 128-entry identity correspondence is the file connector's `CodeSetConversion`, whose `Represents` is the membership `FileConnector.RecordHasCharacterWithoutByteImage` asks) and `CobolClass.CodedSetKind.Ascii`; the same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/8.8.4.4-Simple-class-condition/pb109_class_condition_alphabet`; `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/pb110_code_set_identity`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1542_code_set_unrepresentable_85`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1542_code_set_line_sequential`; `unit:CodeSetConversionTests.Iso646_RepresentsExactlyItsOwn128Characters` |
| DOC-A.1-193 | **STOP and GOBACK statements — mechanism for error termination**, §14.9.42 GR4 (§14.9.42.4) · §14.9.18 GR9 (§14.9.18.4), optional (documented if provided) | **Not provided.** No implementor-defined mechanism can mark a run unit as terminating in error, so a `STOP RUN` or a main program's `GOBACK` written without an ERROR, NORMAL or STATUS phrase always reports a normal termination — process exit code **0** — whatever the program did before it. There is no `RETURN-CODE` special register (a reference to it is `COBOL1639`, not defined), no compiler option and no run-time setting that changes this; only the ERROR / STATUS phrases of the terminating statement (item 192) and an abnormal run-unit termination on a fatal exception condition (item 44), which is not a STOP or GOBACK, produce a nonzero exit code. | `conformance-test:StopGobackExitCodeTests.TerminationStatus_SetsProcessExitCode` |
| DOC-A.1-194 | **Subscripts — mapping of an index value to an occurrence number**, §8.4.2.3 GR1 c) (§8.4.2.3.4), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **The identity.** An index holds its 1-based occurrence number directly — a 64-bit integer, never a byte offset or displacement (the storage of an index is item 211) — so subscripting by `index-name-1` selects the occurrence equal to the index value (`BoundIndexRef`; `NumericRenderer.Visit`). `index-name-1 + integer-1` and `index-name-1 − integer-1` select the occurrence the index value plus or minus the integer names, computed without changing the index. A `SET` of a numeric item to an index, or of an index to another index of the same table, carries that occurrence number unchanged. Example: with `05 E PIC X OCCURS 5 TIMES INDEXED BY I` holding "ABCDE", after `SET I TO 3` the references `E(I)`, `E(I + 1)` and `E(I - 2)` are `C`, `D` and `A`, and `SET N TO I` stores 3. | `conformance:cases/13.18.60-USAGE/pb215_index_windows` |
| DOC-A.1-196 | **SYNCHRONIZED clause — how the records of a file are handled**, §13.18.55 GR11 (§13.18.55.4), optional (documented if provided) | **Not provided.** WiseOwl COBOL has no rule for synchronizing the records of a file: a record area is never aligned or padded as a whole, and a SYNCHRONIZED elementary item in a record sits at exactly the offset it would have without the clause (item 195), so the record written to and read from the file is byte-for-byte the record's own image. Example: `01 R. 05 A PIC X. 05 B PIC S9(4) COMP SYNC. 05 C PIC X.` with "Q", 258 and "Z" writes the 4 bytes `51 01 02 5A` to a sequential file. The same in every edition. | `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_dns_a1_196_sync_file_record_stream` |
| DOC-A.1-197 | **SYNCHRONIZED clause — positioning when neither RIGHT nor LEFT is specified**, §13.18.55 GR3 (§13.18.55.4), required + documented | **The item is positioned exactly where it would be without the clause: it begins at the byte immediately after the preceding item.** WiseOwl COBOL treats every byte position as a natural boundary — a record is a typed .NET structure, not an addressable byte buffer, so an unaligned binary item costs no extra machine operations — and therefore performs no positioning, adds no slack bytes, and does not change the size of the item or of any containing group or REDEFINES (item 195). The same is true of `SYNCHRONIZED LEFT` and `SYNCHRONIZED RIGHT`: with a one-byte natural boundary an item both begins at the left byte and ends on the right byte of the boundaries that delimit it, so GR4 and GR5 are met with no adjustment, and the three forms lay out identically. Example: `01 G. 05 A PIC X. 05 B PIC S9(4) COMP SYNCHRONIZED. 05 C PIC X.` is 4 bytes, and `B` occupies bytes 2–3, with or without LEFT/RIGHT and with no clause at all. The same in every edition. The three forms lay out alike but remain three CLAUSES, and the compiler records which one each item carries (`DataItem.Synchronized`, `SynchronizedPhrase`; kb/Work PB538): §8.5.3.1 requires corresponding elementary items of equivalent type declarations to "have the same … SYNCHRONIZED … clauses", so declarations differing only in `SYNC LEFT` against `SYNC RIGHT` (or either against the bare form) are not equivalent. A clause written on a group is the clause of each subordinate elementary item for which it is permitted (§13.18.55.4 GR1; kb/Work PB539). | `conformance:cases/8.5.1.6.4-Item-alignment-for-increased-object-code/l1_byte_length_implicit_filler`; `conformance:cases/13.18.55-SYNCHRONIZED/pb538-sync-left-right-differ`; `conformance:cases/13.18.55-SYNCHRONIZED/pb539_sync_group_as_if_leaves` |
| DOC-A.1-198 | **System-names — rules for the formation of a system-name**, §8.3.2.3 (§8.3.2.3.1), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided — one restriction.** A system-name is formed as any COBOL word of the target edition — letters, digits, hyphen, and (2002 and later) underscore, not beginning or ending with a hyphen or underscore (`ABC-` is a syntax error), at most 30 characters (COBOL-85), 31 (2002 and 2014) or 63 (2023), the length limit being `COBOL1567` — with ONE added restriction: a system-name shall not consist of digits only, because such a character-string is always read as an integer literal (`OBJECT-COMPUTER. 12345.` is refused at the literal as a token the closed format does not print, `COBOL1970`). Unlike a user-defined word, a system-name need not contain a letter otherwise: `123ABC`, `MY_BOX-9` and `1-2` are all accepted as computer-names. Which system-names are RECOGNIZED is a separate matter: device-names, switch-names and feature-names are a fixed list (items 189–191; an unknown one is `COBOL2241`), code-names are items 183–184, and external-locale-names are item 181. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1c32_system_name_formation`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1c32-system-name-all-digits` |
| DOC-A.1-201 | **Text manipulation — stage of processing at which parameterized classes and interfaces are expanded**, §7.2 (the sentence is in §7.1), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **At compile time, after all text manipulation.** WiseOwl COBOL expands a parameterized class or interface when it BINDS the compilation group (`BinderDriver` → `OoExpansion`): for each `EXPANDS` specifier in a REPOSITORY paragraph it takes the parameterized definition's source text AS IT STANDS AFTER COPY, REPLACE and conditional compilation have been applied, substitutes each actual parameter for the corresponding formal parameter, and compiles the result as an ordinary, non-parameterized class or interface. So text manipulation can build or rename a formal parameter (a `REPLACE` that turns `ZZELEM` into `ELEM` before `CLASS-ID. ... USING ZZELEM` is seen gives the same class as writing `USING ELEM`), but a REPLACE never sees, and cannot alter, the text an expansion produces. Nothing is expanded at run time and no .NET generic type is used. Parameterized classes and interfaces exist from 2002 on; a class definition is rejected below 2002 (`COBOL0900`). | `conformance:cases/11.3-CLASS-ID/pb759_parameterized_class`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1522_replace_before_parameterized_expansion` |
| DOC-A.1-203 | **THROUGH phrase in the VALUE clause and the EVALUATE statement — collating sequence for a range when no alphabet-name is specified**, §14.7.8 rule 2, required + documented | **The PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE of the range's class — the same sequence a relation condition between the same operands uses.** A range of alphanumeric (or alphabetic) values, in a level-88 `VALUE … THROUGH …` or an `EVALUATE … WHEN … THROUGH …`, written without `IN alphabet-name`, is evaluated in the alphanumeric program collating sequence declared by `OBJECT-COMPUTER. … PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE` (§12.3.6), or in the native order (UTF-16 code-unit order) when none is declared; a range of national values uses the national program collating sequence (`… FOR NATIONAL`, 2002 and later), else the native national order (`CollatingSelection.ThroughRangeClass` → `CollatingSelection.ForComparison`). A national or alphanumeric GROUP conditional variable takes the sequence of its own class. A range whose first value collates after its second in that sequence is empty (with EC-RANGE-INVALID when that check is enabled). Example: with `PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE IS EB` where `ALPHABET EB IS EBCDIC`, the value `"_"` is NOT in `"Z" THRU "a"` (in EBCDIC `a` collates before `Z`), while with no PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE it is. Numeric ranges are algebraic (rule 1) and use no sequence. | `conformance:cases/13.18.63-VALUE/pb398_range_in_alphabet`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb728_level88_group_usage_collating` |
| DOC-A.1-213 | **USAGE NATIONAL — size and representation of characters**, §13.18.60 GR8 (§13.18.60.4), required + documented | **Two bytes per national character position, uniform at every length: one UTF-16 code unit, stored MOST SIGNIFICANT BYTE FIRST (UTF-16BE).** `PIC N(2)` occupies 4 bytes (`FUNCTION BYTE-LENGTH` 4, `FUNCTION LENGTH` 2), and a national-form numeric or numeric-edited item takes 2 bytes per symbol (`PIC 9(3) USAGE NATIONAL` is 6 bytes). The value of each position is the character's UTF-16 code unit — `A` is `00 41`, `é` is `00 E9`, `€` is `20 AC` — and this is the image seen through a REDEFINES, in an alphanumeric group that contains the item, and in a record written to a file. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is a surrogate pair and occupies TWO character positions, each half treated as a separate character exactly as §8.5.1.4 rule 2 requires, so a MOVE that truncates between the halves keeps only the first. There is no option to vary the size or representation per compilation unit. USAGE NATIONAL exists from 2002 on (`COBOL0900` below). | `conformance:cases/13.18.40-PICTURE/pb646_national_form_numeric_bytes`; `conformance:cases/8.1.2-Computer-s-coded-character-set/l1_usage_display_character_size` |
| DOC-A.1-220 | **Variable-length data items — actual time when the resources used are freed**, §8.5.1.11.3, required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **Whenever the .NET garbage collector reclaims them — a time the program cannot observe and WiseOwl COBOL does not fix.** No variable-length item has storage of its own to release: a DYNAMIC LENGTH elementary item is a managed .NET string, so the old value becomes unreachable when a new value is stored (a MOVE of "XY" over "ABCDEFGHIJ" leaves an item of length 2), and the collector reclaims it later. A dynamic-capacity table (`OCCURS DYNAMIC`, `CobolDynTable`) holds its occurrences in a managed array that grows by doubling and is NEVER shrunk: lowering the capacity (`SET … TO`, `DOWN BY`) only lowers the current count, keeping the removed occurrences' storage until the table is enlarged again — when each re-created occurrence is created afresh as a new occurrence, never with the value it held before — or until the table itself becomes unreachable. Freeing never affects a program's results. DYNAMIC LENGTH items and dynamic-capacity tables exist from 2014 on (`COBOL0900` below). | — |
| DOC-A.1-13 | **CALL statement — rules for program-name formation for a non-COBOL program**, §14.9.4.4 GR3 b), conditionally required (on support for calling non-COBOL programs) + documented | **Condition absent.** WiseOwl COBOL supports calling no non-COBOL program: no call-convention-name is defined, so `>>CALL-CONVENTION` admits only COBOL and any other word is COBOL1911 (item 68), and there is no way to declare a program written in another language, so §14.9.4.4 GR3 b)'s implementor-defined branch ("If the program being called is not a COBOL program, the rules for program-name formation and for locating the program are defined by the implementor.") never applies. Every program-name is formed by the COBOL rules of §8.3.2.2 (item 143). A name that spells a non-COBOL module — even the WiseOwl COBOL runtime assembly `WiseOwl.Cobol.Runtime.dll`, which is deployed beside every program — is a program that cannot be located: EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND, and the CALL's ON EXCEPTION phrase runs (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule` registers a sibling module only when it carries the WiseOwl COBOL `[assembly: CobolRepository]` record, whose registrar's `EnsureRegistered()` is the module's one way in). Contingent: re-adjudicate if non-COBOL calls are ever supported. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |
| DOC-A.1-15 | **CALL statement — rules for locating a non-COBOL program**, §14.9.4.4 GR3 b), conditionally required (on support for calling non-COBOL programs) + documented | **Condition absent.** No non-COBOL program can be called (item 13), so there are no rules for locating one: the runtime locates only WiseOwl COBOL programs — those registered in the run unit, then a sibling module `<name>.dll` in the application directory that carries the WiseOwl COBOL registrar (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule`). A module without it, however it is named, is never loaded as a program and the CALL is not successful (EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND, §14.9.4.4 GR3 b)). Contingent: re-adjudicate if non-COBOL calls are ever supported. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |
| DOC-A.1-30 | **Compiler directives — the IMP directive (syntax rules and general rules)**, §7.3.3 SR9 + §7.3.4 GR4, conditionally required (on support for an IMP directive) + documented if provided | **Condition absent.** WiseOwl COBOL defines no IMP directive. §7.3.3 SR9 reserves the word ("The compiler-directive word 'IMP' is reserved for use by the implementor.") and §7.3.4 GR4 makes its rules implementor-defined only "If the implementor defines the IMP directive". The recognized directives are exactly the rows of `CompilerDirectiveCatalog`, which has no IMP row, so a `>>IMP` line is left in the text as an unrecognized directive and the compilation is refused at every edition (a syntax error at the `>>`, COBOL0001). Contingent: re-adjudicate if an IMP directive is ever defined. | `conformance:cases/7.3-Compiler-directives/w59h-imp-directive-undefined` |
| DOC-A.1-34 | **Computer's coded character set — for literals, the correspondence between the compile-time and runtime character sets when conversion takes place**, §8.1.2, conditionally required (on the two sets differing) + documented if provided | **Condition absent: the two sets are the same, so no conversion takes place.** §8.1.2 permits them to differ ("The coded character set used during compilation may be the same as or different from the coded character set used during execution of the resultant runtime elements."); in WiseOwl COBOL both are the UTF-16 repertoire (item 33). The source text is decoded to UTF-16 when it is read (`SourceTextDecoder`, item 25), a literal's characters are stored as those code units, and the run time represents every character by the same code unit — so a literal means at run time exactly what it meant at compile time: `FUNCTION ORD("€")` is 8365 (U+20AC plus 1) and `FUNCTION CHAR(8365)` equals the literal `"€"`. | `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide` |
| DOC-A.1-37 | **Computer's coded character set — when more than one encoding is supported, the mechanism for selecting the encoding for runtime**, §8.1.2, conditionally required (on more than one encoding being supported) + documented if provided | **Condition absent: exactly one encoding is supported.** The computer's alphanumeric and national coded character sets are both encoded as UTF-16 code units, one per character position (item 33); no directive, compiler option, environment variable or runtime call selects another, so there is no selection mechanism to document. (The CODE-SET clause and the ALPHABET clause's code-names convert at the FILE boundary; they do not change the computer's coded character set.) An ordinal therefore depends only on the character, never on the host: `FUNCTION ORD("€")` is 8365 on every machine. Contingent: re-adjudicate if a second encoding is ever supported. | `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide` |
| DOC-A.1-88 | **Function-identifier — execution of a non-COBOL function when a function-prototype-name is specified**, §8.4.3.2.4 GR6 d), conditionally required (on support for calling non-COBOL functions) + documented | **Condition absent.** WiseOwl COBOL supports calling no non-COBOL function, so §8.4.3.2.4 GR6 d)'s implementor-defined branch ("the function to be activated is not a COBOL function, the execution is defined by the implementor") never applies. A function-prototype-name locates only a WiseOwl COBOL user-defined function registered in the run unit (`ProgramTable.CallProgram`, function arm); a prototype whose externalized name spells a non-COBOL module is a function that is not found — EC-FUNCTION-NOT-FOUND (§8.4.3.2.4 GR6 b)), fatal unless checking is enabled and a declarative takes it. Contingent: re-adjudicate if non-COBOL functions are ever supported. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |
| DOC-A.1-96 | **Hexadecimal alphanumeric literals — mapping when characters are not multiples of four bits**, §8.3.3.2.4 GR5, conditionally required (on a coded character set whose characters are not multiples of four bits) + documented if provided | **Condition absent.** §8.3.3.2.4 GR5 defers "the mapping of each hex-character-sequence-1 to a character, when the characters do not occupy a multiple of four bits"; in WiseOwl COBOL an alphanumeric character is taken from exactly TWO hexadecimal digits (8 bits, item 9 / §8.3.3.2.3 SR6) and occupies a 16-bit code unit — both multiples of four — so the case cannot arise. A hex-character-sequence of any other digit count is refused (COBOL1635), and every two-digit group maps to the character whose DISPLAY byte is hh (item 95: U+00hh, except FF which is U+FFFF). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1c12_hex_alphanumeric_every_group`; `conformance:cases/8.3.3.2-Alphanumeric-literals/r03-hex-literal-digit-grouping` |
| DOC-A.1-98 | **Hexadecimal national literals — mapping when characters are not multiples of four bits**, §8.3.3.5.4 GR5, conditionally required (on a coded character set whose characters are not multiples of four bits) + documented if provided | **Condition absent.** A national character is taken from exactly FOUR hexadecimal digits (§8.3.3.5.3 SR5) and is one 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, a multiple of four bits, so the mapping §8.3.3.5.4 GR5 defers for characters that are not cannot arise. Any other digit count is refused (COBOL1635); every group is stored verbatim as its code unit (item 97). | `conformance:cases/8.3.3.5-National-literals/l1c12_hex_national_no_character`; `conformance:cases/8.3.3.2-Alphanumeric-literals/r03-hex-literal-digit-grouping` |

Contingent: re-adjudicate if non-COBOL programs are ever supported. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |
| DOC-A.1-149 | **RECORD DELIMITER clause — consistency rules when used with external file connectors**, §12.4.5.3 GR1 c), conditionally required (on the optional feature-name-1 existing) + documented if provided | **Condition absent.** §12.4.5.3 GR1 c) asks for "a consistent value of feature-name-1 in the RECORD DELIMITER clause" and "The implementor shall specify the consistency rules for feature-name-1"; WiseOwl COBOL provides no feature-name-1 (item 150, 'Not provided.'), and the RECORD DELIMITER clause as a whole is declined with a named warning (COBOL1778, `DiagnosticCatalog.RecordDelimiterUnsupported`, bound in `DataBinder.BindFileControl`), so no value exists to be consistent. Contingent: re-adjudicate if a feature-name-1 is ever provided. | `conformance:cases/12.4.5.11-RECORD-DELIMITER/pb292_record_delimiter_witness`; `conformance-test:DocumentedNonSupportWitnessTests.RecordDelimiterFeatureName_NamedNonSupportWarning_PinnedToSpec` |
| DOC-A.1-152 | **Record locking — circumstances other than a locked logical record that return a locked record status**, §9.1.16, conditionally required (on such circumstances existing) + documented if provided | **Provided: one circumstance, a transaction's HOLDING (kb/Work PB3337).** §9.1.16 permits them ("The implementor may specify circumstances other than a locked logical record that result in the return of a locked record status."). Under an active APPLY COMMIT clause, a WRITE, REWRITE or DELETE of a relative or indexed file HOLDS the record it changed — a DELETEd record's identity included, which stays held after the record is gone, so another file connector's WRITE of a record with that prime key or relative record number answers `51` — and every value of an alternate key declared without DUPLICATES that its change frees, so another connector's WRITE or REWRITE that would insert that value answers `51` (docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.1.10, findings R2-3 and R2-4). A record a transaction changed is likewise `51` to another connector's READ that does not specify IGNORING LOCK. Under an active APPLY COMMIT clause on a SEQUENTIAL file (kb/Work PB3340; DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.2.3) the transaction's holdings are read from its journal: every live transaction holds the END of the file, so another connector's WRITE answers `51`; a record it rewrote, and every record it appended, are `51` to another connector's REWRITE and to a READ that does not specify IGNORING LOCK; once its file is replaced (an OPEN OUTPUT or a DELETE FILE) it holds the whole file. Under `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` or `READ ONLY` the host refuses the other connector's handle first, so only `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` meets them. "Another connector" includes a connector of the same run unit that no APPLY COMMIT clause names; a RETRY phrase does not wait for a holding of the executing run unit's own transaction (it cannot end while the statement runs), and RETRY FOREVER then ends with `52` (A.1 item 109). The holdings are kept IN THE FILE, so they outlive the owner's handle, and last until the transaction's COMMIT or ROLLBACK or the rollback its owner's death brings (the next writable statement that meets one rolls a dead owner back and evaluates its own conditions again). The test is made after the statement's invalid key conditions (which ignore locks, §14.9.51.4 GR33/GR42) and before the record is touched, and the RETRY phrase applies (§14.9.51.4 GR16). Otherwise I-O status `51` (§9.1.13.8 item 1) is produced only for a record another file connector holds locked. Its producers are exactly four: `PhysicalFileTable.LockRecord` (the record's lock owner is a different connector), `FileRegistry.ConflictOnLockedRecord` (`PhysicalFileTable.IsLockedByOther`), `KeyedConnector.HoldingsGate` (a holding of another transaction) and `SequentialJournal.Holdings.Conflict` (a sequential file's journaled holding of another live transaction). A new producer turns the pinning drift test red, which is this row's re-adjudication trigger. | `unit:LockedRecordStatusProducersDriftTests.LockedRecordStatus_IsProducedOnlyWhereAnotherConnectorHoldsTheLock`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.A_transactions_changes_are_held_against_every_other_connector`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.Every_holding_of_a_transaction_is_found_by_its_commit_or_rollback`; `unit:SequentialCommitControlTests.A_read_not_ignoring_lock_meets_the_records_a_live_transaction_holds`; `unit:SequentialCommitControlTests.A_statement_meeting_another_run_units_journal_holding_retries_under_its_retry_phrase`; `unit:SequentialCommitControlTests.A_holding_of_this_run_units_own_transaction_is_not_waited_for`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb669_lock_visibility_plain_connector` |
| DOC-A.1-28 | **Commit and rollback — interaction with other facilities and languages**, §9.1.18, optional (documented if provided) | **Provided for every file §9.1.18.2 admits** (§5, A.4.3: Claimed; kb/Work PB3337, PB3338 and PB3492 for RELATIVE and INDEXED files, PB3340 for SEQUENTIAL and LINE SEQUENTIAL ones). **Another program reading a sequential file under commit control** reads it as it stands, uncommitted changes included: the transaction's journal lives in transient files in the file's lock directory and the file itself carries nothing of it (DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.2.4). **File sharing and record locking:** a file subject to an active APPLY COMMIT clause takes the implicit LOCK MODE IS AUTOMATIC WITH LOCK ON MULTIPLE RECORDS (§9.1.16: "For files subject to commit and rollback the LOCK clause and the UNLOCK statement shall not be specified", refused by name, COBOL2974), and the records a transaction changed are HELD against every other file connector, of this run unit or another, until its COMMIT or ROLLBACK (I-O status `51`, A.1 item 152); a dead run unit's holdings are rolled back by the next writable statement that meets one. **Other languages:** the only non-COBOL component a run unit can contain is a .NET host that activates COBOL programs (A.1 item 167); COMMIT and ROLLBACK act on the run unit's COBOL file connectors and APPLY COMMIT data items only, and nothing outside them (a .NET transaction, a database) joins the transaction. | `conformance:cases/14.9.36-ROLLBACK/pb3338_apply_commit_rollback`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.A_transactions_changes_are_held_against_every_other_connector`; `unit:SequentialCommitControlTests.A_live_transaction_refuses_another_run_units_write_and_open_output_and_delete_file` |
