| DOC-A.1-200 | **Text manipulation — stage of processing the LISTING and PAGE directives and the SUPPRESS phrase of COPY**, §7.3.18.1 + §7.3.19.1 + §7.2.3.4 GR4, conditional (on the implementor producing listings), need not be documented | **Condition absent.** The compiler never produces a source listing (item 117), so the stage at which these three listing controls are processed has no effect to document. `>>LISTING` is ignored (§7.3.18.3 GR1, "If the compiler does not produce a source listing, the LISTING directive shall be ignored"), `>>PAGE` has no effect (§7.3.19.4 GR3, "If a source listing is not being produced, a PAGE directive shall have no effect."), and COPY's SUPPRESS PRINTING phrase affects only the listing (§7.2.3.4 GR4): the library text is incorporated in full. All three are accepted and inert (`DirectiveStateRegistry`, NONE HELD; `CopyProcessor.ParseCopyStatement`, which parses SUPPRESS [PRINTING] in its general-format place, before the REPLACING phrase — kb/Work PB1354). Contingent: re-adjudicate if a listing is ever produced. | `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w59h_listing_stage_inert`; `conformance:cases/7.3.18-LISTING/pb725_directive_facility` |
| DOC-A.1-14 | **CALL statement — runtime resources that are checked**, §14.9.4.4 GR3c, required + documented | **One runtime resource is checked: the stack the activation needs.** When the program is located (§14.9.4.4 GR3b), the CALL is not successful if the thread running the run unit has less than an activation's reserve of stack left — 1 MiB on the run unit's own thread, whose stack is 384 MiB and on which the run unit's main program always runs, or the .NET runtime's own 128 KB margin on a host thread that activates COBOL directly. Then **EC-PROGRAM-RESOURCES** is set (GR3c; fatal, Table 13), nothing of the activation has been set up, and execution continues per GR3h: the ON EXCEPTION phrase, a declarative, or the §14.6.12 abnormal termination with its §14.6.11 implicit CLOSE. A minimal RECURSIVE program under `>>TURN EC-ALL CHECKING ON` reaches about 100,000 activations before the check fails (measured 104,585 on Windows and 92,137 on Linux; 256,126 without checking; kb/Work PB2659), and the activation past that is a defined condition, never a process kill. The check comes first, before GR3d–f (`ActivationStack.IsAvailable`, asked by `ProgramTable.CallProgram`). GnuCOBOL defines no outcome here — 3.2 dies of SIGSEGV after 74,687 activations of the same minimal program on its default 8 MB stack — so the standard's own GR3c governs, and the stack size is chosen so that the same program reaches GnuCOBOL's depth under full checking. Locating is not a resource check, and a failure to locate is “the program cannot be located”: a callee is located when it is registered in the run unit's program table — compiled into the calling assembly, or a separately compiled module in the application directory whose registration member `__CobolModule.EnsureRegistered()` has registered it (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule` asks `RepositoryLocator` for the program: the file `<program-name>.dll` first, and only when that file does not carry the program, the `Units` index every module's `CobolRepository` record holds, so a program whose assembly is not named after it is found too; the record, with the registrar it names, is read as metadata before anything is loaded; the rest of the locating mechanics are implementor-defined, see items 15 and 16). A module file that exists but cannot be loaded (a truncated or foreign image, or a dependency the registrar itself needs) or whose registrar throws for any reason, or that the run unit refuses (`ProgramTable.RegisterModule`: another runtime major or call ABI, or an outermost name another module already registered), or of which two different assemblies carry the program's name, or that is of another repository schema, has therefore NOT been located; and neither has a registered program whose class or dependency the CLR cannot load or initialize when its instance is created (`ProgramTable.Create`: a missing dependency assembly, a static initializer that throws), which is the same missing assembly whether the CLR loads it inside the registrar or later, so the condition never depends on when it is loaded. The CALL takes GR3b's arm: **EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND** with the loader's or the module's own reason, the call is not successful, and execution continues per GR3h (ON EXCEPTION, or the checking-state disposition). A trimmed or ahead-of-time application has no dynamic probe: the switch `WiseOwl.Cobol.Runtime.DynamicProbe` is on unless the application sets it false, which such an application does (a native-AOT application that leaves it on finds no assembly loader by path, and the probe's CALL is EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND with that reason). Its CALL to a program no host registered is EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND saying so. Treating a module that cannot be loaded as not located follows GnuCOBOL under CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence — libcob's resolver sets EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND when a module is found but cannot be loaded — except that GnuCOBOL also prints a runtime warning naming the module's path, which WiseOwl COBOL does not issue. The same determination serves a user-defined function (item 89) and an invoked method (item 102). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_call_unloadable_module_not_found`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2101_locate_program_not_named_after_its_file`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2101_locate_two_assemblies_one_name`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2101_locate_named_file_beside_a_copy`; `conformance-test:RunTimeLocateFaultTests.ARegistrarThatThrows_ThroughTheProbe_IsProgramNotFoundNamingTheFault`; `conformance-test:RunTimeLocateFaultTests.ARegisteredProgramWhoseDependencyIsMissing_IsProgramNotFoundWithTheLoadersMessage`; `conformance-test:RunTimeLocateFaultTests.AProgramWhoseStaticInitializerThrows_IsProgramNotFound`; `unit:RepositoryLocatorTests.TheNamedFile_IsTheAnswer_AndNothingElseIsRead`; `conformance:cases/14.9.4-CALL/pb2659_call_resources_recursion`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2659-call-resources-below-2002`; `conformance-test:ActivationResourcesTests.UnhandledCall_PastTheStack_EndsAbnormally_AndClosesTheRunUnitsFiles`; `unit:ActivationStackTests.RecursiveCall_PastTheStack_IsEcProgramResources_AndUnwindsBalanced`; `unit:ActivationStackTests.RunUnitThread_RefusesAnActivation_BeforeTheRuntimesOwnMarginIsReached` |
| DOC-A.1-20 | **Case mapping (compile-time, of the COBOL character repertoire)**, §8.1.3 (§8.1.3.2 GR1 with GR3 b) and GR4 b)), required + documented | **WiseOwl COBOL's compile-time case mapping IS Annex C (C.2 General case mappings) of the edition being compiled, applied as a fold from uppercase to lowercase** — the Unicode simple lowercase mapping of the Annex B characters that the A.1 item 20 NOTE recommends (C.2's own NOTE: the Changes_When_Lowercased property, Unicode 13.0.0). **Basic letters:** A–Z fold to a–z everywhere outside the non-hexadecimal forms of alphanumeric and national literals (§8.1.3.2 GR3 a/b), so `WS-Total` and `ws-total` are one word. **Extended letters** (A.4.6, claimed in §5): an uppercase extended letter folds to the lowercase letter C.2 pairs it with, and a letter C.2 does not list folds to nothing but itself (GR4 b), so `CAFÉ` and `café` are one word while dotless `ı` (U+0131) is distinct from `i` at COBOL 2023. The per-edition differences follow the annex: COBOL 2023 deletes `(0131,0069)` and `(03C2,03C3)` (E.2 item 14) and adds the E.3.3 item 6 pairs, so a 2002/2014 compilation folds by the older list. **Implementation:** ONE fold, `CobolNames` (the C.2 table transcribed from this standard by `scripts/spec/gen_annex_bc.py`, `AnnexBCDriftTests`), keys every name table and every word comparison of the compiler, the frontend and the run-time externalized-name match (`ExternalizedNames`, INVOKE's method-name dispatch); .NET's ordinal-ignore-case comparison, which disagrees with C.2 on the extended letters, is barred there (`CobolNameFoldDriftTests`). The table is COBOL 2023's; below 2023 the lexer writes E.2 item 14's two letters (U+0131, U+03C2) in their edition's fold, which is the only difference a COBOL 2002/2014 word can observe — every mapping E.3.3 item 6 added pairs a character those editions' Annex B lacks (kb/Work PB1402). This compile-time mapping governs COBOL WORDS only; the RUNTIME mapping of the UPPER-CASE / LOWER-CASE functions is the separate §3 determination (the .NET invariant tables, or a locale's LC_CTYPE), and item 43's currency-symbol equivalence is its own rule. | `unit:CobolNameFoldDriftTests.Same_IsTheAnnexCFold`; `unit:AnnexBCDriftTests.AnnexCLists_EqualTheSpec`; `conformance:cases/8.1.3-COBOL-character-repertoire/pb1402_extended_letters_2023` |
| DOC-A.1-23 | **Characters prohibited from use in text-words in COPY … REPLACING and REPLACE**, §7.2.2.5 rule 3, required + documented | **NONE — WiseOwl COBOL prohibits no character in, or as, a text-word.** Any character of the compile-time coded character set (UTF-16, item 25) that is not a separator is an ordinary text-word character, whether or not it is in the COBOL character repertoire: `==éVAL==`, `==@Y~==` and `==€X==` are pseudo-text operands like any other and match exactly the text-words they spell, in both COPY … REPLACING and REPLACE, at every edition. What bounds a text-word is the §8.3.5 separator set (with the §7.2.2.5 rule 1 colon and parenthesis cases), and the end of a source line — and nothing else (a horizontal tab U+0009 never reaches the text-word stage: the line-entry stage expands every tab to spaces before anything reads the line, as GnuCOBOL's reader does, item 157) — so a character that merely LOOKS like a space but is not the COBOL character space — U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE, U+2000–U+200A, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+0085 — is a text-word character, and `==P<U+00A0>Q==` is ONE text-word that matches `P<U+00A0>Q` and never the two words `P Q`. Whether the text that results from replacement is a legal COBOL word is decided afterwards by the ordinary lexical rules, not by the text-manipulation pass. The separator-space set is ONE predicate, `TextWordScanner.IsSeparatorSpace` (space and line end — the lexer's `WS` set), used by every text-word boundary the text-manipulation stage draws (kb/Work PB1543). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1543_nbsp_is_a_text_word_character`; `unit:TextManipulationTextWordTests.UnicodeSpaceLookalike_IsATextWordCharacter` |
| DOC-A.1-25 | **COBOL character repertoire — encoding of, mapping of, substitute graphics**, §8.1.3.2 GR1 and GR5, required + documented | **Mapping:** every basic letter, basic digit, basic special character and extended letter maps to its ISO/IEC 10646 code point, held as UTF-16 — one coded character set serves both the alphanumeric and the national class, so the two share one numbering and GR1's alphanumeric-to-national correspondence is the identity (`A` is U+0041 in both; the figurative and editing values are item 32's row). **Encoding of source text:** decided per file (item 26's row): a byte-order mark selects UTF-8, UTF-16LE/BE or UTF-32, and a file with no mark is read as UTF-8. **A file with no mark that is not well-formed UTF-8 is read as ISO/IEC 8859-1 instead** — every byte is the character with that code point, so no source byte is lost or altered (a 0xE9 byte in `VALUE "A<0xE9>B"` is `é`, U+00E9, `FUNCTION ORD` 234) — and the compiler issues the WARNING COBOL5435 naming the file and the offset of the first byte that is not UTF-8, so the choice is never silent. **A file whose byte-order mark names an encoding its content is not well-formed in** (invalid UTF-8 after `EF BB BF`, a lone surrogate in UTF-16, a UTF-32 unit beyond U+10FFFF) **is the compile-time ERROR COBOL5434 naming the file and the byte offset** — there is no fallback for a marked file, because the mark states the encoding. No source character is ever replaced by U+FFFD or any other stand-in. This is the byte-preserving disposition GnuCOBOL takes under CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence (cobc runs no conversion on source text, so each byte is one character with that byte's code). **Substitute graphics:** none; every character of the COBOL repertoire has its own graphic in ISO/IEC 10646, so GR5 never applies. The same at every edition. Decoded in `SourceTextDecoder`, the one place a source or library text's bytes become characters (`CompilationInputs.ReadSourceText` reads and reports; each file draws a finding at most once). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_encoding_per_file_bom`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_encoding_unmarked_non_utf8_is_latin1`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_encoding_marked_malformed_is_refused`; `unit:SourceTextDecoderTests.UnmarkedNonUtf8_IsLatin1_EveryByteItsOwnCodePoint`; `unit:SourceTextDecoderTests.Utf8Mark_WithInvalidContent_IsMalformed` |
| DOC-A.1-31 | **Computer's coded character set — the characters in and the encoding of the alphanumeric and national coded character sets, and the encoding for USAGE DISPLAY and USAGE NATIONAL**, §8.1.2 (with §8.3.3.2.3 SR2 and §8.3.3.5.3 SR2 for source representation), required + documented | **ONE coded character set serves both classes: the UTF-16 Basic Multilingual Plane, one code unit per character position** (the standing UTF-16 repertoire decision, applied in kb/Work R48's second section; items 33, 188). The alphanumeric and the national coded character set each contain all 65,536 BMP code units; a character outside the BMP is a surrogate pair occupying two character positions (§8.5.1.4, item 213). **In memory** every character is its UTF-16 code unit, whatever the item's class. **USAGE NATIONAL** is two bytes per character position, the code unit most significant byte first (UTF-16BE, item 213). **USAGE DISPLAY** is one byte per character position in ISO/IEC 8859-1 (item 209), under the **storage-byte law** (owner decisions kb/Work R51 / R52; kb/Work PB1759; design WISEOWL_COBOL_FILES D29; `WiseOwl.Cobol.Runtime.StorageByte`): a character U+0000–U+00FE is the byte of the same value and the byte 0xFF is the HIGH-VALUE character U+FFFF (§8.3.3.6.4 GR6 — the highest of the 65,536 native characters), so the characters with a DISPLAY byte image are U+0000–U+00FF and U+FFFF, and **U+00FF and U+FFFF share the byte 0xFF**. The same law images and decodes every byte-form storage position (binary, packed, IEEE, pointer, bit, a national item's UTF-16BE pairs in a record image — a character's byte is its low-order byte), which is what keeps `MOVE HIGH-VALUES TO REC` followed by `IF REC = HIGH-VALUES` TRUE for a record with a COMP field (§14.9.25.4 GR4 moves a group "without conversion of data from one form of internal representation to another"). **Accepted cost (owner R52):** a real `ÿ` (U+00FF) that passes through a byte — the medium of a fixed-record file, or a byte-form storage position — returns as HIGH-VALUE; in an alphanumeric item in memory it stays U+00FF (write it as the literal `"ÿ"` or `FUNCTION CHAR(256)`). **The hexadecimal literal `X"FF"` is the byte 0xFF, not that character** (kb/Work PB2919, which reversed this row's earlier statement that it stayed U+00FF): §8.3.3.2.4 GR4 gives each literal character "the bit configuration specified by" its digit pair, so the pair `FF` takes the law's character, U+FFFF, the HIGH-VALUE character — the same one a binary or packed item's byte 0xFF has through a REDEFINES, so `IF GX = X"FFFFFFFE"` is TRUE for the alphanumeric view of a binary -2, and `X"FF"` equals `HIGH-VALUE` as it does in IBM, Micro Focus and GnuCOBOL. **Any other character above U+00FF has no DISPLAY byte image, and WiseOwl COBOL never loses it silently.** At an in-memory byte channel (the storage image read by CONVERT's ANY, HEX and BYTE legs, a REDEFINES or group image through a national, bit, binary, packed or floating-point view) it becomes `?` (0x3F) and EC-DATA-CONVERSION is set (item 33's decided disposition; `StorageByte.ImageByte` is the one run-time reader, kb/Work PB547, and `StorageByte.ToByte` the same law without the condition, so a class test and the value it guards agree; the condition rides every statement of a checking-on region, `EcBinder.AmbientRaises`). At a FIXED-RECORD file with no CODE-SET clause — record sequential, report, relative and indexed files (owner decision kb/Work R47) — the WRITE or REWRITE of a record holding one is UNSUCCESSFUL with the implementor's I-O status `'91'` (§9.1.13.11; item 110), nothing reaches the medium, and the record area is unchanged. A print line is no exception: it is written one byte per column in the same set, U+0080–U+00FF included, with no print-specific character map (item 159). `FileCharacterSet` is the fixed-record set's one executable copy (`ToChannel` / `FromChannel` apply the law at the medium), and every record write encodes through its STRICT ISO/IEC 8859-1 encoding, whose exception fallback makes a write that skipped the refusal fail loudly instead of writing `?`. Every byte read decodes by the law (0xFF as U+FFFF). **A LINE SEQUENTIAL file with no CODE-SET clause is UTF-8 TEXT** (owner decision kb/Work R51, superseding R47 for that organization; kb/Work PB1760; item 115; `LineSequentialEncoding`): every character a record area holds round-trips, U+00FF included, and only a character outside the line sequential character set is refused (`'71'`). A CODE-SET clause selects the medium encoding instead (§5 row 27), and the CODE-SET alphabet's coded character set then decides what can be written: a character it does not represent is refused with the same '91' / '71' (item 187; kb/Work PB1542). **Source representation:** a source file is read as UTF-8 unless a byte-order mark names UTF-16 or UTF-32 (ISO/IEC 8859-1 when it has no mark and is not well-formed UTF-8, item 25), and every source character is designated a character of both compile-time sets, so an alphanumeric or a national literal may contain any BMP character; the compile-time and runtime sets are the same (item 34), e.g. `FUNCTION ORD("€")` is 8365. Every edition (the national set from 2002). | `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide`; `conformance:cases/15.26.4-Returned-value-rules/pb59_repertoire_identity`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb690_file_character_set_85`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb690_line_sequential_byte_image_2023`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.FileCharacterSet_IsLatin1_AndRefusesRatherThanReplaces`; `conformance:cases/8.3.3.2-Alphanumeric-literals/pb2919_hex_literal_ff_is_the_storage_byte`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb547_redefines_national_view_of_wide_character`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb547_redefines_binary_and_bit_views_of_wide_character`; `unit:StorageImageByteTests.NatReadWindow_ReadsAWideCharacterAsTheSubstituteByte_AndSetsDataConversion` ||
| DOC-A.1-36 | **Computer's coded character set — when alphanumeric and national are one composite set, the characters that map into each**, §8.1.2, conditionally required (condition met: one UTF-16 set serves both classes, item 31) + documented | **Every character maps into BOTH sets: the alphanumeric and the national coded character set are the same 65,536 UTF-16 BMP code units** (the standing UTF-16 repertoire decision, applied in kb/Work R48's second section; item 31). No character is national-only and none is alphanumeric-only, so a PIC X item may hold every character a PIC N item may, a MOVE between the classes is the identity (item 33), and no character in an alphanumeric item is ever mixed alphanumeric and national data (item 38). Which characters have a ONE-BYTE USAGE DISPLAY image (U+0000–U+00FF) is the encoding question, answered by item 31, not a mapping: a character above U+00FF is still an alphanumeric character, and only its byte image is refused or substituted there. Every edition from 2002 (the national set). | `conformance:cases/15.26.4-Returned-value-rules/pb59_repertoire_identity`; `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide` |
| DOC-A.1-38 | **Computer's coded character set — whether UTF-8 or mixed alphanumeric and national characters are recognized in class alphanumeric, and the applicable syntax and general rules**, §8.1.2; §8.3.3.2.3 SR2; §8.3.3.2.4 GR3 c), conditionally required (on providing the capability) + documented if provided | **Not provided — and no character needs it.** Every UTF-16 BMP character is a character of the alphanumeric coded character set (items 31, 36), so a format 1 alphanumeric literal or an alphanumeric data item containing `€` or `Ж` holds only alphanumeric characters, one per character position; mixed alphanumeric and national data cannot arise. UTF-8 is not recognized in class alphanumeric: a UTF-8 source file is decoded before lexing, so `"€é"` is two characters (`FUNCTION LENGTH` 2), never the three or more bytes of its UTF-8 form, and no option keeps the bytes. There are therefore no additional syntax rules (SR2) or general rules (GR3 c) to specify. Every edition from 2002. | `conformance:cases/12.3.7-SPECIAL-NAMES/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide` |
| DOC-A.1-39 | **CONTINUE statement — precision and maximum size of the AFTER interval**, §14.9.9.4 GR1, required + documented | **m = 0, n = 5, and the maximum meaningful value is 86,400 seconds (one day)** (`CobolTiming.MaxSeconds`). The interval behaves as a temporary `9(5)` item with no decimal places: a value of arithmetic-expression-1 **greater than 86,400 — however large, in any arithmetic mode and whatever the expression's form (literal, data item, product, quotient, power) — puts 86,400 in the temporary**, so the program is suspended for one day and never for less; any other value is stored by the implicit COMPUTE without ROUNDED, so a fraction truncates toward zero (`CONTINUE AFTER 1.9 SECONDS` suspends 1 second, `0.999…` suspends none). A value below zero is set to 0 and, with FC-CONTINUE-LESS-THAN-ZERO checking enabled, raises the nonfatal EC-CONTINUE-LESS-THAN-ZERO (GR1 a–c). **A floating-point interval that is not finite takes the rule of its kind** (kb/Work PB2841; an infinity is a number in ISO/IEC 60559 and a NaN is not, the PB2647 determination): −∞ is a value below zero (GR1 a–c), +∞ is a number above the maximum (the program is suspended for 86,400 seconds, exactly as for 10^30), and a NaN is no number and so a zero interval (the disposition a NaN has landing in a fixed-point item): no suspension, no condition. None of them is EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE, which §14.6.13.2 item 3 limits to a sending operand described with a standard floating-point usage and which is raised where such an operand is read, so a `FLOAT-LONG` or `COMP-2` interval never raises it. Because m = 0, the processor-dependent fractional precision of Annex A.3 item 8 is not claimed (§2 row 8). COBOL 2023 only (CONTINUE AFTER is new in 2023). The interval is evaluated once and handed to the runtime on the carrier it evaluated on (the scaled `Int128`, the unsigned-wide `UInt128`, the standard-decimal `CobolDec` or binary64), and `CobolTiming.ContinueAfter` takes its sign and its whole seconds from that value in its own domain through the carrier's saturating reader (`CobolNum.PositionOf`), so a value past every host integer — 2^64, 2^64 + 3, 10^40, a 16-byte unsigned `COMP-5` item at or above 2^127 — is above the maximum and suspends exactly 86,400 seconds (kb/Work PB1529; witnesses are observed through `CobolTiming.SuspensionObserver`, never timed). | `unit:CobolTimingTests.HugeInterval_SuspendsForTheMaximumMeaningfulValue`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.ScaledLane_HugeInterval_SuspendsForTheMaximum`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.UnsignedWideLane_HugeInterval_SuspendsForTheMaximum`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.SdidiLane_HugeInterval_SuspendsForTheMaximum`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.ContinueAfterCall_IsTotalOverTheNumXCarriers_AndNarrowsNothing`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.CompiledProgram_EveryLaneSuspendsForTheMaximum_NeverForTheWrappedValue`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.CompiledProgram_StandardDecimal_EveryExpressionSuspendsForTheMaximum`; `unit:CobolTimingTests.NonFiniteInterval_TakesTheRuleOfItsKind_NeverEcDataNotFinite`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2841_continue_after_non_finite` |
| DOC-A.1-40 | **COPY statement — rules for identifying and locating default library text**, §7.2.3.3 SR5 and §7.2.3.4 GR3 (with GR2), required + documented | **The default COBOL library is an ordered list of places, searched in GnuCOBOL's order** (CLAUDE.md rule 1: the standard leaves both the list and the search to the implementor): (1) the compiler process's current working directory — the name is first tried as a path relative to it, or as written when it is absolute; (2) each `--copy DIR` in command-line order; (3) with `--nist`, the `copylib` directory beside the source file's directory. The source file's own directory is searched only when it is one of these — as in GnuCOBOL 3.2, whose own testsuite carries "COPY: relative copybooks" (a COPY resolved against the including source's directory) as an expected failure, not implemented. The same list serves every COPY in the compilation group, including a COPY inside library text. **Locating a text:** text-name-1 is used as spelled; literal-1's content is a host path (SR5: any non-empty host path is an allowable literal-1 or literal-2) — its VALUE, so a doubled quotation symbol is one character and a hexadecimal-format `X"…"` names the characters its digit pairs encode; a national or boolean literal, a concatenation expression or a figurative constant is refused as COBOL2450 (SR4/SR5; kb/Work PB1354). The literal forms (literal-1, literal-2) are a COBOL-2002 introduction (constructs row `copy-literal-name-2002`, VCR row 7.44, edge derived; kb/Work PB1601): `--std 85` names a text only by a word and refuses a literal as COBOL0900. In each place in turn WiseOwl COBOL tries the name as spelled and then with the suffixes `.CPY`, `.CBL`, `.COB`, `.cpy`, `.cbl`, `.cob`, in that order (a name whose FILE NAME — the part after the last directory separator — already contains a period is tried only as spelled; `"../lib/BOOK"` still takes the suffixes), and the FIRST regular file that exists IS the library text; so a text-name names exactly one text in a library (SR3) and no ambiguity is diagnosed. If `BK3.cbl` and `BK3.cob` sit in one directory, `COPY BK3` is `BK3.cbl`. Whether letter case in the name matters is the host file system's rule; the text found is named, in every diagnostic, the line map and the dependency record, by its directory entry's own spelling and never by the spelling that was probed (on a case-insensitive file system the probe `BOOK.CPY` finds `book.cpy` and the text is `book.cpy`; `CompilationInputs.LocateFile`, kb/Work PB1680). **OF/IN library-name-1 or literal-2** names a subdirectory: the FIRST place (in the same order) that holds a subdirectory of that name IS the library, and the text is located in it alone, with the same suffix rule. **A library that no place holds, or a text the library does not contain, is the compile-time error CBL3620** (GR2: the library shall be available): compilation fails, and there is no fallback from a named library to the default one and no silent omission of the COPY (GnuCOBOL's fallback to the default library, with a warning, is not followed: GR2 controls). The same at every edition. One mechanism implements all of it: `CopyProcessor.FindCopybook` over `LibraryPlaces` (the working directory, then the configured search paths) and `LocateInLibrary` (the name as spelled, then `CopybookSuffixes`); CBL3620 is reported by `CopyProcessor.ResolveOneCopy` on every path (kb/Work PB1355). The test harnesses name a golden's directory as a `--copy` path, as a user does, and the GnuCOBOL differential compiles each case as GnuCOBOL's testsuite runs `cobc`: in the case's directory, with its files at their own relative paths and each `-I DIR` passed as `--copy DIR`. | `conformance:wiseowl/cases/7.2.3-COPY/pb1355_library_text_located`; `conformance:cases/7.2.3-COPY/pb1355-library-text-not-found`; `conformance:cases/7.2.3-COPY/pb1355-library-not-available`; `unit:TextManipulationStatementTests.LibraryText_APeriodInADirectoryPart_IsNotAnExtension`; `conformance-test:DiagnosticPositionTests.Copy_MainLinesStayMain_CopiedLinesNameTheCopybook` |
| DOC-A.1-46 | **Data storage — possible representations when the implementation provides multiple ways of storing data**, §8.5.1.1, conditionally required (the condition HOLDS: WiseOwl COBOL stores data in several usages) + documented | **The complete specification is the USAGE clause's: ONE fixed representation per usage, no per-compilation-unit option, each pinned in full by its own row.** **DISPLAY** — one byte per character position (item 209). A position holds a UTF-16 code unit (items 33 and 188); a code unit above U+00FF has no one-byte image, and at every IN-MEMORY byte channel (the storage image seen through a REDEFINES or a containing group by a national, bit, binary, packed or floating-point view, CONVERT's BYTE/HEX/ANY legs) it reads as `?` (0x3F) **and EC-DATA-CONVERSION is set** — item 33's decided disposition (`StorageByte.ImageByte`, kb/Work PB547), never a silent truncation to the low-order byte; at the FILE channel the WRITE or REWRITE of such a record is refused with the implementor-defined I-O status `'91'` and nothing reaches the medium (item 31, owner decision R47). **NATIONAL** — two bytes per position, UTF-16BE (item 213). **BINARY / COMPUTATIONAL / COMP / COMP-4** — big-endian two's complement of the unscaled value in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes by PICTURE digit count (items 205, 208); **COMP-5** has the same representation and owns its full container range (item 208). **BINARY-CHAR / -SHORT / -LONG / -DOUBLE** — 1, 2, 4, 8 bytes, big-endian two's complement (items 206, 207). **PACKED-DECIMAL / COMP-3** — BCD, two digits per byte, trailing sign nibble (item 215; `PIC S9(5) COMP-3` is 3 bytes). **FLOAT-SHORT / COMP-1 / FLOAT-BINARY-32** — IEEE 754 binary32, 4 bytes; **FLOAT-LONG / FLOAT-EXTENDED / COMP-2 / FLOAT-BINARY-64** — IEEE 754 binary64, 8 bytes; big-endian interchange bytes unless an endianness-phrase says otherwise (items 207, 48). **INDEX** — an 8-byte big-endian occurrence number (item 211). **POINTER, FUNCTION-POINTER, PROGRAM-POINTER, OBJECT REFERENCE** — one managed reference, 8 bytes by `FUNCTION BYTE-LENGTH` (items 216, 210, 214; PROGRAM-POINTER is item 217). **BIT** — one bit per boolean position, rounded up to whole bytes (`PIC 1(8) USAGE BIT` is 1 byte, `PIC 1(9)` is 2); a boolean item of usage DISPLAY is one character position per boolean position. Figurative constants: item 74. **Not provided** (refused by name, COBOL1564 / COBOL1943): FLOAT-BINARY-128 and FLOAT-DECIMAL-16/-34 (§2, Annex A.3 items 17 and 19) and MESSAGE-TAG (A.3 item 4). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb547_redefines_national_view_of_wide_character`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb547_redefines_binary_and_bit_views_of_wide_character` |
| DOC-A.1-49 | **DEFINE directive — mechanism for providing the value of a compilation-variable-name from the operating environment**, §7.3.11.4 GR4, required + documented | **The compiler process's environment variable whose name is the compilation-variable-name in its canonical UPPER-CASE spelling** — `CobolNames.UpperFold`, the Annex C fold of §8.1.3.2 GR3 b) and GR4 b) with the basic letters then written A-Z, the one upper-case key of every COBOL word in the compiler (an extended letter stays in its fold, because Annex C maps only from upper case to lower) — read once, when the `>>DEFINE … AS PARAMETER` directive is processed. A compilation-variable-name is a COBOL word, so every spelling of one name (`MyVar`, `MYVAR`, `myvar`, and a spelling Annex C.2 makes the same word, such as the Kelvin sign for `K`) reads the SAME variable, `MYVAR`, on every host, including a host whose environment names are case-sensitive; two names Annex C keeps apart (a long s and `S`) read two variables (kb/Work PB2990). **No value ⇒ the name is NOT defined** (GR4's second sentence), and a definition it had before the directive is removed. **The FORM of a value is the implementor's (GR4), and GnuCOBOL 3.2 decides it** (`cobc/ppparse.y`, the `PARAMETER` action and `ppp_check_needs_quote`; CLAUDE.md rule 1; kb/Work PB1626): the classification is SYNTACTIC, on the text exactly as the environment holds it, at EVERY edition, and does not depend on a numeric type's range. (1) An absent variable, an EMPTY variable and a variable whose text BEGINS WITH A SPACE make no value available. (2) A text that begins with a quotation symbol is ONE quoted literal when a closing delimiter of that symbol ends it (a doubled quotation symbol is content, §8.3.3.2.3 3)): the name is defined with that literal (`"ab""c"` is `ab"c`, `'x y'` is `x y`, `"7"` is alphanumeric); one that is not so closed — `"abc`, `"a"b"`, `"a" & "b"` — makes no value (GnuCOBOL tests only the first and last characters; this compiler holds the text to one literal). (3) A text that is the SPELLING of a fixed-point numeric literal (§8.3.3.3.2: at least one digit, at most one sign and it the leftmost character, at most one decimal point and never the rightmost — `7`, `007`, `-2.5`, `+.5`) is NUMERIC, of ANY length, and its value is made by the path a numeric literal written in the directive takes (`>>DEFINE X AS 12…`), so a 29-31-digit value is numeric whatever the edition's compile-time arithmetic mode, and a value of more than 31 digits is refused (COBOL1619, naming the directive) where that path refuses the same literal, at the definition (GnuCOBOL reports it at the use). `5.` is not a numeric literal's spelling (§8.3.3.3.2 3)), so — unlike GnuCOBOL, which calls it numeric — it is alphanumeric. (4) Any other text — `1,000`, `1E5`, `7x`, `7 ` (a trailing space is content) — is ALPHANUMERIC with the text exactly as given. The one implementing site is `DefineParameterValue.Classify`. Every read is recorded on the compilation's inputs (`CompilationInputs.EnvironmentReads`). The same lookup serves the DISPLAY directive's PARAMETER operand (item 55). | `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_TwoSpellingsOfOneName_ReadOneVariable`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_ValueCategory_FollowsTheDocumentedTyping`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_Unavailable_NotDefined`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_SourcesFromEnvironment`; `unit:ParameterVariableNameTests.Define_ReadsTheVariableOfTheCanonicalSpelling`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_NoValue_LeavesTheNameUndefined`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_ThirtyOneDigitValue_IsNumericAtEveryEdition`; `unit:ConditionalCompilationDefineTests.Parameter_ThirtyTwoDigitValue_RefusedAtTheDefinition`; `unit:DefineParameterValueTests.Classify_IsSyntactic`; `unit:DefineParameterValueTests.FixedPointLiteralForm_IsThe8_3_3_3_2_Spelling` |
| DOC-A.1-52 | **Devices that allow concurrent access**, §9.1.15 Sharing mode, required + documented | **All of them — the same determination as item 76, which answers the same §9.1.15 sentence.** Every physical file is a path in the host file system (a regular file, or a device path such as `/dev/null` that the host opens as a file), and every such path allows concurrent access: the SHARING clause and the SHARING phrase always apply, and a second connector's OPEN of the same file is decided by §9.1.15 Table 19 without testing the device (`FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt`, `PhysicalFileTable`). `ASSIGN TO PRINTER` and `ASSIGN TO DISK` name the same shareable file (item 71). This row states which devices allow concurrent access and nothing more: how strongly the file lock excludes ANOTHER run unit is §9.1.15's lock rule, open under kb/Work PB833, and the sharing mode used when none is specified is item 77, open under kb/Work PB322. | `conformance:cases/14.9.27-OPEN/l1c11_sharing_every_device_shareable` |
| DOC-A.1-53 | **DISPLAY directive — conversion of data transferred**, §7.3.12.4 GR1 (with GR2, GR4), required + documented | **Each operand is converted to a character image and the images of one directive are written as ONE line to the compiler's standard output, at compile time, during text manipulation.** The compiler produces no source listing (item 117), so GR2 makes the result the implementor's; WiseOwl COBOL follows GnuCOBOL (CLAUDE.md rule 1 precedence), which writes the operands to the compiler's standard output when the directive is processed. Conversion: an **alphanumeric or national literal** transfers its characters without the delimiters and with no other change; a **boolean literal or boolean-expression-1** transfers its value as the boolean characters `0` and `1`; an **arithmetic-expression-1** (a numeric literal included) is evaluated in compile-time arithmetic and transfers its value in the shortest decimal form: a leading `-` only when negative, at least one integer digit, and a `.` followed by the fraction digits only when the value is not an integer, with no trailing zeros (`42`, `-2.5`, `0.125`); a **PARAMETER** operand transfers the environment value's text unchanged (item 55). The images are joined in operand order (GR4) with ONE space between them and the line ends with the host newline — `>>DISPLAY "HELLO-COMPILE" 42` writes `HELLO-COMPILE 42`. With no UPON phrase (GR6's UPON LISTING) the line goes to standard output; UPON compile-time-device-1 is item 54. Nothing is added to the compiled program's own output. | `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.ConversionOfData_FollowsTheDeterminedImages`; `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.OperandsAreTransferredInOrderAsOneLine`; `conformance:cases/7.3.12-DISPLAY/pb807_display_directive_operands` |
| DOC-A.1-54 | **DISPLAY directive — meaning of compile-time-device-1**, §7.3.12.4 GR5 b), required + documented | **compile-time-device-1 is one of the OUTPUT-capable device-names of the SPECIAL-NAMES table (item 189), naming the same stream in the compiler process:** `CONSOLE` and `SYSOUT` — the compiler's standard output; `SYSERR` — the compiler's standard error. `SYSIN` (input only) and any other word are a compile-time error naming the available devices, from the one `ImplementorNames` table, so the directive and a SPECIAL-NAMES entry can never disagree about what a device-name means. `UPON LISTING` (GR5 a) goes to the device used for source listings; no listing is produced (item 117), so that device is the compiler's standard output, the same place as an omitted UPON phrase (GR6, item 53). An UPON phrase naming several devices, or devices and LISTING (§5.2.6.4 choice indicators, each at most once), writes the line once to each named destination, in the order written. | `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.Upon_NamesTheDestinations`; `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.Upon_BreakingItsFormat_IsDiagnosedAndTransfersNothing`; `conformance:cases/7.3.12-DISPLAY/pb807-display-directive-upon-input-device`; `conformance:cases/7.3.12-DISPLAY/pb807-display-directive-upon-listing-twice` |
| DOC-A.1-55 | **DISPLAY directive — mechanism for providing the value of a compilation-variable-name from the operating environment**, §7.3.12.4 GR3, required + documented | **The same mechanism as the DEFINE directive's PARAMETER phrase (item 49): the compiler process's environment variable whose name is the compilation-variable-name in its canonical UPPER-CASE spelling** (`CobolNames.UpperFold`), read when the DISPLAY directive is processed, so `PARAMETER MyVar` and `PARAMETER MYVAR` read the same variable on every host, and so do two spellings Annex C.2 makes one word (kb/Work PB2990). A present variable's text is transferred unchanged, with no numeric conversion and none of the DEFINE directive's classification (item 49 — which reads an empty variable as no value; the lookup is the same, what each directive makes of the text is its own) (item 53); an empty variable transfers an empty image. **When the variable is absent, that DISPLAY directive transfers nothing at all** — no line is written for any of its operands (GR3: "no transfer shall take place"). The name is not thereby defined as a compilation variable; only a DEFINE directive defines one. | `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.Parameter_IsReadFromTheEnvironment_ByTheUpperCaseName`; `unit:DisplayDirectiveTests.AbsentParameter_TransfersNothingAtAll`; `unit:ParameterVariableNameTests.Display_ReadsTheVariableOfTheCanonicalSpelling` |
| DOC-A.1-60 | **Dynamic-capacity table — determination of the highest permissible occurrence number**, §8.4.2.3.4 GR2 (with §8.5.1.9.6 GR2), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY — kept because item 62 and item 61 depend on it) | **The SMALLER of 1,073,741,823 (`0x3FFFFFFF`, `CobolDynTable.MaxOccurrences`) and the largest capacity the process can allocate at the moment the table grows**, for every dimension of every `OCCURS DYNAMIC` table, in every edition that has them. The constant is one fixed number for every element type and size, about HALF the .NET array-length limit (`Array.MaxLength` = 2,147,483,591 = `0x7FFFFFC7`), chosen so the doubling growth of item 61, clamped at the constant, never overflows a 32-bit length; the resource bound is what GR2's "may be affected by the availability of runtime resources" names, and it is reached when the managed heap cannot hold the grown table (item 61: each table is one managed array, grown by doubling). A growth past either bound — implicit, through a receiving reference, or explicit, through `SET … TO` — sets the **fatal EC-BOUND-TABLE-LIMIT** (§8.5.1.9.6 GR2) and leaves the capacity unchanged (§14.9.39.4 GR30); it never ends the run unit with a host out-of-memory failure that no COBOL exception condition names (`CobolDynTable.GrowTo` / `Enlarged` / `FromCurrentImage`; kb/Work PB1410). **The same constant is the maximum permissible value of integer-4 and integer-5** of Format 4 (§13.18.38.3 SR29: "The implementor shall specify a maximum permissible value for integer-4 and integer-5"): an `OCCURS DYNAMIC` FROM or TO value above 1,073,741,823 is refused at compile time, COBOL2647 (`DataBinder.DynamicBoundWithinMaximum`; kb/Work PB1264). | `unit:CobolDynTableTests.SetCapacity_BeyondRuntimeResources_LeavesTheCapacityUnchanged`; `conformance:cases/8.5.1.9.6-Exceeding-capacity/pb463_dyn_implementor_maximum` |
| DOC-A.1-63 | **Dynamic-length elementary items — structure when no dynamic-length-structure-name is specified**, §8.5.1.10.2 / §13.18.19.3 SR3, required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY — kept because it decides what a record holding such items looks like) | **A native .NET `System.String` holding the item's current content, one UTF-16 code unit per character position, with NO length field and NO delimiter**: the current length is the string's own length, from 0 up to the maximum size (item 62). The item is located outside the record it belongs to (§8.5.1.10.3 permits this; the record holds a reference). **In a record image** it contributes exactly its current content (each character position in item 209's or item 213's representation: two bytes, UTF-16BE, a national position, so a character past ISO 8859-1 is sent whole - the image of a record and of a group holding the item is its storage, A.1 item 57; kb/Work PB3441; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb3441_dynamic_national_member_record`), and a record that contains dynamic-length items is written with its extent table beside it on the storage medium (§3 D-FRA (v)): each variable-length member's offset and current length, which is not part of the record area or the record size. So a READ gives every member back at the length it was written with, even when two dynamic-length items are next to each other: `D1` = `ABC` and `D2` = `DE` written as one record read back as `ABC` (length 3) and `DE` (length 2). **A LINE SEQUENTIAL record has no frame to carry the table** (a line is plain text, §12.4.5.10.3 GR2; §3 D-FRA (x)): its contiguous image reads back exactly, but the members are split by the take step, so `D1` = `ABC` and `D2` = `DE` written as one line `ABCDE` read back with `D1` = `ABCDE` (the earlier member takes the excess, up to its maximum size) and `D2` empty. **In a file of FIXED-length records (an explicit RECORD clause Format 1) there is no frame to carry the table, so the record is carried in its FIXED FORM instead — each member at its maximum width, space padded, and read back without the trailing padding (§3 D-FRA (vi); `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb1562_fixed_clause_file_second_description`).** A structure named by a DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause (PREFIXED / DELIMITED) is §3 D-DL3, not this row. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1053_dynamic_members_both_sides` |
| DOC-A.1-66 | **External repository — mechanism for specifying whether checking and updating occur**, §8.13, required + documented | **The external repository is the metadata of compiled WiseOwl COBOL assemblies** (owner decision kb/Work R44): every program, function, class and interface assembly the compiler produces carries its source units' §8.13 signature information as .NET metadata, with a WiseOwl COBOL-owned metadata record for whatever .NET metadata cannot express. A `cobol` command option names the repository assemblies a compilation references; REPOSITORY-paragraph specifiers resolve against those assemblies and the compilation group's own definitions and prototypes, and a name that resolves to neither is diagnosed. **Updating** (§8.13's first mechanism): a compilation updates the repository by emitting that metadata into the assembly it produces, and a user-visible option chooses whether it does. **Checking** (§8.13's second mechanism): a user-visible option chooses whether differences between a prototype or definition in the compilation group and the signature recorded in a referenced repository assembly are flagged. The options' spellings and defaults are fixed by the R44 design doc (not yet written; kb/Work PB1086), which fills them into this row in the same change set. | — |
| DOC-A.1-67 | **External repository — information beyond the required information**, §8.13, optional (documented if provided) | **The external repository is the metadata of compiled WiseOwl COBOL assemblies** (owner decision kb/Work R44, 2026-09-24): the §8.13 information of each source unit is carried as .NET metadata, with a WiseOwl COBOL-owned metadata record for whatever .NET metadata cannot express. Whether that record holds anything beyond the §8.13 list (“any other information that the implementor requires”), and what, is fixed by the R44 design doc (kb/Work PB1086), which writes it into this row in the same change set. ⚠ Not yet implemented: no repository exists today, REPOSITORY-paragraph specifiers are never resolved against one (`CLASS NOSUCHCL PROGRAM NOSUCHPG` compiles and runs clean), and the compiler has no option to reference or update a repository — kb/Work PB1086. | — |
| DOC-A.1-68 | **Externalized names — formation and mapping rules**, §7.3.9.3 GR2 a) and b), §8.3.2.2, required + documented | **Formation.** An externalized name is a string of characters. For a name written as a COBOL word with no AS phrase (a program-name, a user-function-name, a class-name, an interface-name, an EXTERNAL data-name or file-name) it is the word's spelling. For a name given by an `AS literal` it is the literal's content with **leading and trailing spaces removed**; spaces inside the name are kept. A CALL, CANCEL, `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` or `ADDRESS OF FUNCTION` target and an INVOKE method name are formed the same way: a literal's content, or an identifier's content, with leading and trailing spaces removed. A name WRITTEN in source text as a literal (an AS literal, a CALL, CANCEL or `ADDRESS OF` literal, an INVOKE method-name literal) is also written in the edition's Annex C spelling (`ExternalizedNames.FormInEdition`, kb/Work PB2840), as the word it names was lexed: below 2023 `CALL "Z<final sigma>"` reaches `PROGRAM-ID. Z<sigma>` and `INVOKE O "X<final sigma>"` names `METHOD-ID. X<sigma>`, because Annex E.2 item 14 deleted the mappings of final sigma and dotless i at 2023 only; at 2023 they are two names. An identifier's content (a CALL, CANCEL, `SET program-pointer TO ENTRY` or `ADDRESS OF` target, a universal INVOKE's method name) is formed by the same function, which the emitted C# calls with the compiled program's edition (kb/Work PB2991), so `CALL WS-NAME` holding `Z<final sigma>` reaches `PROGRAM-ID. Z<sigma>` below 2023 exactly as the literal does; the run time itself compares every name by the 2023 table. One function forms and maps every one of these names, at bind time and at run time alike (`WiseOwl.Cobol.Runtime.ExternalizedNames`). An AS literal made only of spaces forms the zero-length name, which nothing can name, so it is refused (COBOL2643) wherever the clause itself refuses a zero-length literal: every AS clause except CLASS-ID, whose §11.3.3 SR1 admits one. ISO leaves formation to the implementor (§8.3.2.2). GnuCOBOL removes leading and trailing spaces, with a warning, from a CALL or CANCEL literal and from a literal program-name, but keeps an AS literal as written, so a GnuCOBOL program named `AS "trail  "` cannot be called. WiseOwl COBOL removes them from AS names too, so that every externalized name is formed by one rule, and gives a compile-time warning (COBOL2642) when an AS literal has leading or trailing spaces. **Mapping.** Two externalized names are the same name when they are equal ignoring case: `CALL "sub-p"` and `CALL "SUB-P"` both reach `PROGRAM-ID. SUB-P`, and `EXTERNAL AS "Shared Two"` and `EXTERNAL AS "shared two"` are one data item. A program with an AS phrase is reached by its AS name, never by its declared word. **CALL-CONVENTION (§7.3.9).** WiseOwl COBOL defines no call-convention-name. `>>CALL-CONVENTION COBOL` (the default, §7.3.9.3 GR1) is the only accepted form, so GR2 a) always applies: program-names and method-names in CALL, CANCEL, INVOKE and program-address-identifiers map by the COBOL-word rule above. `>>CALL-CONVENTION` followed by any other word is a compile-time error (COBOL1911), because that word names no convention and therefore no GR2 b) literal mapping (kb/Work PB1383). Because the invocation side can only ever be under COBOL and a method's ENTRY-CONVENTION can only be COBOL (any entry-convention-name-1 is COBOL2385, A.1 item 64), §9.3.6 match rule 2 ("The same calling convention shall be in effect for the invocation as is in effect for the invoked method") holds for every INVOKE by construction. **INVOKE (§8.3.2.2).** Through an object reference that is not universal, the method-name maps by the entry convention of the class or interface that contains the method, and that convention is always COBOL (stated or by §11.9.7.4 GR4), whose §11.9.7.4 GR2 mapping is the rule above. Through a universal object reference the class's ENTRY-CONVENTION is ignored and the COBOL call convention, the only one, maps the method-name as a COBOL word by the same rule (§8.3.2.2 1)); the literal mapping §8.3.2.2 2) gives under a call-convention-name-1 never arises, because no call-convention-name is defined. Both arms therefore reach `METHOD-ID. M2 AS "MixedExt"` by `"MIXEDEXT"` or `"mixedext"`, and neither by the declared word `M2`. | `conformance:cases/8.3.2.2-User-defined-words/pb303_as_externalized_name`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w73d_pb1539_as_name_formation`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/w73d-pb1539-as-literal-all-spaces`; `conformance:cases/7.3.9-CALL-CONVENTION/pb1383_call_convention_cobol`; `conformance:cases/7.3.9-CALL-CONVENTION/pb1383-call-convention-undefined-name`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2840_literal_names_edition_spelled`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2840_literal_names_two_words_at_2023`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2840-invoke-literal-final-sigma-is-another-word-at-2023`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2991_data_item_names_edition_spelled`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2991_function_address_data_item_edition_spelled`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2991_data_item_names_two_words_at_2023`; `conformance:cases/8.3.2.2-User-defined-words/w1095g_pb661_entry_convention_invoke_mapping` |
| DOC-A.1-75 | **File sharing — interaction with other facilities and languages**, §9.1.15, optional (documented if provided) | **Provided: other facilities see COBOL file sharing only as a host lock on the physical file.** When an OPEN succeeds, the connector takes a host lock on the physical file chosen from BOTH its sharing mode (§9.1.15 rules 1–3) and its open mode, so that another opener — in this run unit, in another WiseOwl COBOL run unit, or in another language that honours the lock — is admitted or refused exactly as §9.1.15 Table 19 decides. A connector with no sharing mode specified locks as the implementor-default mode (item 77). The lock lasts until the connector is closed, **except for a relative or indexed file in an active APPLY COMMIT clause (§14.9.6.4 GR9, §14.9.7.4 GR4, §9.1.16; kb/Work PB3480, PB3484): its CLOSE keeps the file lock, the handle that is it and every record lock the connector holds until the next COMMIT or ROLLBACK, or the run unit's end (§9.1.18.5).** The connector's own re-OPEN carries them on, and a connector a registration displaces or an object's deletion drops (§12.4.6.3.4 GR5: a canceled element's clause stays active until a COMMIT or ROLLBACK deactivates it) goes on being the COMMIT's and the ROLLBACK's until then. **Record locks and keyed records cross run units too (kb/Work PB2660).** A RELATIVE or INDEXED connector also holds each record lock it takes as an exclusive byte-range lock (shared and then tested for an `OPEN INPUT` connector on Linux) on one byte of its physical file far beyond any record, derived from the record's identity, so another WiseOwl COBOL run unit's access to that record answers **51** (§9.1.13.8 1)) and a `RETRY` waits for it; and the store is kept coherent across run units by a byte-range statement mutex on the file, held through the connector's own handle (exclusive through a writable one, shared through a reader's; a statement that holds it shared writes nothing, even beside a writable connector of its own run unit, kb/Work PB3335). A RELATIVE or INDEXED connector under every sharing mode but `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` (kb/Work PB3333, PB3334; `docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md` §2.2.1.7) runs each record statement, and its OPEN's adoption of the file, under the mutex: the statement reads ONE page (the store's work meta page) to learn whether another run unit changed the file since this one last saw it, and when it did adopts that page's trees and drops its page cache; it then reads the pages it touches and writes the pages it changes, and the work meta page, before the mutex is given back, so every statement is one step to every other run unit; a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` connector, which no other run unit can open beside, writes its pages at every statement with no mutex. An indexed record's n + 1 entries (its frame and one entry per alternate key) change in that ONE statement, so no run unit ever reads half of another's change and no update is lost to another's CLOSE. These locks are an agreement among WiseOwl COBOL run units: another program sees them only if it takes the same byte-range locks (or, on macOS, the same lock files, below). A SEQUENTIAL connector publishes its record locks the same way, naming a record by its ordinal (kb/Work PB2692). The reverse direction also holds: when the host refuses a WiseOwl COBOL OPEN because another process, in any language, holds the file under an incompatible lock or share mode, the OPEN fails with I-O status **61** (§9.1.13.9 1)); a DELETE FILE refused the same way gets **62**. **On Windows** the lock is the host share mode of the connector's own handle, which is mandatory and per-access, so every process on the machine is bound by rules 1–3, and the connector also publishes its Table 19 column (kb/Work PB3482): it holds exclusively one byte, chosen at random, of that column's 2^32-byte range at 2^62 + 2^61 + 2^60 + 2^32 × the column's number (the same 0 to 4 number the Linux byte offset carries) through a read handle of its own, and, before the OPEN succeeds, tests the ranges of the five columns its request row refuses (its own column's range with its own byte left out), so every WiseOwl COBOL run unit is arbitrated by Table 19 across processes as on Linux; a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` connector publishes nothing, because its handle is exclusive and refuses the read handle and every other open itself. A share mode refuses by ACCESS, so one case it cannot say is carried by the column: an INPUT opener that still owes its transaction's writes (APPLY COMMIT, kb/Work PB3337) holds a handle open for writing, which the `FileShare.Read` of a `SHARING WITH READ ONLY` request refuses, although Table 19 prints *Normal open* for that request beside an INPUT opener. An INPUT opener that owes writes publishes that with its column (one more exclusive byte, of a sixth 2^32-byte range at 2^62 + 2^61 + 2^60 + 5 × 2^32; kb/Work PB3499), and a request refused by the host with its column held, while another WiseOwl COBOL run unit's connector owes writes, is therefore OPENed again with `FileShare.ReadWrite` (`FileLockPosture.WhenOwedWritesAreAdmitted`); every request Table 19 refuses is still refused, by the columns. **Determination:** a program outside the protocol that holds the file open for writing still refuses a READ ONLY request '61', whether or not a WiseOwl COBOL INPUT opener that owes no writes is open beside it; only when an INPUT opener that owes writes is, the share mode cannot tell its writer from the outside one and the READ ONLY connector's handle admits both for the rest of its OPEN. The one thing a share mode cannot refuse is the truncation by an `OPEN OUTPUT` (Table 19 prints *Unsuccessful open* in every OUTPUT cell), so an `OPEN OUTPUT` on an existing file first requests exclusive access of the host and is refused with **61** if any handle holds it, before anything is truncated (on Linux the region lock refuses the OUTPUT like every other cell). **On Linux (x86-64 and arm64, kernel 3.15 or later, a filesystem that holds byte-range locks)** the connector also holds an advisory open-file-description byte-range lock (`fcntl` `F_OFD_SETLK`) on the physical file — its Table 19 column, published as a shared lock on one byte far beyond any record — and, before the OPEN succeeds, tests the five columns its request row refuses for another holder (`F_OFD_GETLK`), so every WiseOwl COBOL run unit is arbitrated by §9.1.15 Table 19 across processes as it is inside one; the lock is removed by the CLOSE (or an unsuccessful OPEN) and dies with a run unit that terminates. Only a regular file is locked: a device node such as `/dev/null` carries no region lock (it is not a file whose bytes another run unit can damage, and the lock would otherwise arbitrate every run unit on the machine that assigns it). The share mode (`flock`) is still taken on the connector's own handle, so rule 1 also excludes an outside process that takes `flock`. **A program in another language, or one that opens the file without taking either lock, is neither stopped nor detected** except by the share mode's strength on that host (on Linux and macOS a shared `flock`, which refuses a writer only under NO OTHER); a program in another language is bound by rules 2 and 3 only if it takes the same region locks (the byte layout is `RunUnitFileLock`'s). **On macOS** (and every Unix that is not Linux on x86-64 or arm64, kb/Work PB2484) the same table is carried by a LOCK FILE PER HOLDER instead of a byte-range lock: the connector creates `.wolk-<16 hex digits>/<column>-<guid>` in a directory beside the physical file (the digits are the SHA-256 of the file's name under the host's case rule, `HostFile.PhysicalFileKey`; the column is the same 0 to 4 number the Linux byte offset carries) and holds it open, so that .NET takes an EXCLUSIVE `flock` on it; before the OPEN succeeds it tests the lock files of the five columns its request row refuses by asking for a SHARED lock on each, which only a live holder's file refuses (so two run units testing one leftover at the same instant never read each other as a holder, kb/Work PB2917), and the kernel drops the `flock` with the descriptor, so a run unit that is killed holds nothing. Two OPENs at the same instant cannot both pass (each publishes before it tests, and a holder never counts its own file); the CLOSE (or an unsuccessful OPEN) deletes the connector's lock file before it closes the descriptor and the directory with its last file, and a leftover of a killed run unit is deleted by the next OPEN. The lock is measured, not assumed: right after creating its file the connector asks for exclusive access to it, and a host that does not refuse that (a network file system without `flock`, `DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING`) or a directory the process may not write beside the file leaves the connector with the share mode alone, exactly as an unavailable region lock does on Linux. The classic `fcntl` locks macOS offers cannot stand in (closing any descriptor of the file drops them, `fcntl` is variadic, which Apple's arm64 calling convention passes differently from a fixed P/Invoke signature, and its open-file-description commands are private). Differences from Linux: two spellings of one file reach one lock directory under the host's case rule (on macOS `Cust.dat` and `cust.dat` are one file), a symbolic or hard link remains a second spelling, a device such as `/dev/null` is unlocked only because no lock directory can be created beside it, and a FIFO in a writable directory is arbitrated like any other file (Linux excludes it by file type). **The record-lock and store-mutex halves of the cross-run-unit protocol above are carried the same way on macOS (kb/Work PB2936).** Each held byte of the region map (the store mutex, the lock-presence byte, one hashed byte per record) is a lock file in the SAME lock directory named `r<the byte as 16 hex digits>-<S or X>-<guid>` (shared or exclusive), published before it is tested exactly as a column is: an exclusive hold is refused by any other live holder of the byte, a shared one by an exclusive holder, so a second run unit's READ WITH LOCK of a record the first holds answers **51** (§9.1.13.8 1)) and two run units no longer overwrite each other's keyed store, as they did before PB2936, silently. A WAITING hold (the store mutex) retries after a jittered pause until the holder gives the byte back. **Determination — a holder the process cannot observe.** A lock file this process may not open (another user's under a restrictive umask, or an entry that is not a file) is neither free nor swept (kb/Work PB2917): a request that its column refuses is refused **61** (§9.1.13.9 1)), a non-waiting record hold answers **51**, and a WAITING hold, which cannot wait for a release it cannot see, proceeds without the cross-run-unit mutex for that statement (the run unit then has the guarantees it can keep alone). The price is that a killed run unit's leftover that nobody may read or delete refuses requests until its owner or an administrator removes the `.wolk-*` directory: a refusal is loud, where a silent grant loses a lock. **Several users.** The lock directory is created with the permissions of the physical file's directory and its files with the directory's read and write bits, not the first holder's umask, so a second user of a shared directory can publish into it and read the first user's files; a user who may not write the lock directory cannot publish its own column, but a live or unobservable conflicting holder still refuses it, and with none its OPEN has the share mode alone, exactly as an unavailable region lock does on Linux. A user who may enter the lock directory but not LIST it cannot look at all: every holder is unobservable to it, so its OPEN is refused ('61') wherever its request row refuses a column, and a record lock it requests without waiting is held by another ('51'). Design: `docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md`; witnesses `unit:RunUnitFileLockDriftTests` (every sharing × open mode pair, in a second run unit, through the host of the machine it runs on) `unit:RunUnitProcessBoundaryTests` (two real processes: the refusal `61` / `62` through every handler, the lock given back by the holder's CLOSE, its implicit CLOSE, an abnormal end and a kill, and not kept by a child process) `unit:SidecarColumnLockHostDriftTests` (the lock-file host over every pair, on every machine) `unit:HandleColumnLockHostDriftTests` (the Windows byte-range host over every pair, release, retake, the race and many holders; the cases run on Windows) and `unit:RegionLocksDriftTests` with `unit:CrossRunUnitKeyedStoreDriftTests` / `unit:CrossRunUnitSequentialLockDriftTests` (the record locks and the store mutex on the host of the machine AND on the lock-file host). **A run unit that dies under APPLY COMMIT (kb/Work PB3337).** Its uncommitted changes to a relative or indexed file are rolled back (§9.1.18.5) by the FIRST statement any connector with a writable handle runs on the file afterwards, in any run unit: a record statement's entry or an OPEN, under the statement mutex, before that statement touches anything; a statement whose lock test meets one of the dead transaction's holdings rolls it back there (A.1 item 152). Whether the owner is alive is one byte of the lock region per transaction, held through the owner's writable handle, which the operating environment releases with the handle; the records the transaction changed stay held in the file meanwhile, so no other run unit changes them before the rollback. A connector opened INPUT in the interval reads the file as it stands, the dead transaction's changes included (docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.1.10). **A sequential file under APPLY COMMIT (kb/Work PB3340; DESIGN-runtime-library.md 2.2.2)** keeps its transaction in the SAME lock directory, on every host: `txn-<id>.live` (a lock file held for the transaction's life: the owner's liveness, probed as the column and record lock files are), `txn-<id>.journal` (readable by every run unit while its owner lives) and `txn-<id>.before`, and its ENTRY MUTEX is one more held byte of the region map, `2^62 + 0x102`, carried on every host as a lock file (`r…0102-X-<guid>`) because the file it guards may not exist. A covered connector's CLOSE keeps its handle, its file lock and its record locks until the COMMIT or ROLLBACK, as a keyed one's does. A directory beside the file this process may not create or write is a refused first change ('30', the statement's permanent error, with the file unchanged); a journal it may not read holds the whole file ('51' or '61') until its owner or an administrator removes the directory. **Determination — the directory sync** the journal's write-ahead rules need (2.2.2.5; .NET has none): on Linux and macOS `open(dir, O_RDONLY)` and `fsync` (on macOS `fsync` orders the metadata in the kernel without forcing the drive's cache, the reach `FileStream.Flush(true)` has there too); on Windows nothing is called: NTFS and ReFS journal every creation and removal of a name, and the next `FlushFileBuffers` of any file on the volume forces that journal through the point it was written at, so the sync of the record or of the file the protocol makes after each directory sync carries it (`HostFile.SyncDirectory`). | `unit:RunUnitFileLockDriftTests.ASecondRunUnitsOpenIsArbitratedByTable19`; `unit:RunUnitProcessBoundaryTests.AKilledHoldersLockDiesWithItsProcess`; `unit:SidecarColumnLockHostDriftTests.ASecondHolderIsArbitratedByTable19`; `unit:HandleColumnLockHostDriftTests.ASecondHolderIsArbitratedByTable19`; `unit:HandleColumnLockHostDriftTests.AHolderThatOwesWritesIsSeenByAnotherHolderAndOnlyByAnother`; `unit:FileLockPostureDriftTests.AnInputOpenerThatOwesNoWritesDoesNotAdmitAReadOnlyOpenBesideAnOutsideWriter`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.An_input_opener_that_owes_its_transactions_writes_admits_what_Table_19_admits`; `unit:RegionLocksDriftTests.TwoSimultaneousExclusiveHolds_NeverBothHold`; `unit:FileLockPostureDriftTests.TheHostsShareModeSemanticsAreTheDocumentedOnes`; `unit:CommitRollbackRuntimeTests.A_dead_owner_is_rolled_back_by_the_next_writable_statement` |
| DOC-A.1-77 | **File sharing — the default sharing mode when none is specified**, §9.1.15, §14.9.27.4 GR23 (and §9.1.3), required + documented | **It depends on the open mode.** When neither the OPEN statement's SHARING phrase nor the file control entry's SHARING clause gives a mode, the OPEN establishes one of §9.1.15's own modes for the connector: **`OPEN INPUT` opens `SHARING WITH READ ONLY`**, and **`OPEN OUTPUT`, `OPEN I-O` and `OPEN EXTEND` open `SHARING WITH NO OTHER`**. The mode lasts until the connector is closed, and every other connector is arbitrated against it by §9.1.15 Table 19, whether that connector is in this run unit or in another one. So with two clause-less connectors on one file: `OPEN INPUT` and a second `OPEN INPUT` both succeed with 00; `OPEN INPUT` followed by a second connector's `OPEN I-O`, `OPEN EXTEND` or `OPEN OUTPUT` fails with 61; and any OPEN of a file that a clause-less connector holds open in OUTPUT, I-O or EXTEND mode fails with 61. The host lock for these modes is described in item 75. This follows GnuCOBOL, which locks a file shared for input and exclusive for every other mode; ISO leaves the choice to the implementor (CLAUDE.md rule 1). This paragraph covers COBOL 2002, 2014 and 2023. **COBOL-85 (`--std 85`) is the other determination, the owner's of 2026-10-23 (kb/Work PB670, option (i)): the file sharing facility is not in effect.** File sharing and record locking is an optional module (Annex A.4.7), §A.4.1 makes "any associated syntax rules, general rules, other rules, exception conditions, and I-O status values" optional with it, and the SHARING and LOCK MODE clauses are COBOL-2002 introductions, so a COBOL-85 program is compiled for a processor that does not have it. §9.1.15 lets the implementor define the default as "a mode completely specified by the implementor", and for such a program that mode **restricts no other connector**: Table 19 is not asked, no file lock is established against other run units, and I-O status 61 (a status the 1985 edition does not define) is never answered. Two connectors of one run unit open the same physical file in any pair of modes, every OPEN answers 00 (an `OPEN OUTPUT` beside a connector that holds the file creates it empty, §14.9.27.4 GR18, and the holder's next READ is at end), and a second run unit is not refused either; a process outside the run unit that holds the file exclusively makes the OPEN answer 30, §9.1.13.6 item 1. This is GnuCOBOL's measured `-std=cobol85` behaviour (cobc 3.2: every OPEN of a file another connector of the run unit holds answers 00). The edition decides it in one place, `DialectBehavior.FileSharingFacility` (ledger row 7.39 of `docs/VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE.md`), read through `FileConnector.SharingFacilityInEffect`. Implemented by `FileRegistry.ImplementorDefaultSharing` (read once, in `FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt`; its COBOL-85 answer is ALL OTHER, the mode whose host share mode admits every sibling handle) and `Table19.Conflicts`, a plain lookup of the printed table, asked only where the facility is in effect. | `conformance:cases/14.9.27-OPEN/pb322_default_sharing_by_open_mode`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb670_cobol85_no_sharing_facility`; `unit:OpenTable19Tests.ImplementorDefault_IsAFunctionOfTheOpenMode`; `unit:SharingFacilityEditionTests.AtCobol85_EveryPairOfOpensIsANormalOpen` |
| DOC-A.1-81 | **Floating-point numeric item — alignment when used as a receiving operand**, §14.6.8.3 rule 1, required — documentation NOT required by A.1 (VOLUNTARY) | **One correctly rounded conversion to the receiver's own format.** The sending operand's algebraic value (for a decimal sender, every digit it holds) is converted in ONE step to the nearest value the receiver can represent. Ties go to even, ISO/IEC 60559 round-to-nearest. `FLOAT-SHORT` and `COMP-1` hold IEEE binary32. `FLOAT-LONG`, `FLOAT-EXTENDED` and `COMP-2` hold binary64 (item 207). `FLOAT-BINARY-32`/`-64` convert the same way, as §14.6.8.3 rule 2 requires. The value is never rounded first to a wider binary format and then narrowed. A value too small for the normal range becomes the nearest subnormal, or zero when it is closer to zero than half the smallest subnormal. A value too large for the format is the §14.9.25.4 GR6 d)4.a case covered in §3 ("EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE / EC-DATA-OVERFLOW applied to EVERY floating-point usage"): with checking off the result is ±Infinity, and with EC-DATA-OVERFLOW checking on the exception condition is raised. So `MOVE 0.1 TO` a FLOAT-SHORT stores 0.100000001490116…, and `MOVE 1.000000059604644775390625000001 TO` a FLOAT-SHORT stores 1.00000011920928955 (the binary32 neighbour nearer the value), not 1. This holds for EVERY statement that lands a value in a binary32 receiver: MOVE, a ROUNDED arithmetic resultant, INITIALIZE, the VALUE clause and the ACCEPT device transfer. Two statements round by their own rule rather than to nearest: an arithmetic resultant with no ROUNDED phrase truncates (§14.7.4.3 rule 2; a CALL BY CONTENT or BY VALUE crossing into a binary32 formal lands through that same no-ROUNDED store, so it truncates too), and a value produced by a function is converted as the sender it is (a NUMVAL-F result is the exact decimal parse, kb/Work PB3839, so it is converted exactly as the decimal literal of the same value is; a SQRT result is a binary64 sender). Each is still ONE rounding of the value it receives (kb/Work PB1110). | `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb271_float_receiver_overflow` (out-of-range half); `conformance:cases/14.6.8.3-Floating-point-numeric-receiving-data-items/pb1110_binary32_receiver_single_rounding`; `conformance:cases/14.6.8.3-Floating-point-numeric-receiving-data-items/pb1110_float_short_every_landing` |
| DOC-A.1-89 | **Function-identifier — the runtime resources checked before a user-defined function is executed**, §8.4.3.2.4 GR6 c), required + documented | **One runtime resource is checked: the stack the activation needs** — the determination item 14 makes for CALL, applied to a user-defined function. When the function is located (GR6 b) and the thread running the run unit has less than an activation's reserve of stack left (1 MiB on the run unit's own 384 MiB thread), **EC-PROGRAM-RESOURCES** is set (GR6 c), the function activation is not successful, and execution continues as GR6 f) specifies — the same check, in `ProgramTable.CallProgram`, that a CALL makes (kb/Work PB2659). Locating is not a resource check: a function is located when its externalized name (item 68) matches a function registered in the run unit — compiled into the calling assembly, or a separately compiled module beside the application whose registration member `__CobolModule.EnsureRegistered()` has registered it (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule`, the lookup CALL uses: the file `<name>.dll` first, then the `Units` index of every module's record). A module file that exists but cannot be loaded (a truncated or foreign image, or a dependency the registrar itself needs) or whose registrar throws for any reason, or that the run unit refuses (`ProgramTable.RegisterModule`: another runtime major or call ABI, or an outermost name another module already registered), or of which two different assemblies carry the name, has therefore NOT been located, and neither has a registered function whose class or dependency the CLR cannot load or initialize when its instance is created (`ProgramTable.Create`): **EC-FUNCTION-NOT-FOUND** is set, the function activation is not successful, and execution continues as GR6 f) specifies. **Available memory is not checked**: running out of it is a host failure, the run unit ends abnormally and no exception condition is set. Treating a module that cannot be loaded as not found follows GnuCOBOL under CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence — libcob's resolver sets EC-FUNCTION-NOT-FOUND for a function module that is found but cannot be loaded (`call.c` `set_resolve_error`); for the stack GnuCOBOL defines no outcome, so the standard's own GR6 c) governs. | `conformance-test:ActivationResourcesTests.RecursiveFunction_PastTheStack_IsEcProgramResources`; `unit:ActivationStackTests.RecursiveCall_PastTheStack_IsEcProgramResources_AndUnwindsBalanced`; `conformance-test:FunctionLocateResourceWitnessTests.UnloadableSiblingModule_IsNotFound_NeverProgramResources`; `conformance-test:FunctionLocateResourceWitnessTests.LoadableSiblingModule_IsLocatedAndRuns`; `conformance-test:FunctionLocateResourceWitnessTests.ThrowingRegistrarSiblingModule_IsNotFound_NeverProgramResources`; `unit:RepositoryLocatorTests.AFunctionIsFoundByItsWord_TheWordRowsOfTheIndex` |
| DOC-A.1-99 | **Implementor-defined exception conditions, EC-IMP-*suffix* — specification and meaning of each suffix**, §14.6.13.1.6 Table 13 (§14.6.13.1.1, the 'EC-IMP-' type), optional (documented if provided) | **Not provided.** WiseOwl COBOL specifies no EC-IMP-*suffix* exception-name. The level-2 name **EC-IMP** is still valid wherever Table 13 allows a level-2 name, and no level-3 condition exists under it. The EC-level-2-IMP names of item 100, such as EC-PROGRAM-IMP, fall under their own level-2 parents, not under EC-IMP. `EC-IMP-` followed by any suffix names no exception condition, so a program that writes one is refused at compile time with COBOL0711: in `RAISE EXCEPTION`, in a `>>TURN` directive (reported at the directive's line) and in a `USE AFTER EXCEPTION CONDITION` declarative. `ExceptionCatalog.TryGet` answers only the catalogued names and the user-defined `EC-USER-suffix` family, which §14.6.13.1.1 makes open by definition ("The name is defined by specifying it"). The implementation never sets an EC-IMP-*suffix* condition at run time. The standard still reserves the EC-IMP-*suffix* spelling in compiler directives (§8.12), so `CompilerDirectiveWords.IsReserved` tests the spelling (`ExceptionCatalog.IsImplementorSuffixForm`) although no such name resolves. | `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1531-ec-imp-suffix-raise`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1531-ec-imp-suffix-turn`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1531-ec-imp-suffix-use`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/l1_dns_a1_99_ec_imp_level2_valid`; `unit:EcImplementorNamesDocumentationDriftTests.Item99_NoEcImpSuffixNameExists` |
