| DOC-A.1-102 | **INVOKE statement — the runtime resources checked before a method is executed**, §14.9.23.4 GR7 b) — Annex A.1 cites GR7 e), but the resource sentence is GR7 b); required + documented | **Two resources are checked: the stack the activation needs, and that the class which provides the method can be loaded and initialized.** The stack is the CALL's resource (item 14): at the head of every method that executes statements, before its GR7 d) external-item check and before anything of the activation is set up, the method is not successful when the thread running the run unit has less than an activation's reserve of stack left (1 MiB on the run unit's own 384 MiB thread), and **EC-OO-METHOD** is set (`ActivationStack.RequireForMethod`, kb/Work PB2659); a PROPERTY clause's accessor executes no statement and activates nothing, so it is not checked. For the class, when §9.3.6 resolution finds the method, the INVOKE checks that the class's type initialization completes. That initialization runs when the class's factory object is first referenced in the run unit (§9.3.14.2: the factory object is created before it is first referenced; `RunUnit.FactoryObject`), and it covers the class's static data. If it fails, **EC-OO-METHOD** is set (fatal, Table 13), the method invocation fails, and execution continues as GR7 g) specifies. The CLR remembers the failure, so every later INVOKE of that class fails the same way. The standard gives this outcome to both "method not found" and "resources not available". **Loading the class's assembly is not a checked resource.** A class a program can INVOKE is compiled into its own compilation group's assembly, or comes from a referenced repository assembly (item 67), and the host binds that assembly when it first prepares the INVOKE's enclosing method for execution, before any statement of that method runs. A binding failure is a deployment failure the host reports, and no exception condition is set. **Available memory is not checked.** Running out of it is a host failure: the run unit ends abnormally and no exception condition is set. The CALL twin (item 14) and the function twin (item 89) count a module that cannot be loaded as NOT LOCATED rather than as a resource failure; for INVOKE the distinction has no observable effect, because GR7 b) gives both outcomes EC-OO-METHOD. EC-OO-METHOD is raised by `CobolObject.__CobolInvoke` when no class in the hierarchy declares a matching method, and by `RunUnit.FactoryObject` when the class cannot be initialized (kb/Work PB1422). | `conformance-test:ActivationResourcesTests.RecursiveMethod_PastTheStack_IsEcOoMethod`; `unit:ActivationStackTests.RecursiveMethod_PastTheStack_IsEcOoMethod`; `unit:FactoryInitializationFailureTests.ClassWhoseTypeInitializerThrows_IsEcOoMethod_EveryTime`; `unit:FactoryInitializationFailureTests.ClassThatInitializes_IsTheSameFactoryObjectEveryTime` |
| DOC-A.1-103 | **I-O status — the action taken for a fatal exception condition**, §9.1.13.1 (with §14.6.13.1.3 rule 3), required + documented | **Continue only when the program is equipped to see the failure; otherwise terminate.** The fatal I-O statuses are those that begin with 3, 4 or 7, and every 9x status WiseOwl COBOL defines (item 110). The action is decided after the I-O status is stored and any applicable USE procedure has run. **With checking for the EC-I-O condition not enabled (the default):** execution **continues** if the file connector has a FILE STATUS clause or a USE procedure applied to the statement. Control passes to the end of the statement that produced the status, and its NOT AT END or NOT INVALID KEY phrase is not executed (§9.1.13.1). If the connector has **neither**, the run unit **terminates abnormally** (§14.6.12): the message names the exception-name, the I-O status, the file and the statement (`EC-I-O-PERMANENT-ERROR (fatal): I-O status 35 on F (OPEN); the file has no FILE STATUS clause and no USE procedure applies`), and the exit code is nonzero (§2 row 44). **With checking enabled** (`>>TURN EC-I-O CHECKING ON`, or a level above it), WiseOwl COBOL adds nothing: §14.6.13.1.3 rules 4–7 apply after the I-O rules. A PERFORM WHEN phrase or a RESUME in the declarative can continue execution; otherwise the run unit terminates abnormally, even when the file has a FILE STATUS clause. This follows GnuCOBOL, which ends the run unit on a fatal status only when no declarative applies and the file has no FILE STATUS clause; ISO leaves the choice to the implementor (CLAUDE.md rule 1). A host failure inside a READ or WRITE is reported as status 30 and handled by this rule the same way. Implemented at the statement: every I-O statement's after-hook (`SequentialIoEmitter.EmitUseHook`) ends in `CobolFile.TerminateOnUncoveredFatalStatus` for a file that has no FILE STATUS clause, when the status is fatal, no USE procedure ran and the statement has no ON EXCEPTION phrase. **A SORT or MERGE implicit transfer asks the same question** (kb/Work PB2700): each of its as-if OPEN, READ, WRITE and CLOSE statements is performed "as if" that statement "had been executed" (§14.9.40.4 GR12, GR15; §14.9.24.4 GR7, GR12), so a missing non-OPTIONAL USING file ('35') or a GIVING file that cannot be created ('30') with no FILE STATUS clause and no USE procedure ends the run unit (`EC-I-O-PERMANENT-ERROR (fatal): I-O status 35 on F (SORT USING implicit OPEN); …`). The verb's own rules — "the SORT is terminated", MERGE's bypass and continue cells (`SortEmitter.RuleFor`, §3) — are what the CONTINUED run unit does with the statement, and they are read after this question (`SortEmitter.EmitDisposition`). The one rule that continues past a status nothing covers is the GIVING write's boundary paragraph ("if no such USE procedure is specified, the processing of the file is terminated as in General rule 15c"), which is tested first. With EC-I-O checking enabled for the condition, §14.6.13.1.3 rule 2 gives the status to the verb's rules (kb/Work PB993): the statement is terminated and the run unit continues. GnuCOBOL 3.2 (measured) continues after a SORT or MERGE whose USING file is missing — its sort runtime opens the file without passing through the error handler its explicit statements use — so WiseOwl COBOL applies the one determination above to the implicit statement as to the explicit one rather than reproduce that omission, which would leave the program running with nothing sorted and no way to see why. A program whose files all carry FILE STATUS emits nothing new. COBOL-85 programs are held to the same rule: two official NIST programs that depended on continuing (NC401M opens a file that does not exist; ST146A's dump READs a closed file) are recorded in `tests/nist/corpus.tsv` as `divergent` with a `TERMINATES` note, and the harness asserts the termination. **The report writer's transfers do not ask it** (kb/Work PB1956). INITIATE, GENERATE and TERMINATE are not among the statements §9.1.13.1 says set an I-O status ("a CLOSE, DELETE, OPEN, READ, REWRITE, START, UNLOCK or WRITE statement"), and unlike SORT and MERGE no rule of theirs makes a report line a WRITE "as if" executed (§14.9.16.4, §14.9.46.4). So the line the report writer cannot write is item 159's refused line: the report file keeps a blank line in its place, the FILE STATUS item is not stored, no USE procedure runs, and the run unit continues. The standard leaves the action to the implementor, so CLAUDE.md rule 1 takes GnuCOBOL's. GnuCOBOL 3.2 (measured 2026-10-08) continues past a GENERATE and a TERMINATE whose report file was closed under the active report, with no FILE STATUS clause, with one, and with a USE procedure for the file: it does not terminate, store a status or run the procedure. | `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.FatalStatus_NoFileStatusNoUse_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.FatalLogicErrorStatus_OnWrite_NoFileStatusNoUse_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.FatalStatus_WithFileStatusClause_Continues`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.FatalStatus_WithApplicableUseProcedure_Continues`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.CharacterWithoutByteImage_Status91_WithFileStatusClause_Continues`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.CharacterWithoutByteImage_Status91_CheckingEnabled_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item218WitnessTests.CheckedFatalIo_Format1UseCompletesNormally_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.SortUsingFileMissing_NoFileStatusNoUse_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.MergeUsingFileMissing_NoFileStatusNoUse_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.SortGivingOpenFails_NoFileStatusNoUse_TerminatesAbnormally`; `conformance-test:DocA1Item103WitnessTests.SortUsingFileMissing_CheckingEnabled_FollowsTheVerbRule`; `conformance:cases/14.9.24-MERGE/pb2700_sort_merge_missing_using_covered`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb690_report_line_byte_image_85`; `conformance-test:AssignConstantNameTests.ConstantNamedFile_FatalStatus_NeitherFileStatusNorUse_TerminatesTheRunUnit`; `unit:KeyedClosePermanentErrorWitnessTests.A_keyed_close_that_answers_30_runs_the_use_procedure_stores_the_status_and_continues_or_terminates_by_the_rule` |
| DOC-A.1-105 | **I-O status, permanent error — the technique for correcting it**, §9.1.13.1, optional + documented if provided | **Provided: the technique is CLOSE.** A permanent error condition (an I-O status beginning with '3', §9.1.13.6) belongs to the file connector that got it, and it stays in effect until that connector is closed. **After a failed OPEN** ('30', '31', '35', '37', '38' — COBOL-85 to 2014 only: CLOSE WITH LOCK and status '38' were removed at 2023 — or '39') the connector is left closed. That closed state is already the corrected state, so the next OPEN of the file starts fresh. **After a failed READ, WRITE, REWRITE, DELETE or START** on an open connector ('30' or '34'), the condition stays in effect. Every later input-output statement on that connector, except CLOSE, is unsuccessful. It does not touch the physical file, it sets the same I-O status again, and it raises that status's exception condition again (§9.1.13.1). A CLOSE runs normally, and a completed CLOSE — successful or not, since an unsuccessful one also leaves the connector closed — ends the condition, so the next OPEN starts clean. This applies to every organization and every edition. Example: a random relative WRITE with relative key 0 answers '34' (§14.9.51.4 GR29 b). The next WRITE, with key 1, also answers '34' and writes nothing. CLOSE answers '00', and after OPEN I-O the WRITE with key 1 answers '00'. **The condition outranks every other status the later statement would have taken** — the not-open and mode statuses ('41', '47', '48', '49'), GR21's '46' and the '43' gate — because §9.1.13.1 says it remains in effect "for all subsequent input-output operations on the file": READ, WRITE, REWRITE, DELETE, START, UNLOCK, DELETE FILE and a second OPEN of the open connector all answer the status that began it. **A WRITE ... WITH LOCK is a WRITE**: it answers the status that began the condition, stores nothing and sets no record lock (§14.9.51.4 GR11 sets the lock only when the WRITE is successful), and that answer comes BEFORE the §12.4.5.9.4 GR7 lock ceiling is judged, so a connector that holds its maximum number of locks answers '34', not '54'. It is started in ONE place, the I-O status assignment itself (`FileConnector.Status`'s setter: a status beginning '3' on a connector that is open), so no producer — a host failure '30', a boundary '34', a READ of an OCCURS DEPENDING ON record made too long (D-ODO2) — can forget to start it, and each verb family asks `FileConnector.PermanentErrorReplay` once in the precondition it already shares (`PermanentErrorInEffectTests` pins every organization x verb). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1541_permanent_error_remains_in_effect`; `unit:PermanentErrorInEffectTests.RecordSequential_EveryVerbReplaysThePermanentError_AndCloseEndsIt`; `unit:PermanentErrorInEffectTests.Indexed_EveryVerbReplaysThePermanentError_AndCloseEndsIt`; `unit:PermanentErrorInEffectTests.Relative_RegistryVerbs_ReplayTheBoundaryError_UnlockAndDeleteFileToo_AndCloseEndsIt`; `unit:PermanentErrorInEffectTests.FailedOpen_LeavesNoConditionInEffect_TheNextOpenStartsFresh`; `conformance:cases/14.9.51-WRITE/pb1880_write_with_lock_under_permanent_error`; `unit:WriteWithLockPermanentErrorTests.Relative_RefusedWriteWithLock_SetsNoRecordLock_TheControlWriteDoes`; `conformance:cases/9.1.13.6-Permanent-error-condition-with-unsuccessful-completion/pb1880_odo_read_34_exception_paths` |
| DOC-A.1-107 | **I-O status 24 — the manner in which the boundaries of a relative or indexed file are defined**, §9.1.13.5 item 4 + §14.9.51.4 GR33 b) / GR42 d), required + documented | **The keyed store engine, both organizations (kb/Work PB3333 RELATIVE, PB3334 INDEXED; `docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md` section 2.2.1.9).** The boundary of a physical relative or indexed file is the host file system's maximum file size, capped by the format at 2^32 pages of 4 096 bytes (16 TiB). A WRITE or REWRITE whose record would take the store past that boundary is unsuccessful with I-O status '24' (§14.9.51.4 GR33 b) relative, GR42 d) indexed; the invalid key condition exists, the INVALID KEY phrase runs, no record is released and the file is unchanged); the host's answer that the file cannot grow further (`EFBIG`, `ERROR_FILE_TOO_LARGE`) is the same boundary. The '24' is a record WRITE's or REWRITE's alone, in both organizations: §9.1.13.5 item 4's condition is an attempt "to write outside the externally-defined boundaries", and §14.9.10.4 gives DELETE no boundary condition, so a DELETE, an OPEN or a CLOSE whose pages meet the boundary is unsuccessful with §9.1.13.6 item 1's '30' and never the invalid key condition (`KeyedConnector.RecordWriteFailed` vs `Failed`; kb/Work PB3333 review finding R1-1, PB3334 review finding R1-1). A medium with no room for the statement's pages (`ENOSPC`, `EDQUOT`, `ERROR_DISK_FULL`, `ERROR_HANDLE_DISK_FULL`, `ERROR_DISK_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`) makes THAT statement unsuccessful with §9.1.13.6 item 1's '30' and leaves the file as the previous statement left it; nothing is deferred to the CLOSE. An indexed record is n + 1 entries (its frame under the prime key and one entry per alternate key) and they are released, replaced or removed by ONE statement of the page layer, so the boundary and the medium's refusal reach every key at once: a WRITE answered '24' or '30' is released under no key. A record's own size is bounded by the host, not the format (overflow pages), and an empty relative record number costs nothing (a record is one entry of a B+ tree keyed by its number), so a record in the billions is one leaf entry. **The relative key's own range is separate.** A random or dynamic relative WRITE whose relative key is less than 1, or greater than 2 147 483 647 (the highest relative record number permitted for the file — the §12.4.5.13 key item's domain, kept by the engine though its tree would hold 2^63 keys), answers '34' as §14.9.51.4 GR29 b) states, and takes no INVALID KEY branch. GR29 b) names that case explicitly, so it governs over the general GR33 b); GnuCOBOL's '24' for key 0 is not followed because the standard decides it. On a sequential-access WRITE, a relative record number with more significant digits than the relative key answers '24' (§14.9.51.4 GR33 c), §9.1.13.5 item 4); in random or dynamic access the record number comes from the key, so it cannot happen. Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/9.1.13.5-Invalid-key-condition-with-unsuccessful-completion/pb1192_relative_write_boundary_85`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.RelativeWrite_BoundaryIsTheHosts_AndTheKeyRangeIs34`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.RelativeWrite_TheHostsRefusalIsAtTheStatement_24ForTooLarge_30ForFull`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.IndexedWrite_TheHostsRefusalIsAtTheStatement_24ForTooLarge_30ForFull`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.RelativeDeleteAndCreate_AtTheHostsBoundary_Are30_NeverTheInvalidKey`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.IndexedDeleteAndCreate_AtTheHostsBoundary_Are30_NeverTheInvalidKey`; `unit:IndexedEnginePermanentErrorWitnessTests.Boundary_UseAndFileStatus_InvalidKeyTakenOrUseRun_TheDeleteIs30_AndTheFileIsUnchanged`; `unit:IndexedEnginePermanentErrorWitnessTests.Boundary_NeitherUseNorFileStatus_ContinuesPastThe24s_AndTerminatesAtTheDelete` |
| DOC-A.1-108 | **I-O status 34 — the manner in which the boundaries of a sequential file are defined**, §9.1.13.6 item 3 + §14.9.51.4 GR20, required + documented | **The boundary of a physical sequential file (record sequential or line sequential) is the capacity of the host medium.** A WRITE is outside the boundary when the host cannot store the record because the medium is full or a host quota or file-size limit is reached (POSIX ENOSPC / EDQUOT / EFBIG; Windows ERROR_DISK_FULL / ERROR_HANDLE_DISK_FULL). The failure is detected at the WRITE (`HostFile.IsMediumBoundary` classifies the host's refusal; `FileStatusCode.ForWriteFailure` answers the WRITE, WRITE ADVANCING and REWRITE entry points of `SequentialConnector`). The writer buffers records — a flush per record is paid only when another connector may read the file — so the refusal is reported on the WRITE whose record the host is asked to store; a CLOSE whose final flush is refused answers '30' (§9.1.13.6 item 1). The WRITE is unsuccessful with I-O status '34', a permanent error (EC-I-O-PERMANENT-ERROR). No part of the record counts as written, and the file stays open. Under item 105 the condition then stays in effect on that connector until it is closed. Any other host failure during a WRITE is '30' (§9.1.13.6 item 1), never an escaped .NET exception. No other sequential boundary exists: there is no record-count or size limit below the medium's. Same in every edition. | `unit:FileBoundaryTests.SequentialWrite_OnAFullMedium_Is34_AtTheWrite`; `unit:FileBoundaryTests.WriteFailure_MediumExhaustionIs34_AnyOtherFailureIs30` |
| DOC-A.1-113 | **Life cycle for objects — timing and algorithm for deciding that an object can no longer take part in continued execution**, §9.3.14.3, required (A.1 does not require it to be documented; documented here because it decides when §9.1.4's implicit CLOSE of an object's files happens) | **Reachability, decided by the .NET garbage collector.** An instance object is a managed instance of a class derived from `CobolObject`. It can no longer take part in continued execution once no object reference in the run unit reaches it. The .NET tracing garbage collector decides that at a time of its own choosing, which is nondeterministic, as §9.3.14.3 permits. When it has decided, the object is destroyed. Its finalizer implicitly CLOSEs every per-object file connector the object owns (§9.1.4, 'when the object is deleted'), **in the run unit that created the object**, and the object's storage is reclaimed. A later OPEN of the same physical file is therefore arbitrated only against connectors that are still live. At run-unit termination every object not yet destroyed is destroyed, and its files are closed with the run unit's (`CobolFile.CloseAll`). Whichever of the two happens first is the destruction. An object that owns no file has no observable destruction beyond its storage being reclaimed. COBOL 2002 and later. | `unit:InstanceFileFinalizerTests.AnUnreachableObjectsFile_IsClosedInItsOwnRunUnit_BeforeTheNextOpen` |
| DOC-A.1-114 | **Line delimiter — specification of**, §12.4.5.10.3 GR2 (+ §9.1.13.2 item 5's '06'), required + documented | **The line delimiter is the host platform's newline:** CR LF (U+000D U+000A) on Windows and LF (U+000A) on Linux and macOS (`Environment.NewLine`). **WRITE** ends every record with that delimiter, and ADVANCING and LINAGE positioning add their own line and page controls around it. **READ** ends a record at an LF, or at a CR LF pair on any host, so a file written on either platform reads back on the other. A final line with no delimiter ends at end of file. **A lone CR (one not followed by LF) is not a delimiter.** It is record data, and because CR is outside the line sequential character set (item 115), the READ that delivers it answers '09'. A line longer than the record area is delivered truncated with '06' (§9.1.13.2), and the rest of the line is the next record. This follows GnuCOBOL, which writes a line sequential file in the host's text mode and drops a CR only when an LF follows it; ISO leaves the delimiter to the implementor (CLAUDE.md rule 1; kb/Work PB1540). Implemented once, in `SequentialConnector` (`LineSequentialDelimiter` for every line end it writes, `ReadPhysicalLine` for every line it reads). COBOL 2023 (ORGANIZATION LINE SEQUENTIAL). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1540_ls_lone_cr_is_data`; `conformance-test:LinageConformanceTests.Bytes_LineSequential_EveryPlacementMix`; `conformance:cases/14.9.51-WRITE/pb964_ls_plain_write_after_after` |
| DOC-A.1-116 | **Linkage section — whether access to linkage items is guaranteed, and their initial value, when a non-COBOL runtime element activates the program**, §13.7.4 GR3 + GR5, conditionally required (a .NET host can activate a WiseOwl COBOL program) + documented | **The only non-COBOL activator is a .NET host (item 141), and its one interface is the program's generated host entry, `Cobol.<assembly>.<NAME>.Call(...)`: access IS guaranteed, exactly as for a COBOL CALL whose USING phrase names every formal.** Each `Call` parameter is the formal in its position (§14.2.3 GR2), and the formal's initial value is the host's value, landed into storage of the formal's description by §14.2.3 GR9 or GR10 (for a group, its published record's image), whose content reaches the host's variable when the call ends (item 141). An OPTIONAL formal whose parameter is `null` is OMITTED (§14.9.4.4 GR11). The RETURNING item is `Call`'s return value; its initial value is undefined, as for every activator (§14.2.3 GR7). A linkage VALUE clause is not applied (§13.18.63.4 GR3). A program activated by the operating system — the `Main` of a `cobol` executable — is §13.7.4 GR3's other case, where the effect is undefined; there each formal refers to storage private to the program instance that holds the item's category-default value (independent of any OPTIONS paragraph INITIALIZE clause, which governs working storage, not the linkage section): spaces for an alphanumeric, national or edited item; zeros for a boolean item; zero for a numeric item of any usage (display, binary, packed or floating-point); length zero for a dynamic-length item; NULL for a pointer; for a group, each subordinate elementary item's own default; and the formal is not OMITTED. Same in every edition. Witness: `NonCobolActivatorLinkageTests` (kb/Work PB2671, PB2099). | `conformance-test:NonCobolActivatorLinkageTests.ANetHost_CallsTheEntry_WhichGuaranteesLinkageAccessAndOmitsANullOptionalFormal`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2671_omitted_formal_category_default` |
| DOC-A.1-121 | **METHOD-ID paragraph — the actual method-name used when the PROPERTY phrase is specified**, §11.7.4 GR1 a), required + documented | **`__GET_<P>` for a GET PROPERTY method and `__SET_<P>` for a SET PROPERTY method.** `<P>` is the property-name in upper case (the Annex C fold) written as a .NET identifier by the one injective mapping, `DataItem.IdentifierCharacters`: each hyphen an underscore, each underscore `_u005F_`, and a character a .NET identifier cannot hold `_uXXXX_` by its code point, so two property-names never share an accessor (kb/Work PB2839): `GET PROPERTY my-bal` is `__GET_MY_BAL` and `GET PROPERTY my_bal` is `__GET_MY_u005F_BAL`. The rule is the same for every legal property-name, including one spelled like a .NET keyword or starting with a digit (a user-defined word needs only one letter): `GET PROPERTY long` is `__GET_LONG` and `GET PROPERTY 2nd-val` is `__GET_2ND_VAL`, never an escaped, guarded or otherwise altered spelling. It is the name of the public virtual method on the generated .NET class, so a .NET caller invokes the accessor by that name. Override, interface-conformance and inheritance checks match accessors by it. A COBOL program reaches the property through an object-property reference (`long OF obj`, which needs `PROPERTY long` in the REPOSITORY paragraph), not by spelling the accessor name. COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:cases/11.7-METHOD-ID/oo_property_methods`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/oo_property_ref`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1520_property_keyword_spelled_name`; `unit:IdentifierInjectivityTests.PropertyAccessorNames_AreTheDocumentedPrefixPlusTheWholeWord` |
| DOC-A.1-124 | **Native arithmetic — when an operand represents an integer**, §5.5 3) a), required + documented | **An operand represents an integer exactly when its value has no nonzero digit to the right of the decimal point.** The test uses the operand's own exact value, never a rounded or truncated copy. A fixed-point data item is tested at its full declared scale. An arithmetic expression is tested on the value the native intermediate data item (item 123) holds for it. A floating-point operand is an integer only when its binary value is exactly integral: COMP-2 `2.0` is an integer, `2 + 1.0E-10` is not. The same value gets the same answer at every rule that asks: a subscript, a reference-modification start or length, a SET index or amount, and an integer argument of an intrinsic function. A subscript or reference-modification bound that is an arithmetic expression or a floating-point item is evaluated once, before the statement, and tested on the carrier it evaluated on — the exact scaled value, the SDIDI under standard arithmetic, or binary64 — before its integer position is stored (`CobolTable.OccValue*` / `CobolString.RefModValue*`, kb/Work PB1890; it used to be stored into a 9-fraction-digit temporary first, which hid a fraction past the 9th digit). When checking for the rule's exception condition is enabled, a non-integer is refused by that condition (for example EC-BOUND-SUBSCRIPT; for an intrinsic function's integer argument, §15.3 type 6, it is EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION — every carrier of the operand asks the test, the exact scaled value, the SDIDI and binary64, narrow and wide, kb/Work PB1526) and, with that checking off, the truncated integer is the result the implementor defines (§15.3's last sentence; a reference-modification position is the exception — an unchecked EC-BOUND-REF-MOD violation terminates the run unit, owner decision R60). A floating-point operand (which reaches an intrinsic function's integer argument only under `--permissive`) whose integer lies beyond ±1.7×10³⁸, outside the implementation's 128-bit integer carrier, cannot be represented, so it is EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION — never a nearer integer substituted for it — except at TEST-DATE-YYYYMMDD and TEST-DAY-YYYYDDD argument-1 and FIND-STRING argument-3, which answer the same for every integer past their bound and so answer it (kb/Work PB651). The compile-time screen of §5.5 2) is separate (COBOL1627) and fails open on an expression it cannot prove non-integral (`FACTORIAL(X / 2 + 1)`), which is why the VALUE is tested at run time. Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/5.5-Integer-operands/pb1526_integer_argument_has_integral_value`; `conformance:cases/5.5-Integer-operands/pb1526_integer_argument_integrality_standard_decimal`; `conformance:cases/5.5-Integer-operands/pb1890_position_expression_exact`; `conformance:cases/5.5-Integer-operands/pb1890_position_expression_standard_decimal`; `conformance:cases/8.4.2.3-Subscripts/pb41_position_not_integer`; `unit:IntrinsicCarrierAgreementDriftTests.TheIntegerIntake_RaisesOnAFractionOnEveryCarrier_AndAcceptsAnIntegralValue`; `unit:IntrinsicIntegerPositionPermissiveDriftTests.AFloatAtAnIntegerPosition_UnderPermissive_AnswersAsTheIntegerItHolds`; `unit:IntrinsicCarrierAgreementDriftTests.OnlyAnArgumentWhoseAnswerIsConstantPastABound_Saturates` |
| DOC-A.1-131 | **OPEN statement with no SHARING phrase and no SHARING clause — the sharing mode established for the file connector**, §14.9.27.4 GR23 (+ §9.1.15), required + documented | **The default sharing mode depends on the open mode.** OPEN INPUT establishes **SHARING WITH READ ONLY**. OPEN OUTPUT, OPEN I-O and OPEN EXTEND establish **SHARING WITH NO OTHER**. Both are the standard's own modes, so §9.1.15's rules and Table 19 apply to them unchanged. Clause-less readers can share a file. A clause-less updater or writer has the file to itself: its OPEN is refused with '61' while any other connector has the file open, and while it is open every other connector's OPEN is refused with '61'. A clause-less OPEN INPUT is refused with '61' while another connector has the file open in a mode other than input. The same default applies to a file control entry that has a LOCK MODE clause but no SHARING clause, and to an OPEN whose only sharing-related phrase is RETRY. Record locking for such a connector is item 153. Example (three clause-less SELECTs on one file): A OPEN INPUT '00', B OPEN INPUT '00', C OPEN I-O '61', C OPEN EXTEND '61', C OPEN OUTPUT '61'. After A and B close: A OPEN I-O '00', B OPEN INPUT '61', C OPEN I-O '61'. COBOL 2002 and later. At COBOL-85 the facility is not in effect: no connector restricts another, so the same three SELECTs answer 00 for every OPEN above, C OPEN OUTPUT included (A.1 item 77, kb/Work PB670). | `conformance:cases/14.9.27-OPEN/pb322_default_sharing_by_open_mode`; `conformance:cases/14.9.27-OPEN/pb322_clauseless_reader_sees_record_lock`; `conformance:wiseowl/cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb670_cobol85_no_sharing_facility`; `unit:OpenTable19Tests.ImplementorDefault_IsAFunctionOfTheOpenMode`; `unit:SharingFacilityEditionTests.AtCobol85_EveryPairOfOpensIsANormalOpen` |
| DOC-A.1-146 | **RECORD clause — the calculations to derive the size of records on the storage medium**, §13.18.43.4 GR2, required + documented | **Start from the record size in bytes (GR1/GR3/GR8)**: every alphanumeric, alphabetic, numeric-display or edited character position is ONE byte (item 209: ISO/IEC 8859-1, owner decision kb/Work R47 — a record holding a character above U+00FF is refused, item 31), a national character position TWO bytes (UTF-16BE, D-N1), and a binary, packed or floating item its item-205–215 width; the implicit or explicit RECORD clause then fixes the size (implicit clause: item 147; format 3: item 148). **Then add the control information of the file's organization:** **(a) record sequential, fixed-length records** (format 1, explicit or implied) — **exactly integer-1 bytes per record, no control information**: a record description shorter than integer-1 is written followed by the rest of the integer-1-byte record area — positions that no record description of the file covers are spaces (national spaces in a national record area; `FileModel.RecordWidth` sizes the area, `FileConnector.FitRecord` fills it) — so the file is `n × integer-1` bytes (`FD F RECORD CONTAINS 20 CHARACTERS` + `01 R PIC X(10)` → 20 bytes per record; an implied format 1 over `01 A PIC X(5)` and `01 B PIC X(10)` → 10 bytes per record, whichever is written); **a record holding DYNAMIC LENGTH members under an explicit format 1 is carried in its FIXED FORM — every member at its maximum width, space padded, still exactly integer-1 bytes with no frame and no table (§3 D-FRA (vi), kb/Work PB1562)**. **Such a file records no record boundaries**: §9.1.7.2 makes a record sequential record's length "determined by any information the implementor may add to the record on the physical storage medium", and this format adds none, so a READ takes the next integer-1 bytes of the READING file description as the physical record — GnuCOBOL's fixed-length sequential format (CLAUDE.md rule 1; kb/Work PB1514). A physical record is therefore never longer than the reading description's fixed length, and it is shorter only at the end of the file: that final partial record is §9.1.13.2 item 3's '04' (§14.9.30.4 GR14 — the rest of the record area is undefined). A file written under another record length is read in the reading description's lengths (`conformance:cases/9.1.13.2-Successful-completion/io_status_04`: three 5-byte records read as a 10-byte record and a 5-byte '04' record; one 15-byte record read the same way); `RecordLayoutNotice` reports a file whose length is not a whole number of records at OPEN, without changing the I-O status; **(b) record sequential, variable-length records** (format 2, format 3, or an implied format 2) — **4 + the record's own byte size**: a 4-byte little-endian length word before each record (item 151), plus `4 + 8 × k` bytes when the record is a variable-length group with k variable components (its extent table, D-FRA (v)); **(c) line sequential** — the record's characters less the trailing spaces §14.9.51.4 GR21 does not transfer (a file whose RECORD clause has the DEPENDING phrase is filled to data-name-1's length instead, GR22), one byte each, plus the line delimiter of item 114 (CR LF on Windows, LF on Linux and macOS); a record area holding a character outside the line sequential character set is not written at all ('71', item 115); **(c′) record sequential PRINT files** — a record sequential file written with an ADVANCING phrase or described with a LINAGE clause (and every report file) is a print stream, not framed records: each record is presented as its characters less trailing spaces (a variable-length record at its §13.18.43.4 GR13 length, and a WRITE whose length is outside the RECORD IS VARYING bounds presents nothing — '44', §14.9.51.4 GR14/GR15), one byte each, and the page is advanced with line ends and a form feed for ADVANCING PAGE; no length word is written. **The line end is a function of the file's shape, in three arms** (§9.1.7.2, §13.4.5.4 GR4 and §12.4.5.10.3 GR2 leave the on-medium form to the implementor, so CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence decides, and GnuCOBOL 3.2 answers; kb/Work PB1664, `SequentialConnector.SelectLineEnd`): **a record sequential print stream with no LINAGE clause that is not a report file — a LINE FEED on every host** (GnuCOBOL keeps it a binary sequential file and writes `\n`); **a file with a LINAGE clause, and every report file (a LINE SEQUENTIAL one included, §13.4.5.3 SR4) — the host newline of item 114** (GnuCOBOL reclassifies both LINE SEQUENTIAL and writes them in the C library's text mode); and a LINE SEQUENTIAL file — the host newline (item 114). The controls are not line ends and do not move: ADVANCING 0 is a bare carriage return (§14.9.51.4 GR25 c), §4 "ADVANCING 0"), ADVANCING PAGE on a file with no LINAGE clause is a form feed (GR25 h); **(d) relative and indexed** — the keyed store engine's paged store format 6 (`docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md` 2.2.1.4): the file is a whole number of 4,096-byte pages (its length is `4,096 × pages`), pages 0–2 the meta pages that carry the §9.1.6 fixed file attributes and the key descriptors (item 129), the rest the pages of the record trees and of the engine's own bookkeeping trees, and pages a deleted record or a superseded page released, which the file keeps for reuse rather than giving back. **EVERY record, fixed-length or variable, is framed as in (b)**, and an indexed record's frame carries 8 bytes per key (prime first) between its length word and its payload: its release ordinals, the §14.9.30.4 GR26 order of its duplicates under each key (`RecordFraming.EncodeFrame`). **A relative record is ONE leaf entry of 6 + 8 + F bytes** — a 2-byte key length and a 4-byte value length, the relative record number as 8 bytes, and its frame of F = 4 + the record's byte size (+ its extent table) — and an empty record number is no entry at all; **an indexed record is one leaf entry of 6 + k + F bytes in the prime key's tree** (k the prime key's byte length, F = 4 + 8 × the key count + the record's byte size) **and one entry of 6 + a + 8 + k bytes in each alternate key's tree** (a that key's byte length, then the record's 8-byte ordinal, the prime key as its value), none in a tree whose SUPPRESS WHEN value the record carries. A leaf holds ⌊4,064 / entry bytes⌋ such entries when full, and a page split leaves both halves part full. A frame longer than 1,016 bytes, or whose entry would pass 2,032, is kept on overflow pages of 4,056 payload bytes each and its entry holds a 16-byte reference instead. Example: a RELATIVE file whose one record description is `01 R PIC X(80)` (implied format 1, integer-1 = 80) — each record is a 98-byte entry, 41 to a full leaf; 100 records written in record-number order make a 45,056-byte file (11 pages). **CODE-SET** never changes a size: every claimed code set (the identity sets, and EBCDIC = CCSID 37) is one byte per alphanumeric character, and the framing in (b)–(d) stays native (A.3 item 27). The **FORMAT clause** cannot arise: A.4.8 is not claimed and a FORMAT clause is refused with COBOL1705 (A.1 items 84 and 85 cannot arise). | `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb1276_record_contains_sizes_file`; `conformance:cases/9.1.13.2-Successful-completion/io_status_04`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1540_ls_lone_cr_is_data`; `conformance-test:PrintStreamLineEndConformanceTests.RecordSequentialPrintStream_EndsLinesWithLfOnEveryHost`; `conformance-test:PrintStreamLineEndConformanceTests.LinageAndLineSequentialFiles_EndLinesWithTheHostNewline`; `unit:RelativeEngineTests.A_relative_records_size_on_the_medium_is_the_documented_leaf_entry_in_a_file_of_whole_pages` |
| DOC-A.1-147 | **RECORD clause — the implicit RECORD clause when no RECORD clause is specified**, §13.18.43.4 GR5, required + documented | **One rule for every file description entry, FD and SD alike** (§3 D-FRA (iv)). **(a) Implied format 2** when any record description of the entry is VARIABLE-LENGTH — a dynamic-length elementary item or a variable-length group (§8.5.1.12.1; `FileModel.IsVariableLengthRecord`): integer-2 is the smallest record description's byte size with every dynamic-length item at zero length, integer-3 the largest with each at its maximum size (GR5 b / GR8 b), and no DEPENDING phrase. **(b) Implied format 1 otherwise**: integer-1 is the byte size of the LARGEST record description entry (GR5 a), an OCCURS DEPENDING ON table counted at its maximum (GR3), so every record of the file is integer-1 bytes — a WRITE or RELEASE of a shorter record description sends the whole integer-1-byte record area (§14.9.51.4 GR13), as does a REWRITE of a relative or indexed file (§14.9.35.4 GR15, GR18), and an ODO record is always sent at its maximum. A REWRITE of a RECORD SEQUENTIAL file cannot: §14.9.35.4 GR16 requires record-name-1's own byte count to EQUAL the record being replaced, so a shorter record description's REWRITE is unsuccessful with '44' and the record is left as it was (kb/Work PB1168; `conformance:cases/9.1.13.7-Logic-error-condition-with-unsuccessful-completion/pb1168_rs_rewrite_size_gr16`). Sizes are in BYTES (GR1): a national character position counts two (D-N1). Example: `FD F.` or `SD S.` with `01 A PIC X(4)` and `01 B PIC X(10)` and no RECORD clause is fixed-length 10: `MOVE ALL "Z" TO B`, `MOVE "AAAA" TO A`, `WRITE A` (or `RELEASE A`) sends `AAAAZZZZZZ`. Same in every edition (a dynamic-length item exists from COBOL-2014, so arm (a) arises only there). An SD takes the same arm as an FD: `RELEASE A` releases the 10-byte record, and `SORT … GIVING` writes `AAAAZZZZZZ` (kb/Work PB322 F; D-WRT1). | `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb322_release_short_record_fixed_sd`; `conformance:cases/14.9.51-WRITE/pb1907_write_past_record`; `conformance:cases/13.18.33-Level-number/pb981_fd_variable_length_records`; `conformance:cases/13.18.43-RECORD/pb1276_varying_unstated_max_dynamic`; `conformance:cases/13.4.6-Sort-merge-file-description/pb1277_record_size_in_bytes` |
| DOC-A.1-156 | **Reference format — the control characters that terminate a free-form line, and whether they may appear in comments and literals**, §6.1 3) b), required + documented | **Exactly one terminator: LINE FEED (U+000A).** A CARRIAGE RETURN (U+000D) immediately before a LINE FEED is part of that terminator and is not a character of the line, so LF and CR LF files read identically. **No other control character terminates a free-form line** — not a lone CR, not FORM FEED, VERTICAL TAB, NEL or any other C0/C1 control — and ONE set serves every stage that asks where a line ends, because ONE stage answers it — the line-entry stage (`PhysicalLines`, kb/Work PB1800), which every later stage reads: the reference-format and compiler-directive stage (where `>>` must begin a line), the floating-comment indicator `*>` (whose comment runs to the end of the line), and literal scanning; the lexer's line end is the same LINE FEED, so no stage ends a line at a lone CR. The end of the source text also ends its last line. **In comments and literals:** the terminator cannot appear in a comment or in the content of an alphanumeric or national literal — it ends the line (a literal that must span lines ends the first line with the floating literal continuation indicator, §6.2.3.1) — while every other control character, a lone CR included, MAY appear in comment-text and in literal content and is taken as that character: `"A<FF>B"` and `"A<CR>B"` each hold three characters, and a lone CR in a `*>` comment does not end it. The one exception is the horizontal tab, which is never a character of a comment or a literal because it is expanded to spaces at line entry (item 157; owner decision kb/Work R55). Free-form reference format exists from COBOL-2002 (`>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE`, and the auto-detection of item 158). This is GnuCOBOL's line model (rule 1 precedence; the standard leaves the set to the implementor). | `conformance:cases/6.5-Logical-conversion/pb1496_lone_cr_is_a_character`; `unit:PhysicalLinesTests.ALoneCrIsACharacter`; `unit:PhysicalLinesTests.ALoneCr_DoesNotStartADirectiveLine` |
| DOC-A.1-157 | **Reference format — the meaning of lines and character positions, free-form and fixed-form**, §6.1 1) c), required + documented | **A character position is ONE CHARACTER of the decoded source text — one Unicode code point** (each file decoded by its byte-order mark, UTF-8 without one, ISO/IEC 8859-1 when it is not well-formed UTF-8 — item 25, item 26): a character of the Basic Multilingual Plane is one position and so is a supplementary-plane character such as an Annex B extended letter of the Adlam or Linear B script, which is two UTF-16 code units of the in-memory string (a surrogate that is not half of a valid pair is a character of its own). The unit is the character because §6.1 1) a) describes reference format "in terms of character positions" and the standard counts the length of a word in characters, the base character and each combining character apart (§8.1.3.2 GR4 c)); a count of UTF-16 code units put margin R, the indicator area, every tab stop and the free-form 255 limit early by one position per supplementary character, so legal source whose text ends at position 72 was cut short (kb/Work PB1966; this row once read "a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is two"). One definition serves every site — `CharacterPositions` (count, index of a position, position of an index) and `FixedFormLine` (the sequence area, the indicator, the program-text area and margin R of a fixed-form line) — and `PhysicalLinesDriftTests.NoPipelineStage_ReadsAColumnAsAStringIndex` refuses a column read as a string index; a diagnostic's column is a character position too (kb/Work PB2983: the parser reports a UTF-16 index of the resultant text and the source map's origin spans, which end at each tab and at each supplementary-plane character, convert it, so a parser diagnostic and a reference-format gate on one line name the same column; the indicator-column gates name position 7 because a tab in positions 1–7 fills through position 8, kb/Work PB2982). The exception is a horizontal tab (U+0009), which advances to the next tab stop — positions 1, 9, 17, 25, … (a tab width of 8, GnuCOBOL's default `tab-width`; rule 1 precedence) — so it occupies one to eight positions. **A tab is expanded to those spaces EVERYWHERE, at line entry and before anything else reads the line** (the `PhysicalLines` stage, kb/Work PB1800) — in the sequence and indicator areas, in the program-text area, in a free-form line and inside an alphanumeric or national literal alike (owner decision kb/Work R55: the tab is an input-medium positioning control, not a character of the literal; `X"09"` is how a program puts a TAB character in data). So `<TAB><TAB>DISPLAY` in fixed form starts DISPLAY at position 17 with a space indicator; `000100<TAB>` fills positions 7–8, leaving the indicator area a space; and text a tab carries past margin R is truncated like any text past it. No tab reaches a later stage. **A line is the text of a source or library file between two line terminators** (item 156: LF, or CR LF), the terminator not included; the file's end also ends its last line. There is no record or block structure below the file. **Free-form:** a line has 0 to **255** character positions (§6.1 3) a)), counted on the expanded line; a longer line is diagnosed (COBOL2653, an error at every edition, asked wherever a line is read as free form — a `>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE` segment of a fixed-form file too), and program text may begin at any position. A fixed-form line has no such limit: §6.1 2) b) lets a logically converted line be longer, and only its program-text area counts. **Fixed-form:** positions 1–6 are the sequence number area, position 7 the indicator area and positions 8–72 the program-text area; margin R follows position 72 and anything beyond it is ignored (item 158). **A line shorter than 72 positions is read as if space-filled to margin R**, so its program-text area is always the 65 positions 8–72 — which is what an alphanumeric or boolean literal continued by the fixed continuation indicator carries to its continuation (§6.3.5: “any spaces at the end of the fixed-form continued line are part of the literal”), e.g. `000100 01 X PIC X(80) VALUE "AB` ending at position 29, continued by `000100-    "CD".`, gives `AB` + 43 spaces + `CD`. Fixed-form is available at every edition, free-form from COBOL-2002. This follows GnuCOBOL and IBM Enterprise COBOL, which both pad a short record to the margin (rule 1 precedence). The padding is applied by the ONE §6.5 logical conversion (`ReferenceFormatProcessor`), which also joins a continuation line to the latest LOGICAL line, so comment lines and blank lines interspersed among the parts of a literal leave it intact (kb/Work PB1491; golden `85/pb1491_continued_literal_logical_line`). | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1586_tab_stops_fixed_form`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1586_tab_in_literal`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb1586_tab_free_form`; `conformance:cases/6-Reference-format/pb1496_free_form_line_255`; `conformance:cases/6-Reference-format/pb1496-free-form-line-256`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb1966_supplementary_letters_margin_r`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb1966-supplementary-letters-past-margin-r`; `unit:CharacterPositionsTests`; `unit:PhysicalLinesTests.ATabAdvancesToTheNextTabStop`; `unit:PhysicalLinesTests.FreeForm_LineOfMoreThan255Positions_IsDiagnosed`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2983-supplementary-letters-parser-error-column`; `conformance:cases/_unassigned/pb2983-supplementary-letters-gate-error-column`; `unit:PhysicalLinesTests.ColumnMapFollowsTheDefinition_AndNoTabSurvives` |
| DOC-A.1-159 | **Report file — the report writer logical record structure**, §13.4.5 FD entry, GR4 (§13.4.5.4), required + documented | **One print line is one record: the line's character positions written as plain text, one byte per column in ISO/IEC 8859-1, with no length prefix and no file header whatever the file's ORGANIZATION.** Each line is followed by the HOST newline (CR LF, 0x0D 0x0A, on Windows; LF, 0x0A, on Linux and macOS — GnuCOBOL reclassifies a report file LINE SEQUENTIAL and writes it in the C library's text mode, `SequentialConnector.SelectLineEnd`, kb/Work PB1664; the ORGANIZATION the file names changes nothing), except that when the next line begins a new page the line is followed by a form feed (0x0C) instead (GnuCOBOL 3.2.0 writes no representation of a page advance in a report file, so there is none to follow — measured with PAGE LIMIT 5, HEADING 1, FIRST DETAIL 2, LAST DETAIL 4: every intermediate page is its four lines run straight into the next page heading, with no blank line and no page control, and only the LAST page is padded with empty lines at TERMINATE, so a reader of its file cannot find the page boundaries the report's PAGE-COUNTER counted; §14.9.16.4 GR6 makes a failed page fit test result in a page advance and §13.4.5.4 GR4 leaves the representation to the implementor, and where GnuCOBOL does represent a page advance on a print stream, WRITE … ADVANCING PAGE on a record sequential file, it writes the same form feed; kb/Work PB2510). A report record is the CODE characters, when the RD has a CODE clause (§13.18.12.4 GR2: they "are included in the logical record size"), followed by the line, and the record is the size the FD's RECORD clause gives it: integer-1 bytes in Format 1, at most integer-3 in Format 2 or integer-5 in Format 3 (§13.18.43.4 GR6, GR7, GR18; kb/Work PB1934, PB2519). A column of the line past the record's size less the CODE is NOT recorded: the standard states no outcome for the cut (§13.4.5.4 GR4 leaves the structure to the implementor; this item is where it is documented), and the other choices contradict GR6, GnuCOBOL widening the record for a file without CODE and refusing the write of one with it. The cut is not a condition of its own and the exception conditions are untouched by it: the column occupancy EC-REPORT-COLUMN-OVERLAP (§13.18.14.4 GR4) reads reaches as far as the page width (§13.18.39.4 GR2 b)), so two items that overlap past the record are still reported. With no RECORD clause, or a Format 2 clause without its TO phrase, a line holds exactly the columns its report group description places (the widest item), national printable items included at one column per character position (item 160). The report file has no CODE-SET clause, so it uses the file coded character set of item 31 (owner decision kb/Work R47): a character U+0000–U+00FF is written as the byte of the same value, and a print line holding a character above U+00FF is NOT written — the write the report writer performs is unsuccessful with I-O status `'91'` in the report file's connector for every report file, whatever ORGANIZATION it names (§14.9.51.4 GR23's `'71'` is the answer for a line sequential file's WRITE, and a report file is never one to its connector: `FileRegistry.RegisterReport` registers every report connector as not line sequential, which is what makes the line end the host newline whatever the ORGANIZATION; kb/Work PB1664, PB2556; items 31, 110, 115), never a `?`. GENERATE is not among the statements §9.1.13.1 lists as setting an I-O status, so the FILE STATUS item is not stored by it, no EC-I-O exception condition is raised for the refusal and no USE procedure of the file runs (INITIATE and TERMINATE likewise; kb/Work PB1603 asked whether the refusal should be observable and this is its determination: no rule of §14.9.16.4, §14.9.21.4 or §14.9.46.4 writes the line "as if a WRITE statement", as §14.9.24.4 GR12 does for MERGE and §14.9.40.4 GR15 b) for SORT GIVING, the choice is the implementor's, and GnuCOBOL 3.2.0 answers it — measured on a report file assigned to `/dev/full`, whose plain WRITE answers `'34'` at the 68th record, the report's FILE STATUS stays `'00'` through 300 GENERATEs, TERMINATE and CLOSE and its USE AFTER EXCEPTION procedure never runs; the same holds for a medium that is full, `'34'`, as for a line the file refuses, `'91'`; measured on a report file ORGANIZATION LINE SEQUENTIAL with a FILE STATUS item and a USE AFTER STANDARD ERROR procedure, a GENERATE whose national source item holds U+0100 leaves a blank line between its neighbours, the FILE STATUS item reads `'00'` after every GENERATE and after CLOSE and the USE procedure never runs, kb/Work PB2556); the refused line leaves a BLANK line in the report file, because §14.9.51.4 GR15's unsuccessful write "does not take place" (its advance included) and the next line's advance then covers the refused line's slot — every later line of the page still lands on its own LINE-COUNTER line (`ReportWriter` moves its device line only when the write succeeded). Every edition. | `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb690_report_line_byte_image_85`; `conformance:cases/A.1-Implementor-defined-language-element-list/pb2556_report_line_refusal_line_sequential`; `conformance-test:PrintStreamLineEndConformanceTests.ReportFiles_EndLinesWithTheHostNewline`; `conformance-test:ReportLineRefusalConformanceTests.RefusedReportLine_IsNotAnIoStatementException`; `conformance-test:ReportLineRefusalConformanceTests.RefusedReportLine_RaisesNoEcIo_WhenCheckingIsEnabled`; `conformance-test:ReportLineRefusalConformanceTests.ReportLine_RefusedByAFullMedium_IsNotAnIoStatementException` |
| DOC-A.1-161 | **REPOSITORY paragraph — how the external repository and the class-specifier determine which class is used**, §12.3.8.4 GR6, required + documented | **The §8.13 external repository is the metadata of compiled WiseOwl COBOL assemblies** (owner decision kb/Work R44, 2026-09-24): a compiled class assembly carries the class's §8.13 information (externalized name, kind, methods, parameters, returning items, raised exceptions, entry convention, properties, type declarations, DECIMAL-POINT IS COMMA, currency symbols, locale identification), in a WiseOwl COBOL-owned metadata record wherever .NET metadata cannot express it natively; a compiler option names the repository assemblies a compilation references; a class-specifier resolves against the compilation group's definitions and that referenced repository, and a specifier neither answers is diagnosed (§12.3.8.3 SR6); two further options choose whether a compilation updates the repository (records the classes it defines) and whether differences from the repository are flagged (§8.13). **Within the compilation group** the specifier names the definition item 163 describes — by its declared word, or by its externalized name when `AS literal-1` is written — and otherwise the standard class BASE (§16.1), a group definition taking precedence. The precedence between the group and the referenced repository, how externalized names are compared across assemblies, and a name more than one referenced assembly answers are settled by the R44 design (kb/Work PB1086) and written here when it lands. ⚠ **Only the compilation group and BASE are searched today** (kb/Work PB1086): `OoNameResolution.Lookup` searches the per-group `OoClassTable` alone, the compiler offers none of the three options, a specifier no source answers compiles clean, and a class compiled separately cannot be named (COBOL0823). | `conformance:cases/8.3.2.2-User-defined-words/pb974_repository_as_phrase` |
| DOC-A.1-162 | **REPOSITORY paragraph, INTERFACE phrase — how the interface-specifier and the external repository determine which interface is used**, §12.3.8.4 GR9, required + documented | **The item 161 determination, for interfaces** (owner decision kb/Work R44, 2026-09-24): the §8.13 external repository is the metadata of compiled WiseOwl COBOL assemblies, an interface assembly carries the interface's §8.13 information, an interface-specifier resolves against the compilation group's definitions and the referenced repository, and a specifier neither answers is diagnosed (§12.3.8.3 SR9); the reference, update and flag options are item 161's. **Within the compilation group** the specifier names the interface item 163 describes — by its declared word, or by its externalized name (its INTERFACE-ID `AS literal-1`, §11.6.4) when `AS literal-2` is written. §16 defines no standard interface, so there is no BASE step. The remaining resolution details are the R44 design's (kb/Work PB1086), as for item 161. ⚠ **Only the compilation group is searched today** (kb/Work PB1086): an interface compiled separately cannot be named, a specifier no source answers compiles clean, and an interface's literal-1 is only an in-group key — the emitted CLR interface carries the declared word. | `conformance:cases/8.3.2.2-User-defined-words/pb974_repository_as_phrase` |
| DOC-A.1-164 | **RESERVE clause — the number of input-output areas when the clause is not specified**, §12.4.5.14.3 GR1, required + documented | **One input-output area per file connector, separate from its record area** (§12.4.6.4.4 GR1, *"The area being shared includes all storage areas assigned to the files"*, distinguishes the storage areas assigned to a file from the area for the current logical record). **An input-output area is 4,096 bytes** (`HostFile.InputOutputAreaBytes`) of the ONE buffer a connector keeps between its record area and the medium: a sequential connector's reader or writer (the host handle beneath it holds none, kb/Work PB753); for a relative or indexed connector, PAGES of the keyed store engine's page cache for its physical file (`docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md` 2.2.1.13): every byte of the store passes between the medium and that cache one 4,096-byte page per positional read or write (`HostFile.OpenConnectorStore`, the store handle, is itself unbuffered, kb/Work PB2693), so one input-output area is one page, and the OPEN that attaches the connector raises the cache's capacity to at least its areas' pages (`KeyedConnector.Attach` → `KeyedStore.AttachHandle` → `PageCache.Reserve`; a cache is never smaller than its own floor of 256 pages, 1 MiB, `PageCache.DefaultPages`, the engine's working set with room to spare). **With the clause, the connector's areas are exactly integer-1** (GR1's first sentence; `FileConnector.InputOutputAreas`, sized once by `HostFile.InputOutputAreaBuffer`, kb/Work PB643), at every edition and for every organization, report files included: a sequential connector's buffer is integer-1 × 4,096 bytes, allocated by the OPEN, and a run unit that cannot supply the memory gets '30' on that OPEN (§9.1.13.6 1)); a relative or indexed connector's are integer-1 pages of its file's cache, which the OPEN reserves and the cache fills as pages are read. **Limit (§4.2.15):** integer-1 at most 524,287, the largest count whose areas one buffer can hold; a larger one is refused at compile time (COBOL2897), never silently reduced. **When the areas are emptied** depends on the organization and, for a sequential connector, on its sharing mode, and no program can tell the difference (kb/Work PB1587): a relative or indexed connector writes every page a statement changed to the medium before that statement completes, in every sharing mode (the engine's crash-consistency rule, `docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-runtime-library.md` 2.2.1.6); a sequential connector that admits no other connector (`SHARING WITH NO OTHER`, which Table 19 makes exclusive) releases its records to the medium as its areas fill, and at CLOSE; one whose sharing mode admits a reader or a writer (`FileLockPosture.AdmitsAnotherRunUnit`: READ ONLY or ALL OTHER) releases each record during its own WRITE or REWRITE, because §14.9.51.4 GR12 (*"The successful execution of a WRITE statement releases a logical record to the operating environment"*) puts it in the physical file at the statement and §9.1.15 2) admits an INPUT connector beside a READ ONLY writer, whose READ selects from that file (§14.9.30.4 GR21); it also discards what it has read ahead when a sibling releases one. **So the count of areas is not observable through a sibling connector**: `OPEN EXTEND` under `SHARING WITH READ ONLY`, 100 WRITEs of 64-byte records, then a second connector's `OPEN INPUT` and READs reach all 100 before the writer's CLOSE, with one area, with `RESERVE 2 AREAS` and under `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` alike. The earlier determination, under which a READ ONLY writer's records waited in its area until it filled (64 of the 100 visible, none with two areas), made the RELATIVE organization, which writes at every statement, answer the same program the other way, and is retired; GnuCOBOL 3.2 agrees for a SEQUENTIAL file. Same in every edition. | `conformance:cases/12.4.5.14-RESERVE/pb643_reserve_areas_visibility`; `conformance:cases/12.4.5.14-RESERVE/pb643_reserve_areas_all_organizations`; `conformance:cases/14.9.51-WRITE/pb1587_write_released_to_input_reader`; `unit:ReadOnlyWriterReleaseDriftTests.AWriteIsInThePhysicalFileWhenItReturns`; `unit:SharedReadCoherenceDriftTests.TheConnectorKeepsOneBuffer_ItsInputOutputAreas_SizedInOnePlace` |

## 8. Rules with no observable obligation — owner-signed derivations (§4.4 / Annex A.2)

> **⛔ THIS SECTION IS THE ONE ALTERNATIVE TO A SPEC-DERIVED TEST, AND THE OWNER OPENED IT** — decision
> `kb/Work/PB386`, 2026-09-03, implementing `docs/rearchitecture/DESIGN-spec-conformance-review.md` **§1.1**.
> Some normative rules impose no obligation a conforming program can observe, and for those §1(c)'s covering
> test is not merely unwritten, it is **unmeetable**: any golden would pin an IMPLEMENTATION CHOICE as though it
> were the standard's answer, which is the exact thing the traceability inventory's `spec-derived` clause exists
> to prevent. A determination here stands in place of that test — **and in place of nothing else**. The verdict,
> its evidence, and (for an Annex A.1 row) the §7 determination and a greenfield implementing site are all still
> paid in full.
>
> ⚙ **The row key is `DRV-` plus the inventory `rule-id`, and the inventory row's `derivation` field carries
> `docs/CONFORMANCE.md#DRV-<rule-id>` COMPUTED from that same id** — never typed, for the reason §7's key is
> computed: a determination filed against a neighbouring rule cannot be *spelled*. Every cell below is machine
> read: `scripts/spec/audit_derivations.py` and `SpecTraceabilityInventoryDriftTests` both evaluate the arm, and
> `Schema.state_for` refuses to close a row whose determination does not stand.
>
> ⚙ **Four arms, and only one of them is MECHANICAL.**
> · **`undefined-A.2`** is MECHANICAL. Annex A.2 is *"a list of the COBOL language elements within this Working
> Draft International Standard that are explicitly undefined"* (§A.2), and §4.4 2) makes the point that matters
> here: *"A COBOL run unit that allows these situations to happen is a conforming run unit, although the
> resultant execution is not defined by standard COBOL."* Each A.2 item ends in the standard's own citation of
> the rule it is about, so `scripts/spec/extract_annex_a2.py` resolves item → `rule-id` and the checker requires
> the named item to cover **this** row. Naming a real item about a different rule is refused.
> · **`unpopulatable-antecedent`** and **`indistinguishable-consequent`** are reviewed ARGUMENTS. Their shape is
> checked — the closed set must be STATED, the named rule must EXIST and not be this one — and the `Signed`
> cell is the record that the argument was read. An unchecked argument would make the GAP metric cheaper to move
> than the work it stands for, which is the failure this whole register is built against. The cell is one of the
> dated owner signatures `inventory-schema.json` lists under `derivation.signatures`, each mapped to the decision
> that read the rows it signs: `owner: 2026-09-03` (PB386, and the rows signed under it through 2026-09-25, whose
> text names a later decision where there was one) and `owner: 2026-10-08` (the PB1636 batch of 32), and `owner: 2026-10-23` (PB3539 option (i); PB1636's last derivation, DRV-GR-12.4.5.9.4-2).
> · **`definitional`** (owner decision `kb/Work/R43` item 4, 2026-09-24, extending `PB386` — answers `PB468`
> Q9) is a reviewed argument too: the rule DEFINES a property of the USER'S program and imposes no obligation on
> the implementation, so there is nothing an implementation can do that a program could observe as meeting or
> failing it. The `Names` cell must open `defines` and state the property and whose it is; a rule that says what
> an implementation or implementor SHALL do is never this arm. Its first population was §4.4 GR1/GR2; the owner
> extended it on 2026-10-08 (kb/Work PB1636, the five definitional rows of that batch) to a CONSTRAINT on the
> user's run unit that no rule gives a consequence (§4.4 2) then leaves a violation undefined) and to a TERM
> DEFINITION that no other rule reads.
>
> ⚖ **This does not reverse `kb/Work/PB280` Q2.** An Annex A.1 row asks the implementor to STATE a choice, so
> "there is nothing to observe" is unfalsifiable there and still cannot close a row: the A.1 row below is
> admitted because its determination **is** stated, in §7, and it names implementing code — only its WITNESS is
> impossible. `Schema.state_for` encodes that by ORDER, charging a DOC row's anchor and observability costs
> before it ever consults this register.

| DRV-GR-14.9.5.4-11 | undefined-A.2 | A.2 item 4 | **§14.9.5.4 GR11** — *"If a program-pointer has been set to point to the program to be canceled, the result of referencing the program-pointer in a subsequent CALL statement is undefined."* (`cite.py --check 14.9.5.4` → OK, rule 11). **Annex A.2 item 4 repeats it verbatim**, and §4.4 2) makes a run unit that reaches the situation a conforming one, so every behaviour conforms and there is no expected value to compute. WiseOwl COBOL's behaviour is nevertheless determinate: `ProgramTable.CancelNode` assigns `Node.Instance = null` and nothing structural, leaving the entry in `_byPath` and the per-kind name dictionary, so `CallPointer` re-resolves the canonical name the pointer holds and re-enters `CallProgram`, which re-instantiates the program in its initial state. | DRV-GR-14.9.30.4-3 | undefined-A.2 | A.2 item 41 | **§14.9.30.4 GR3** — *"the content of any data item, where any part of that data item lies beyond the range of the current record, is undefined"* (`cite.py --check 14.9.30.4` → OK, rule 3). **Annex A.2 item 41** carries it, and unlike Annex A.1 the A.2 list creates no documentation obligation, so there is not even a documented choice to assert. | DRV-GR-14.9.34.4-2 | undefined-A.2 | A.2 item 46 | **§14.9.34.4 GR2** — *"the content of any data item, where any part of that data item lies outside the range of the current record, is undefined"* (`cite.py --check 14.9.34.4` → OK, rule 2). **Annex A.2 item 46** carries it. | DRV-GR-14.9.20.4-9 | undefined-A.2 | A.2 item 20 | **§14.9.20.4 GR9** — *"If identifier-1 occupies the same storage area as identifier-2, the result of the execution of this statement is undefined, even if they are defined by the same data description entry."* (`cite.py --check 14.9.20.4` → OK, rule 9). **Annex A.2 item 20 carries it** ("INITIALIZE statement. The result of the execution of the INITIALIZE statement is undefined if the receiving operand and the sending operand occupies the same storage area even if they are defined by the same data description entry. (14.9.20, INITIALIZE statement, General rule 9)"). The rule WIDENS undefinedness rather than requiring anything: it overrides §14.6.10 rule 2 ("When the data items are described by the same data description entry, the result of the statement is the same as if the data items shared no part of their respective storage areas." — `cite.py --check 14.6.10` → OK, rule 2) so that the overlap is undefined *even then*. Every behaviour conforms, so there is no expected value to compute and any golden would pin an implementation choice. WiseOwl COBOL's behaviour is nevertheless determinate and inside the envelope: `INITIALIZE G REPLACING ALPHANUMERIC DATA BY A1`, where `A1` is subordinate to `G`, compiles and runs, and §14.9.20.4 GR4's implicit MOVEs are executed per elementary item in the GR8 definition order, so a sender that is itself overwritten mid-statement is read as it then stands (measured: `A1`/`B1` both read `AAA`). (Signed by the owner on 2026-09-09 — decision Q26, after a plain-language brief; DEVLOG 1577.) | owner: 2026-09-03 |
| DRV-GR-4.4-1 | definitional | defines the conforming run unit — a property of the USER's run unit (that each of its runtime modules results from a successful compilation of a conforming compilation unit), not an obligation of the implementation | **§4.4 1)** — *"A conforming run unit is one that:"* … *"is composed of one or more runtime modules, each resulting from a successful compilation of a conforming compilation unit, and"* (`cite.py --check 4.4` → OK, 1)). The sentence DEFINES a term, and the term names the user's program: its subject is *a conforming run unit*, it contains no *shall*, and it asks nothing of the implementation. What an implementation owes a run unit is written elsewhere — §4.2's conforming implementation and every rule of Clauses 7–15, each a row of this inventory with its own verdict and witness — so a program cannot observe §4.4 1) apart from those rules, and a golden written "for" it would test them, not it. Owner decision `kb/Work/R43` item 4 (2026-09-24), extending `kb/Work/PB386`; answers `kb/Work/PB468` Q9. | owner: 2026-09-03 |
| DRV-GR-4.4-2 | definitional | defines the conforming run unit's runtime-behaviour half and the standing of undefined results — properties of the USER's run unit, not obligations of the implementation | **§4.4 2)** — *"complies with the explicitly stated provisions and specifications of standard COBOL with respect to the runtime behavior of that run unit"*, with the paragraph that follows it: *"The results of violating the formats or rules of standard COBOL are undefined unless otherwise specified"* and *"The inclusion of non-COBOL components in the run unit does not affect the conformance of the run unit."* (`cite.py --check 4.4` → OK, 2)). Every sentence classifies a USER'S run unit (conforming or not; what is predictable about it); none says what an implementation SHALL do. The runtime behaviour it refers to is specified — and verified row by row — by the rules it points at, and the undefined situations it names are exactly Annex A.2's, which this register's `undefined-A.2` arm already closes rule by rule. Owner decision `kb/Work/R43` item 4 (2026-09-24), extending `kb/Work/PB386`; answers `kb/Work/PB468` Q9. | owner: 2026-09-03 |
| DRV-GR-14.9.28.4-2 | undefined-A.2 | A.2 item 37 | **§14.9.28.4 GR2** — *"The results of executing the following sequence of PERFORM statements are undefined and no exception condition is set to exist when the sequence is executed: a) a PERFORM statement is executed and has not yet terminated, then b) within the range of that PERFORM statement another PERFORM statement is executed, then c) the execution of the second PERFORM statement passes through the exit of the first PERFORM statement."* (`cite.py --check 14.9.28.4` → OK, rule 2). **Annex A.2 item 37 carries it** ("PERFORM statement. The results of the execution of overlapping PERFORM statements are undefined. (14.9.28, PERFORM statement, General rule 2)"). ⛔ The rule's second clause — *no* exception condition is set — cannot be witnessed either, and that is not for want of trying: the only place a witness could observe it is after the sequence has run, and where control goes after (c) is precisely what the first clause leaves undefined, so no expected output line is derivable. NOTE 1 makes the point the standard's own way ("On some implementations it causes stack overflows, on some it causes returns to unlikely places"). WiseOwl COBOL's behaviour is determinate: `DispatchEmitter.EmitDispatchMethod` models no overlap and Table 13 defines no exception-name for it, so nothing can be raised; measured under `>>TURN EC-ALL CHECKING ON`, a `PERFORM PA THRU PB` whose range performs `PC`, which `GO TO PB`, runs PA/PC/PB, falls past PB and exits 0 with no EC and no diagnostic — one admissible realization, and the no-exception half is honoured. (Signed by the owner on 2026-09-09 — decision Q27, after a plain-language brief; DEVLOG 1577.) | owner: 2026-09-03 |
| DRV-RV-15.4.1-4 | unpopulatable-antecedent | the set item 4 governs is CLOSED by the standard itself and is EMPTY: the functions that have an equivalent arithmetic expression are exactly §15.7 ABS, §15.9 ANNUITY, §15.17 COMBINED-DATETIME, §15.23 DATE-TO-YYYYMMDD, §15.25 DAY-TO-YYYYDDD, §15.36 FACTORIAL, §15.60 MEAN, §15.74 PRESENT-VALUE, §15.79 SECONDS-FROM-FORMATTED-TIME, §15.81 SIGN, §15.86 STANDARD-DEVIATION, §15.88 SUM, §15.98 VARIANCE and §15.100 YEAR-TO-YYYY — the fourteen clauses containing “The equivalent arithmetic expression is as follows” — and NOT ONE of those fourteen function clauses contains the words “implementor-defined”, “implementor defines” or “defined by the implementor” anywhere in it | **§15.4.1 NOTE 1 item 4** — *“The result is explicitly implementor-defined”* (`cite.py --check 15.4.1 "The result is explicitly implementor-defined"` → OK, rule 4), the fourth disjunct of *“The result of an equivalent arithmetic expression is implementor-defined if any one or more of the following applies”*, whose normative twin under a standard mode is the same clause’s rule 2 c), *“The returned value is explicitly implementor-defined”* (`--check` → OK, rule 2). **Its antecedent is false for every equivalent arithmetic expression THE STANDARD DEFINES**, so it is unpopulatable before it is ever an implementation question. NOTE 1’s own lead-in scopes item 4 to *the result of an equivalent arithmetic expression*, so it reaches only functions that HAVE one; that set is closed and enumerable, and the enumeration in the Names cell was taken mechanically over §15 rather than recalled. Each of the fourteen was then searched for an explicit implementor-defined result and none carries one. The three functions this row’s own history named — §15.75 RANDOM, §15.80 SECONDS-PAST-MIDNIGHT and §15.38 FORMATTED-CURRENT-DATE — are not members of the set at all: they have no equivalent arithmetic expression, so their implementor-defined results are §4.2.5 Annex A.1 determinations (§7 items 144/145, 171, 112, 87) and instances of §15.4.1’s LAST paragraph (*“When a numeric or integer function does not have an equivalent arithmetic expression, its returned value is implementor-defined”*), never of item 4. §15.27 E and §15.73 PI do make a native returned value an implementor-defined approximation of a stated expression, but that is NOTE 1 item 1 (*“Native arithmetic is in effect”*) and those clauses print no equivalent arithmetic expression either. ⚠ The vacuity is the STANDARD’s, not this implementation’s, so unlike the device- and medium-set rows above it cannot be voided by a later implementation choice — only by a future edition that makes some EAE-bearing function’s returned value explicitly implementor-defined, at which point the rule-digest changes and the row is re-adjudicated by construction. The row’s companion `RV-15.4.1-1` (*“the returned value shall equal the value of the equivalent arithmetic expression”*) carries the observable half and keeps `conformance:cases/8.8.1.5.4-Exponentiation-in-standard-decimal-arithmetic/exp_standard_decimal_eae`; that test-ref was on THIS row and is cleared here, because a test about rule 1 is not evidence about rule 4. (kb/Work PB245.) | owner: 2026-09-03 |
| DRV-GR-13.18.10.4-3 | unpopulatable-antecedent | the set of run-time consumers of a physical-record size is empty: BLOCK CONTAINS is claimed inert under A.3 item 5 (DataBinder.BindBlockContainsClause screens SR1 and models nothing), and the minimum and maximum physical record size is outside the A.1 item 129 OPEN-validated fixed-attribute set | **§13.18.10.4 GR3**: *"If the CHARACTERS phrase is specified, the physical record size is specified in terms of the number of bytes required to store the physical record, regardless of the types of characters used to represent the items within the physical record."* (`cite.py --check 13.18.10.4` → OK, rule 3). GR3 fixes only the UNIT in which a physical-record size is counted. A program could see that unit only if some statement's result depended on the physical size. None does here. Blocking is inert under **§A.3 item 5** (*"The BLOCK CONTAINS clause has no effect if the operating environment does not support the required features"*, `--check A.3` → OK 5)), and §5 row 5 claims it so. The size is a §9.1.6 fixed file attribute, but §14.9.27.4 GR10 (*"The implementor defines which of the fixed-file attributes are validated during the execution of the OPEN statement"*, `--check 14.9.27.4` → OK 10)) leaves validation to the implementor, and §7's A.1 item 129 excludes the physical record size, so OPEN never answers `'39'` over it. A golden for GR3 would print the same records under a bytes reading and a characters reading. That is what the gn1 draft `gn1_block_contains_characters_bytes` did before it was withdrawn. ⚠ CONTINGENT: re-adjudicate if blocking is implemented or item 129 adds the physical record size. | owner: 2026-10-08 |
| DRV-GR-13.18.10.4-4 | unpopulatable-antecedent | the set of run-time consumers of a physical-record size is empty: BLOCK CONTAINS is claimed inert under A.3 item 5 (DataBinder.BindBlockContainsClause screens SR1 and models nothing), and the minimum and maximum physical record size is outside the A.1 item 129 OPEN-validated fixed-attribute set | **§13.18.10.4 GR4**: *"If integer-1 is not specified, integer-2 represents the exact size of the physical record. If integer-1 and integer-2 are both specified, they refer to the minimum and maximum size of the physical record, respectively."* (`cite.py --check 13.18.10.4` → OK, rule 4). GR4 says how the two integers are READ: an exact size, or a minimum and maximum. A program could tell the readings apart only through a statement whose result depends on the physical size. As for GR3, there is none. **§A.3 item 5** makes the clause inert (`--check A.3` → OK 5)). The min/max physical record size is a §9.1.6 fixed file attribute, but it is outside the §14.9.27.4 GR10 validated set (§7's A.1 item 129), and logical READ and WRITE never see the physical record. The integers' only compile-time consequence, their order, is §13.18.10.3 SR1, a separate row pinned by its own goldens. ⚠ CONTINGENT, as DRV-GR-13.18.10.4-3. | owner: 2026-10-08 |
| DRV-GR-7.3.9.3-3 | unpopulatable-antecedent | the call-convention set is closed at one member, COBOL: CompilerDirectiveCatalog admits only >>CALL-CONVENTION COBOL, and any call-convention-name-1 is refused (COBOL1911; owner 2026-10-03, kb/Work PB1383/PB1945), so the directive has no second value whose other details could differ from the default's | **§7.3.9.3 GR3**: *"The CALL-CONVENTION directive may also be used by the implementor to determine other details needed to interact with a function, method, or program."* (`cite.py --check 7.3.9.3` → OK, rule 3).
